Title: ProofStudio: Five Proof Assistants in the Browser
Yutaka Nagashima
Comments: The tool is available at: this https URL
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

Recent advances in AI-assisted proof automation are extending the use of proof assistants in software verification and mathematics. However, greater proof automation does not remove users' responsibility to assess whether formal statements capture their intended requirements, making education in formal specification and reasoning essential. To lower the installation and learning barriers associated with mature proof assistants, we present ProofStudio, a browser-based environment integrating Isabelle/HOL, Lean, Rocq, HOL4, and HOL Light with corresponding worked examples, preconfigured proof search, and contextual AI assistance. With ProofStudio, users can explore formal specifications and proofs across five systems without local installation, inspecting native prover feedback and experimenting with automation through a common interface.

[57] arXiv:2611.05542 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Towards Efficient Whole Page Ranking with One-Pass Inference
Qi Xu, Zhigang Hua, Zijie Lei, Yan Xie, Jizhe Zhang, Lynn Lu, Delun Du, Sha Hua, Ren Mao, Ke Pan, Haomin Yu, Sandeep Pandey, Luke Simon
Comments: 12 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Whole-page ranking jointly optimizes advertisements and organic content to balance business outcomes and user engagement under complex layout and business constraints. Existing non-autoregressive (NAR) approaches enable efficient page generation but typically score candidate items independently of previously selected items, limiting their ability to capture order-dependent interactions. Autoregressive (AR) methods address this limitation through sequential conditioning, but incur substantial inference overhead that challenges large-scale deployment. Bridging this quality-efficiency gap remains a challenge in industrial whole-page ranking.
We propose Multi-Item Scoring (MIS), a prefix-aware NAR-style framework that incorporates sequential context into efficient multi-item scoring. MIS integrates global candidate interactions, localized prefix conditioning, and position-aware scoring within a shared representation architecture. By computing reusable representations once per request and performing lightweight prefix-conditioned scoring during constrained beam search, MIS captures important sequential dependencies without repeated full-model inference.
Experiments on KuaiRand-1K and RL4RS demonstrate that MIS approaches the generation quality of an autoregressive CGA baseline while achieving 4.07x and 3.54x faster CPU decoding, respectively. In a randomized evaluation on a large-scale social-video platform, MIS improves the realization metric by 0.104% and watch time by 0.058%, while reducing ranking-service CPU consumption by 9.73%. These results demonstrate that prefix-aware multi-item scoring can narrow the quality gap between NAR and AR generation while retaining the efficiency required for industrial scalability.

[58] arXiv:2611.05546 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FedSharp: Byzantine Robust Decentralized Federated Learning Under Noisy Channel
Ojaswi Sinha, Amin Farajzadeh, Animesh Yadav, Melike Erol-Kantarci
Comments: 6 pages, 4 figures, submitted for possible publication
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Decentralized federated learning (DFL) eliminates the central aggregation server but remains vulnerable to data heterogeneity, Byzantine attacks, and channel noise. We show that noise accumulates as models propagate across nodes, becoming increasingly significant as the learning rate decays. Moreover, accumulated noise enables Byzantine attackers to exploit loss-based model selection by mimicking honest model averages. To address these challenges, we propose screened, hop-aware, ranked, proximal averaging, a robust DFL framework (FedSharp). In this approach, each node maintains models from its 2b predecessors, ensuring at least b honest candidates when at most b nodes are Byzantine. FedSharp screens suspicious models using coordinate-wise median deviations, averages the b lowest-loss candidates to reduce fresh channel-noise variance by a factor of b, and applies noise-adaptive gradient-norm regularization and proximal training to mitigate accumulated noise and non-IID drift. Experiments on a 100-node ring with 33 Byzantine nodes show that FedSharp achieves 93.5-94.9% accuracy on MNIST, compared with 29.4-38.1% for a state-of-the-art single-model-selection benchmark, and 32.8-48.8% on CIFAR-10, compared with 10.0-30.5%, across Gaussian and hidden attacks under IID and non-IID data. On MNIST, FedSharp also achieves accuracy within approximately one percentage point of the benchmark operating without channel noise.

[59] arXiv:2611.05548 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Iterated creation, grading, and revision of data science projects by language models
Rohan Alexander
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

We evaluate the extent to which agentic AI models can complete an end-to-end data science project, and how this improves with feedback. A 'writer' model with specific tools creates a complete data science project including downloading, cleaning, and analyzing a dataset, and writing a short paper about it. The project is executed and a 'grader' model evaluates it. The writer can then revise its submission, and this repeats for a total of three rounds. We consider seven models from five developers: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and this http URL. Each model is both a writer and a grader, so there are 49 writer-grader pairs and we run each pair three times. Of the 147 initial submissions, 107 run and render, and the average score increases from 59 per cent to 76 per cent after the final round of feedback. By writer the extent of the increase ranges from 3 percentage points for Anthropic's Opus 5.5 to 46 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5, and by grader it ranges from 13 percentage points for Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash to 32 percentage points for Anthropic's Haiku 4.5. When a model grades its own writing the score tends to be about 9 percentage points higher than the average of what the other models give it. About half of the difference that we see from round to round is within the grader's own noise. Feedback generally results in the highest marks, but even just having the chance to revise, or having the additional budget, in terms of time or tool calls, without any feedback, results in considerable increases for some of the models but not for others. We find that how much such a loop helps depends on which model plays which role, but weaker models generally do not improve stronger models.

[60] arXiv:2611.05549 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Whose Transparency is it Anyway? Understanding Generative AI Transparency Needs and Gaps Across Stakeholders
Genevieve Smith, Sahiba Chopra, Natalia Luka, Min Kyung Lee
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computers and Society (cs.CY); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

Transparency has become a central principle in AI governance, yet there is little agreement about what transparency means, for whom, and in what contexts. Drawing on interpretive flexibility within the Social Construction of Technology, this paper examines how different stakeholders understand and experience transparency in generative AI. This study draws from a global survey of 400 end-users, AI builders, and policymakers, complemented by a structured focus group with end-users, grounding the quantitative findings in qualitative insights from the group most underserved by current transparency practice. We present three key findings. First, all three groups share similar understandings of what transparency means and what it should afford, centered on ensuring accuracy and privacy. Second, gaps between the importance of transparency features and their perceived availability are substantially larger for end-users than builders, revealing how power shapes what gets built and who it serves. Only 28% of end-users report that current transparency practices reflect their needs very well, compared to 53% of builders and 49% of policymakers. Third, transparency is situationally constructed, priorities shift with context and task structure, with role-specific frames activating when context demands them and receding when it does not. We argue that meaningful AI transparency requires moving beyond a one-size-fits-all solution, including current emphases on AI disclosure and static documentation, toward pluralistic transparency infrastructures that reflect the needs of diverse users and stakeholders.

[61] arXiv:2611.05550 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Energy-efficient End-to-End Communication System with Spiking Neural Networks
Pooja Plavilayil Anil, Te-Chuan Chiu, Nguyen Van Huynh
Comments: 6 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, conference
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)

2030 is expected to witness the first commercial 6G systems. However, traditional modular communication architectures cannot meet the latency, optimisation, and integration requirements demanded by various sub-millisecond, data-intensive emerging 6G applications. End-to-end (E2E) communication addresses these limitations by replacing traditional processing blocks with neural networks. Nevertheless, conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs) in E2E systems use dense computation. This results in substantial energy consumption and computational resource requirements, which may not be feasible in resource constrained devices. This paper addresses the aforementioned challenge by developing a spiking neural network (SNN) encoder that targets lower encoder inference energy while maintaining communication reliability. In particular, the SNN encoder combines sparse spike activity, sinusoidal temporal modulation, and weighted temporal aggregation to map one-hot encoded messages to distinguishable transmit signals. The model is evaluated across antenna configurations and SNN timesteps to investigate the bit error rate (BER)-energy trade-off. The simulation results show that the SNN encoder achieves comparable BER under suitable timestep selections, while reducing the average estimated encoder energy by 68.93%, 52.20%, and 35.69% for SNN timesteps 2, 3, and 4, respectively, across five antenna configurations. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed SNN encoder for energy-efficient E2E communication systems.

[62] arXiv:2611.05551 [pdf, other]
Title: VirtualTrialHarness: Coordinating Agentic Operationalization of Virtual Trial Protocols Across Complex Clinical Schemas
Pengze Li, Jingna Feng, Yue Yu, Yining Wu, Xinyue Hu, Jie Lin, Avanti Bhandarkar, Cui Tao
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Virtual trials use routinely collected clinical data to evaluate treatment strategies, but translating a study protocol into an executable analysis requires determining how clinical concepts and study requirements should be represented in the available data and applied consistently across the workflow. These decisions depend on local data representations and operational conventions and can involve source selection, patient and encounter identity, linkage, and temporal interpretation. Here we introduce VirtualTrialHarness (VTHarness), an agent framework that coordinates virtual-trial operationalization by selecting reusable procedural skills for each workflow stage and uses explicit contracts to maintain consistent study decisions across stages. We also introduce VTBenchmark for evaluating source selection and cohort construction. Across three complex synthetic environments, VTHarness successfully produced all required cohort outputs matching the references in 95.1% of workflows after requirement clarification, compared with 60.4% using retrieval from the same procedural corpus. Procedural skills improved source recovery across three language models and increased source overlap with analyst code in 13 Mayo Clinic cases. Site-specific adaptation enabled reference-matched cohort execution across eight MIMIC-IV tasks. Within the Mayo Clinic Virtual Trials Program, the framework supported investigator review of cohort construction and endpoint analysis. These findings support coordinating procedural guidance with workflow decisions to improve virtual-trial implementation across complex clinical schemas.

[63] arXiv:2611.05556 [pdf, html, other]
Title: AGORA: Reliability-Aware Aggregation of LLM Judges via Item-Response Theory
Junhyung Ahn
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

LLM-as-a-judge is a common substitute for costly human evaluation, and aggregating several judges is the standard remedy for any single judge's bias. Judge pools mix judges of very different reliability, while the human-labeled sets that validate them hold a few hundred items or fewer. In this regime the per-item mean weights weak judges as heavily as strong ones, and confusion-table models such as Dawid-Skene must estimate a per-judge error table from too few items. We propose AGORA (Aggregation Of Reliability-weighted Assessments), an item-response-theory aggregator that places every item on one latent quality scale and describes each judge by a sensitivity parameter and ordered rating thresholds, so judge reliability is learned from all items jointly and without human labels. Across three benchmarks, AGORA matches or exceeds Dawid-Skene on large evaluation sets, and its advantage widens as the set shrinks toward a few hundred items. It remains accurate as pools grow more uneven, a label-free dispersion statistic indicates in advance when trust weighting helps, and its learned trust weights track per-judge human validity.

[64] arXiv:2611.05557 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Support Vector Machines Directly Minimise KL Divergence
Ivan Silajev
Comments: 11 pages, 1 table
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Support vector machines (SVMs) are fundamentally grounded in geometric margin maximisation and currently lack a mainstream probabilistic interpretation. This keeps them theoretically isolated from probabilistic machine learning models that are naturally comparable and combinable. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proving that the dual objectives of both support vector classification and support vector regression are exact, constrained Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence minimisation tasks between two Gaussian measures. We further show that this same divergence formulation recovers the exact objective function for kernel ridge regression when domain constraints are removed and $L^2$ regularisation is applied. By demonstrating that SVM duals directly minimise relative entropy, our results provide a unified information-theoretic model for standard kernel machines and lay the foundation for unifying broader kernel-based algorithms under probability theory.

Title: Easy Multi-Precision Acceleration via Vectorization
Chansup Byun, Piotr Luszczek, Jeremy Kepner, LaToya Anderson, William Arcand, David Bestor, William Bergeron, Alex Bonn, Daniel Burrill, Vijay Gadepally, Michael Houle, Matthew Hubbell, Hayden Jananthan, Michael Jones, Lauren Milechin, Julie Mullen, Andrew Prout, Albert Reuther, Antonio Rosa, Charles Yee, Peter Michaleas
Subjects: Performance (cs.PF); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

High level programming languages and accelerators are powerful enablers for a wide range of applications. Accelerators offer significant performance via diverse numeric precision and increased memory bandwidth and capacity. These enable new algorithms to be explored. Construction of these algorithms can be enabled by the ready accessibility of these performance features in high-level languages. Achieving scalable vertical (within a compute node), precision (over various numeric precisions), and temporal (over different generations of hardware) performance while retaining productivity requires effective abstractions. Vectorized coding that expresses operations as high-level matrix mathematics has historically been an important method for achieving portable performance. This paper examines the performance availability across a wide range of precisions and hardware using simple vectorized coding techniques applied to several example programs that highlight bandwidth, real and complex matrix multiplication, and 2D convolution. The systems evaluated span nearly a decade of computing hardware, enabling direct comparison of performance gains over this period. This work demonstrates that near hardware peak performance is readily accessible from high-level programming environments. In particular for memory bandwidth, real and complex matrix multiplication in double/single/half precision, and 2D convolutions using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). Furthermore, algorithms that trade decreased compute intensity for increased memory intensity have significant potential.

Title: How Finely Can Vision-Language Models See Biology? Bio-VQA: A Benchmark for Taxonomic, Morphological, Spatial and Individual Reasoning
S M Rayeed, Qian Ma, Charles V. Stewart, Yao Ma
Comments: Accepted to WACV 2027, 8 pages main paper; 4 figures, 4 tables
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

In biodiversity monitoring, a single image raises several questions: which taxon, how many, which trait, and whether the individual has been seen before. Vision-language models (VLMs) could answer all of these from the image, but their ability is largely untested in biology, as existing benchmarks focus mostly on species identification within a few taxonomic groups. We present Bio-VQA, the largest biological visual question answering (VQA) benchmark and the only one to span four aspects of biological visual understanding: hierarchical taxonomic reasoning, fine-grained attribute grounding, quantitative spatial reasoning, and individual re-identification. Bio-VQA contains 1.86M questions over 217K images from 11 public datasets, and extends right-or-wrong scoring to graded scoring, so a near-miss counts for more than a distant one. Evaluating 18 open-weight models from 3.75B to 38.4B parameters, we find that general visual capabilities do not transfer to biological organisms: the best model counts animals exactly on 41.7% of images with 2 to 10 individuals, less than half its accuracy on everyday objects at the same counts. Taxonomic accuracy falls to one sixth, from 0.72 at phylum to 0.12 at scientific name, and scaling helps mostly at coarse ranks. The gap to a domain specialist widens accordingly, from 0.731 against BioCLIP-2's 0.874 at class (1.2x) to 0.269 against 0.544 at scientific name (2x). On trait size measurement, 15 of the 18 models do no better than an image-blind baseline that predicts one fixed number for every specimen, and on re-identification, 17 of the 18 models fall below chance under adversarial conditions. Title: Lesion Overlap Ranks PET Segmentation Models but Does Not Certify Patient-Level Tumor Burden
Tushar Kataria, Gerald Sabin, Ponnuswamy Sadayappan, Shireen Y. Elhabian
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Metabolic tumor volume (MTV) summarizes whole-body PET disease burden for prognostic stratification and treatment assessment. Automated MTV is useful only if its estimate is reliable for the individual patient, yet segmentation models are usually evaluated with overlap metrics such as Dice rather than burden error. We examined whether overlap metrics identify unreliable MTV estimates using 1,014 autoPET FDG PET/CT studies. We evaluated LesionTracer predictions held out from fine-tuning, compared five selected released models on 489 tumor-positive patients, and examined the findings in 597 PSMA studies. Across the five FDG models, ranking by higher mean Dice gave the same order as ranking by lower mean relative MTV error ($\rho=-1.00$, exact $p=0.017$). At the patient level, however, out-of-fold Dice tracked relative MTV error strongly ($\rho=-0.75$), yet 82 of 489 patients (16.8\%) fell on opposite sides of the Dice 0.80 and MTV-error 25\% thresholds. Within the training-exposed released models, correlations ranged from $-0.47$ to $-0.74$ over narrower, high-Dice ranges. Out of fold, opposing false-positive and false-negative volumes cancelled about one third of spatial error in net MTV. In 236 of 489 patients, each of the five models missed at least one lesion, though not necessarily the same lesion. Thus, agreement in average model rankings did not establish the reliability of individual MTV estimates or reveal shared lesion misses. Comments: Code, stimulus generators, and all result files: this https URL
Journal-ref: WACV 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Contrastive vision-language models score left/right relations near chance, but the symptom has two causes that call for opposite repairs: the relation may survive in the pooled embedding yet be unreachable by native image-text similarity, or pooling may discard it while the dense features retain it. On clean two object photographs, across ten encoders, the lateral polarity is linearly decodable from the flip odd component of the pooled vector at 0.77-0.99, yet a search over a million captions leaves nine of the ten at chance under native scoring: an access failure. On controlled C4 orbits, where the relation is the only thing that varies, pooling keeps the arrangement axis at 0.998-1.000 and loses its polarity, which the patch grid retains: a pooling failure. Both sit downstream of the dense features, so one readout covers both. Our zero parameter, query conditioned spatial moment recomputes the geometry from the patch grid and stores it as a vector beside the native embedding. On a 118,287 image index it raises left/right pairwise accuracy against reversed geometry negatives from 0.51-0.53 to 0.81-0.96 and conditional R@1 among 21 category matched candidates from 0.05 to 0.37-0.75, at under a millisecond per batched query, while reproducing the native ranking exactly for queries that name no relation.

Albert Wilcox, Frank Chang, Nhi Nguyen, Aishani Chakraborty, Jeremy A. Collins, Vaibhav Saxena, Benjamin Joffe, Siddharth Karamcheti, Animesh Garg
Comments: 51 pages, 12 figures, including appendices. Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL), 2026. Project website: this https URL
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. [70] arXiv:2611.05569 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Role-based Effectiveness of an Epistemic Uncertainty Estimate in Training Models for Semantic Segmentation of 3D LiDAR Point Clouds
Krishnakumar N, Jaya Sreevalsan-Nair
Comments: 23 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Point cloud segmentation is a fundamental task in 3D data analysis, with applications across robotics, augmented and virtual reality, and remote sensing. However, the inherent sparsity, noise, and unordered nature of point clouds introduce significant challenges, particularly in achieving reliable classification. While the state-of-the-art rely on training models for explicit modeling of uncertainty, there is a gap in exploring different roles that estimated uncertainty using generative approaches can play. This work investigates the impact of deterministic uncertainty in point cloud segmentation by explicitly modeling epistemic uncertainty and using it in different roles, namely, as a feature and in loss function. We evaluate a baseline artificial neural network (ANN) and two uncertainty-aware variants (uncertainty as an additional input feature and as a per-sample confidence weight in the training loss) on four large-scale LiDAR benchmarks spanning airborne and mobile acquisition, namely ISPRS Vaihingen, AHN3, Paris-Lille-3D, and Toronto-3D, together with PointNet++ and RandLA-Net references and their uncertainty-augmented counterparts under canonical spatially disjoint train and test splits. Under this protocol, uncertainty-aware modeling improves mean Intersection over Union, recovers minority classes that the baseline ANN never predicts at all, and in half of the configurations improves the alignment between prediction error and estimated uncertainty as measured by Patch Accuracy versus Patch Uncertainty. Our findings indicate that uncertainty can play multiple roles in the segmentation pipeline rather than as a device for improving accuracy alone.

[71] arXiv:2611.05570 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ChangeJEPA: Predict Before You Compare for Remote Sensing Change Detection
Buddhi Wijenayake, Dhananjaya Jayasundara, Vishal M. Patel
Comments: 15 pages
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Remote sensing change detection is typically formulated as Siamese feature comparison, where two images are encoded independently and a decoder determines which discrepancies correspond to meaningful change. This is challenging because the encoders preserve both true scene changes and nuisance variations such as illumination, seasonal, radiometric, and geometric differences. We introduce ChangeJEPA, a bitemporal joint-embedding predictive architecture that reformulates change detection as latent post-state prediction. Given a pre-change image and partial post-change evidence, ChangeJEPA predicts the full post-change representation under two complementary conditions: a prior hypothesis derived from the pre-change scene and an updated hypothesis conditioned on observed post-change context. A joint-embedding predictive loss aligns both hypotheses with the target latent representation, encouraging semantic consistency while suppressing transient appearance variations. Change is then inferred from the disagreement among the pre-change representation, the observed post-change target, and the predicted latent states, capturing complementary evidence of change, prior surprise, contextual update, and prediction reliability. Across SYSU-CD, LEVIR-CD+, and CDD, ChangeJEPA consistently outperforms its decoder matched Siamese baseline by up to 1.51 IoU points and achieves the best IoU and F1-score on all three benchmarks, demonstrating the advantage of latent post-state prediction over direct feature comparison. Page: this https URL

[72] arXiv:2611.05571 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ELA: End-to-End Latent Action Policy Learning from Video Demonstrations
Cheng-Chun Hsu, Peter Stone
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: this https URL

[73] arXiv:2611.05572 [pdf, other]
Title: Just the Facts: How Dialogues with AI Reduce Conspiracy Beliefs
Thomas H. Costello, Gordon Pennycook, David G. Rand
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Personalized dialogues with AI substantially reduce conspiracy beliefs. To identify why, we conducted two experiments with U.S. adults recruited online (total N = 2,193) that removed possible causes one at a time. The debunking effect was robust to disclosing the AI's persuasive goal, framing the exchange as a debate, instructing the AI to inform rather than persuade, halving its response length, altering how beliefs were measured, and replacing the dialogue with a single tailored message. Only instructing the AI to persuade without factual evidence and arguments substantially reduced the debunking effect. Content analyses of the AI's output and participants' own accounts linked larger reductions in conspiracy beliefs to factual argumentation rather than rapport, storytelling, or appeals to empathy. AI dialogues appear to reduce conspiracy beliefs primarily by supplying relevant, well-reasoned counterevidence. Our results suggest that humans might be similarly effective if they could supply comparable evidence.

[74] arXiv:2611.05573 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Optimal Marginal Mixing for Transvection-Based Trapdoored Matrices over Large Fields
Mark Braverman, Aayush Jain, Stephen Newman
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

\emph{Trapdoored matrices} are pseudorandom matrices admitting a fast matrix-vector multiplication algorithm given the secret key. We study a candidate family of such matrices: matrices generated by short random \emph{transvection walks} on \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), whose steps are given by adding a random multiple of a random row of the current state to another.
We show that the worst-case time for any nonempty set \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq [n]\times[n]\) of matrix entries to come within TV distance \(\varepsilon\leq \frac{1}{4}\) of its stationary marginal under this walk is \(\Theta(|\mathcal{S}|+n\log(n/\varepsilon))\), uniformly over all \(\mathcal{S}\) and \(q\geq Q_\mathrm{all}(n)\). This is asymptotically optimal, and resolves open questions about the mixing times of transvection walks. We derive concrete upper and lower bounds for \(n\geq 256\). Surprisingly, our bounds also hold conditioned on the row-pair structure of the walk, except on a fraction at most \(\varepsilon\) of such structures. This implies that these walks may be pseudorandom even after conditioning on the row-pair structure, and therefore that trapdoored matrices built with these walks may be universal.
Assuming the conjectured structure-conditioned pseudorandomness of short walks, we exhibit highly efficient, highly parallelizable, and universal trapdoored matrices over \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\), and \(\mathbb{F}_q^{n\times n}\). The families over \(\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\) and \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)\) admit equally efficient trapdoors for their inverses, making them the first to do so for finite-field trapdoored matrices. We discuss attacks, analyzing one in detail, and lay out directions for further investigation.

[75] arXiv:2611.05574 [pdf, html, other]
Title: What Do We Mean When We Say 'F*ck AI'?: Moral Panic, Semantic Indeterminacy, and the Reification of Techno-Capitalism
Sasha Luccioni, Travis LaCroix
Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Academic and (increasingly) public resistance to artificial intelligence (AI) often blurs the line between legitimate critique of techno-capitalist exploitation and (inflated) existential risk. Moreover, discourse around AI can sometimes resemble a "moral panic" where an apparently clear and identifiable scapegoat is targeted in lieu of the complex systemic problems that are causing (genuine and justified) social anxieties. However, AI is not a monolith. In this paper, we explore the environmental, political, and socio-technical consequences of the semantic indeterminacy of discourse about "AI" in conjunction with the increasing moral panic encompassing these technologies. We argue that since the umbrella term "AI" lacks a coherent, singular referent, the moral panic about AI inadvertently reifies the concept of an autonomous, singular agent with inherent and often autonomous tendencies, which aligns with corporate narratives. Hence, well-intentioned critique, activist pushback, and public protest paradoxically amplifies hype-based discussions of AI, thus validating the "threat" narrative that tech leaders deploy to exaggerate their products' capabilities and market value, further consolidating and centralising their political and socio-economic power. Moreover, if "AI" does not refer to a unified class of technologies, then policy intended to govern "AI" will systematically (and necessarily) fail. We conclude by proposing ways forward to improve AI literacy, enforce accountability, and repurpose existing regulation in order to imagine a more positive AI future.

[76] arXiv:2611.05576 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A First Closed-Form Robin Parameter for Optimized Schwarz Waveform Relaxation as a Function of Iteration Count, Overlap, and Time Window Length
Alejandro Alfonso Rodriguez, Martin J. Gander, Felix Kwok
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

Schwarz waveform relaxation (SWR) is a parallel-in-time iterative method for the solution of evolution problems and belongs to the class of Parallel-in-Time algorithms that have received increasing attention over the past three decades. For parabolic problems, SWR converges linearly over long time intervals and exhibits superlinear convergence on short time intervals. Since the introduction of optimized variants (OSWR) nearly three decades ago, determining the optimized Robin parameter when OSWR is applied on bounded time windows has remained an open problem.
We introduce here a new analytical approach that, for the first time, yields a closed-form expression for the optimal Robin parameter in the transmission conditions for the one-dimensional heat equation with two overlapping subdomains. The resulting formula explicitly characterizes the dependence of the optimal parameter on the iteration number, the overlap size, and the length of the time window. Beyond resolving this long-standing optimization problem, our analysis provides a framework that can be extended to more general settings, including higher-dimensional problems, multiple subdomains, and higher-order transmission conditions.

Title: Readable Is Not Steerable: Pre-Registered Tests of Physical Structure in Learned Fluid Representations
Manvendra Modgil
Comments: 30 pages, 9 figures. Code, pre-registrations and checkpoints: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Fluid Dynamics (physics.flu-dyn)

Self-supervised world models are often said to organize their latents around physical quantities. We test this on 2D decaying Navier-Stokes flow in three pre-registered studies, each tested once on held-out data. In Study 1, a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) trained to predict the flow fails the pre-registered criteria for organizing its latent around fluid quantities better than an untrained network of the same architecture (not supported); a JEPA trained on non-physical linear dynamics and a static invariance model that never sees time do as well or better. In Study 2, plain autoencoders that render the field make enstrophy prominent in their slowest unsupervised latent directions (best r 0.80-0.86 vs 0.38 untrained; fresh seeds, sealed data). Adding VICReg lowers this prominence in every comparison, though not by the pre-registered margin for vorticity, while raising the autoencoders' linear decodability (partially supported). In Study 3, we build steerable directions ("dials") by routing: the decoder gets overall scale only through a small conditioning code, while its other pathway carries a degraded copy of spectral shape. Label-free rules find a loudness dial in all 8 trained models and a shape dial in 3 of 5 fresh seeds on sealed data, against a pre-registered bar of 4; neither control shows a shape dial (partially supported). Across the studies, what a latent contains and what can be controlled through it come apart. In exploration, a supervised direction reading spectral shape almost perfectly moved nothing when steered. During the build, the loudness dial had to be found by its effect on the output (closest to a pure rescaling), not by data variance; for shape, a variance rule and an effect-constrained rule each worked in 3 of 5 seeds. The program used about 70 logged hours on one consumer GPU; all pre-registrations, deviations, code and outputs are public.

Title: Whose Values Are Generated? Measuring Visual Value Leakage in Multilingual Text-to-Image Generation
Zucan Lyu, Binwei Yao, Rheeya Uppaal, Jing Yao, Xiaoyuan Yi, Junjie Hu
Comments: 38 pages
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Text-to-image (T2I) systems serve users across languages and cultural contexts. However, evaluations of cultural representation focus mainly on recognizable elements such as landmarks, clothing, and activities, overlooking the cultural values that generated images convey. To bridge this gap, we introduce VisionValueBench, a multilingual benchmark that operationalizes six of Hofstede's cultural value dimensions (e.g., individualism versus collectivism) to investigate how T2I systems frame neutral social situations through a particular cultural orientation. We find that value-neutral prompts, which admit diverse cultural interpretations, nonetheless yield images that favor particular value orientations, a phenomenon we call visual value leakage. We evaluate prompts varying in language and geographic cues across 960 social scenarios and six T2I configurations. Generated images consistently favor the same value orientations across all six dimensions, for example, equality over hierarchy (low power distance), individual autonomy over group obligation (individualism), and enjoyment over restraint (indulgence). Prompt language has limited influence on these orientations, whereas geographic cues shift some dimensions toward the associated cultural values while largely preserving the prevailing orientations. These findings reveal substantial homogeneity in the cultural values conveyed by T2I systems worldwide.

Title: Learning vs. Optimizing Players in Budgeted Games
Giannis Fikioris, Balasubramanian Sivan, Éva Tardos
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We study repeated general games over $T$ rounds between a utility-maximizing optimizer and a learning agent, where budget constraints couple the players' decisions across rounds. Without budgets, low swap regret simultaneously guarantees the learner sublinear regret and caps the optimizer at its Stackelberg value. Budgets break this picture: adversarial no-regret becomes impossible, so the natural goals are non-manipulability---no adaptive optimizer earns more than $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + o(T)$, where $\mathtt{BSE}$ is its Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium value---and low stochastic regret when the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy.
We give an efficient, budget-feasible learning algorithm that achieves both goals in every budgeted game: any adaptive optimizer, budgeted or not, earns at most $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + O(\sqrt{T})$ in expectation, and if the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy on each of a constant number of intervals, the learner has $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret on each such interval. Our learner best responds to forecasts of the optimizer's play that are calibrated in two novel senses, since under budgets the calibration that prevents manipulation no longer yields low stochastic regret. Response calibration, which conditions on the learner's own mixed response by embedding its continuous mixing weight as a step function in $L^2([-1,1])$, prevents manipulation without discretizing responses; dual-weighted Lagrangian calibration ensures low regret. Although low calibration error requires randomized forecasts---distributions over a continuous space that need not have a succinct representation or be directly computable---we construct such forecasts in polynomial time by simulating online gradient ascent.

Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Title: Exploring the Privacy--Size Tradeoff for Differentially Private Self-Attentive Variational Autoencoders

Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Data tends to be most useful when it is shared, and the data most worth sharing is often the data that privacy obligations restrict. Synthetic data from a generator trained under differential privacy (DP) is one way to reconcile the two, but its utility depends on the privacy budget $\varepsilon$ and on how much data the generator sees - a parameter that most data sharing applications of synthetic data control. We find that, under the same DP guarantee, more data generally means more utility. For the marginal mechanisms it absorbs most of what a strict budget costs, and a noise-scaling argument suggests DP-SGD exchanges data fo budget at a worse rate. Title: Contact-Implicit Whole-Body Trajectory Optimization for Dynamic Humanoid Locomotion on Parameterizable Uneven Terrain

This letter presents a trajectory planner for humanoid robots to perform dynamic motions on complex, parameterizable terrains using a contact-implicit whole-body optimization framework. Title: Anduin: A sybil-resistant agentic marketplace reputation system

Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

As autonomous AI agents enter permissionless onchain markets, selecting new service providers remains a core challenge. Existing reputation systems depend on scarce resources like human curation, identity credentials, or voluntary reviews, while naive volume rankings are vulnerable to Sybil attacks.

Evaluating these algorithms against simulated adversaries across 813 buyers, we show that rating manipulation costs 20% of those buyers' total spend and is around 23x harder to manipulate than the standard similarity rule (collaborative filtering).

[85] arXiv:2611.05587 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Cibersapiens: Gamifying Cybersecurity Education to Engage Secondary Students
Soraya Frías-Guadalupe, Pedro Paredes, Carlos Castaneda-Marroquín
Comments: 9 pages, 2 tables. Presented at JNIC 2025, Zaragoza, Spain, June 4-6, 2025
Journal-ref: Actas de las X Jornadas Nacionales de Investigacion en Ciberseguridad (JNIC 2025), Universidad de Zaragoza, 2025, pp. 485-493. ISBN 978-84-10169-61-6
Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Cybersecurity education and awareness are often tailored for businesses, leaving general citizens, especially young people, unprepared. Despite the availability of educational resources, cybersecurity training is not provided equally to all individuals, particularly children and teenagers. As digital risks such as sexting, grooming, and cyberbullying, among others, increase, young users remain vulnerable. However, existing awareness efforts fail to engage them effectively and current content lacks the motivation needed to drive meaningful behavioral change. This paper introduces "Cibersapiens: Digital Well-being for a Connected Generation," an interactive, gamified environment designed to teach cybersecurity to secondary school students. The project focuses on developing and implementing gamified educational resources that actively engage students, improve their understanding of cyber risks, and promote best practices in digital security. By leveraging active learning methodologies, this approach transforms cybersecurity education into an engaging and meaningful experience.

[86] arXiv:2611.05590 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Verified but Vacuous: Three Failure Surfaces of LLM-Driven Verified Code Generation
Aditya Vempaty, Himaneesh Sompalle, Manan Tayal, Mowafak Allaham, Prasenjit Dey, Ashish Jagmohan, Ravi Kokku
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

What should ``verified'' mean when evaluating LLM-generated code? Many existing pipelines report a single verification number. We argue this collapses three distinct properties measured in a conditional audit sequence: verifier acceptance (Surface A), \emph{syntactic specification binding (Surface B: does the proof obligation bind to the spec?), and \emph{semantic specification fidelity} (Surface C: does the spec capture the informal requirement?). Two empirical demonstrations show the surfaces separate. \textbf{First ($A \neq B$), via Li@Opus (a same-model reproduction of \citet{li2025dafny}'s Dafny-as-intermediate-representation (IR) pipeline under Claude Opus 4.7) on three Python benchmarks}: it reaches \textbf{99.1\% verifier acceptance} on HumanEval while only \textbf{1.9\%} carry a certificate binding to a spec-defined predicate or function. \textbf{Second ($B \neq C$), via VCG on two Rust benchmarks}: we use VCG (which is our own in-house Dafny-as-intermediate pipeline) on Rust because the Rust target lets us enforce fully-verifiable output (every component ships as a Dafny certificate, ensures-binding gate passing by construction). Even inside that construction, \textbf{11.48\% (MBPP-Rust) and 14.82\% (VeriContest LC slice) of structurally-verified samples still fail hidden tests}. On the LC slice of VeriContest, \textbf{VCG's reported End2End rate is 7.79\% (535/6870).} The cited external rates are 5.51\% (GPT-5.5) and 1.88\% (single-shot Opus 4.7). [87] arXiv:2611.05591 [pdf, html, other]
Title: C-GRPO: Conformal Group Relative Policy Optimization
Arya Fayyazi, Seyedarmin Azizi, Mehdi Kamal, Massoud Pedram
Comments: Proceeding of NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Reasoning-oriented language model training increasingly relies on multiple on-policy rollouts, but standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses a fixed group size, wasting compute on easy prompts and under-exploring hard ones. Existing adaptive-budget methods alleviate this inefficiency, yet their stopping rules are heuristic and do not provide a finite-sample calibration guarantee. [88] arXiv:2611.05593 [pdf, html, other]
Title: GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats
Shahaf Valencia Levy, Sagie Benaim
Comments: Under review at TMLR. 32 pages. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: this https URL

[89] arXiv:2611.05594 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Relevance Propagation as Entropic Optimal Transport on Filippov Neural Networks: Sinkhorn Propagation and Region Relevance in Image Classifiers
Olivier Gibaru, Eric Nyiri
Comments: 41 pages, 17 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Relevance propagation, which redistributes a network's prediction backward through the layers, is usually treated as a heuristic. We show that it is the solution of a single variational problem: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) is the divergence-free flow on the active computational graph of zero relative entropy to the backward transition law of the forward activation flow; for a non-negative reference, this is a relative entropy between Markov measures on backward paths. The rules LRP$_0$, LRP$_{z^+}$ and LRP$_{\alpha,\beta}$ follow from this principle by the choice of a reference, and are instances of one rule, LRPN$_{\alpha,\beta}$, whose weights may vary from node to node, for instance with the node's activity, in the spirit of Hebb's principle. The principle rests on a measure-theoretic formalization of feed-forward networks as directed acyclic graphs of Filippov operators, which covers piecewise-smooth and discontinuous architectures (e.g. hard-routed Mixture-of-Experts) with a Clarke-Filippov generalized-gradient calculus; it also characterizes backpropagation as the adjoint equation of a Lagrangian relaxation. On networks of ReLU and max-pooling nodes, LRP$_0$ is Gradient$\times$Input, with an explicit jump across a kink where LRP$_{z^+}$ stays continuous. Taking the entropy edge by edge yields a new rule, Sinkhorn Relevance Propagation. Aggregated over an input region, the flow of a non-negative reference tells, with exact accounting, which hidden units carry its evidence, the conditioned flow being a Schrödinger bridge. On VGG-16, the conservation identities hold to round-off, and the rules are told apart by the sign of their maps, the share of the output left to the bias nodes, faithfulness, localization and class dependence; on ConvNeXt-Tiny, LRPN$_{\alpha,\beta}$ conserves the output and its Hebbian weights give the highest ABPC of the rules tested.

[90] arXiv:2611.05596 [pdf, html, other]
Title: RAGCompass: Generalizable Retriever Routing via Reranking
Valentin Six, Mufei Li, Dongqi Fu, Yinglong Xia, Hong Li, Pan Li
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

Different retrievers exist for retrieval-augmented generation, yet none performs best for all queries. Therefore, the key question is: given a query and retrieved passages from different retrievers, which one is most suited for that query? Existing routers usually make predictions from query-specific features and a fixed pool of retrievers; such routers have no output for an unseen retriever and are incapable by design on a new corpus. To fill these gaps, RAGCompass reads the retrieved passage sets themselves: passages from an unfamiliar retriever or corpus stay directly comparable to other passages, so routing stays well designed where a query-only map would fail. We contrastively fine-tune a reranker against the answer each evidence set produces, which accounts for most of the gain; a small comparison head adds a moderate improvement, and neither component has retriever-specific parameters. RAGCompass improves answer F1 by 28% relative to the best fixed retriever, and outperforms fusion baselines, three query-only routers, and a prompted 8B language model. Generalization experiments show that RAGCompass keeps most of its gain under an unseen corpus, retriever, or reader, while query-only baselines fall to the best fixed retriever or below.

[91] arXiv:2611.05598 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Fast Quantum Byzantine Agreement with Nearly Linear Quantum Communication
Jan Olkowski
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We consider synchronous binary Byzantine agreement among $n$ processes connected by authenticated point-to-point classical and quantum channels. The adversary is computationally unbounded, sees all classical information, adaptively corrupts up to $t\le(1/3-\varepsilon)n$ processes, and may suppress messages sent by a process in the round in which it is corrupted.
We give a quantum algorithm that solves Byzantine agreement in this model with probability $1$. It uses $O(\log^4 n)$ rounds, $O(n\log^8 n)$ qubits, and $O(n^2\log^8 n)$ classical bits in expectation, with constants depending on $\varepsilon$. This reduces the quantum communication of the protocol of Ben-Or and Hassidim (STOC~2005), which achieves $O(1)$ expected rounds but whose Byzantine coin implementation requires $\Omega(n^4\log n)$ qubits and classical bits.
We also extend the quadratic message lower bound of Abraham et al.\ (PODC~2019) to quantum channels, obtaining an $\Omega(t^2)$ lower bound on worst-case expected total communication. For $t=\Theta(n)$, the communication and round complexity of our algorithm are therefore optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.

[92] arXiv:2611.05599 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CAPTOR: text-encoder-free grounding by counting caption co-occurrence over the visual words of a frozen encoder
Elad Yoshai, Natan T. Shaked
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Grounding a text query in an image needs a matrix scoring every term against every patch. Vision-language models compute it with an aligned text encoder, which many image encoders, such as histopathology-related models trained on slides alone, lack. The Caption-Anchored Patch-Term Occurrence Representation (CAPTOR) estimates the matrix without a text encoder. It clusters a frozen image encoder's patch tokens into visual words and describes each captioned image by its share of patches in each word. A term signature is the standardized difference of those shares between images whose captions mention the term and the rest. The matrix factorizes into a term-by-word table and a query-independent image factor, so an image is encoded once and a new term adds one table row. Against every training-free baseline, CAPTOR leads on Common Objects in Context (COCO), Pascal Visual Object Classes (VOC) and Cityscapes. On COCO, scored on the cells one object owns, it reaches 0.565 mean intersection over union (mIoU) against 0.502. On all three, it is also level with a text alignment trained on the same backbone, which needs gradients, a text encoder and several times the captions. On held-out breast-cancer slides, it exceeds the strongest baseline scoring patches with a pathology text encoder by 0.160 mIoU. Read through CAPTOR, UNI, an encoder trained on slides alone, exceeds such baselines by 0.132 on a common grid. Counting can therefore give a text interface to any image encoder trained without language, wherever captioned images exist.

[93] arXiv:2611.05601 [pdf, html, other]
Title: RIDGE: State-Conditioned Reward Blending for Behavioral Coverage in Deep RL Game Agents
AL Muqshith Mohammed Shifan, Kevin Christopher Chua, Ali Neshati, Loutfouz Zaman, Cristiano Politowski
Comments: Conference of Games, 4 pages, 3 figures, reinforcement learning, automated playtesting, procedural personas,reward shaping, PPO, Crafter
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Software Engineering (cs.SE)

A deep RL agent trained on a fixed persona reward plays one way: an Explorer keeps exploring while starving, a Survivor hoards on an empty map. Since each persona fixes its own reward, automated playtesting trains N agents for N styles. Changing reward composition mid-episode runs into the switching-stability dilemma: PPO degrades under non-stationary rewards. We present RIDGE, a single-agent architecture that sidesteps the dilemma with two design choices: a state-conditioned blender that computes softmax-normalized sigmoid weights from slow-moving state variables, and a multi-head critic that trains one value head per persona on its own stationary signal. On Crafter with four personas, one \ridge agent acquires both branches of the wood-tier crafting/combat split that no fixed-persona baseline solves jointly, and a sharpness ablation confirms state-conditioning drives the gain. We position these results as demonstrations of the blending mechanism's dynamics across n=3 seeds per condition; larger multi-seed sweeps remain future work.

[94] arXiv:2611.05602 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Private Online Release of Adaptive Linear Queries
Aleksandar Nikolov, Haohua Tang
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

In this paper we study answering counting and other linear queries online under differential privacy constraints. Recent work by Nikolov, Tang, and Ullman [STOC 2026] gave the first online algorithm that answers \emph{obliviously chosen} online linear queries privately, and achieves poly-logarithmic competitiveness against an optimal offline factorization mechanism. This also implied poly-logarithmic competitiveness against arbitrary private offline mechanisms when the private dataset is large enough. The error guarantees of their algorithm, however, can fail when the queries are adaptive. We give a new algorithm that also achieves poly-logarithmic competitiveness, while being able to handle \emph{adaptively chosen} queries. This implies that there is no large separation between the optimal error bounds for privately answering, respectively, offline linear queries, obliviously chosen online linear queries, and adaptively chosen online linear queries. Our algorithm combines the online factorization approach from prior work with a novel layered Euclidean iterative database construction, presenting a new way to use factorization in private algorithms.
We also give a lower bound that shows that some poly-logarithmic factor in the competitive ratio is unavoidable. Our lower bound first shows that any interactive private mechanism implies a deterministic online factorization algorithm, and then gives a new lower bound for the competitive ratio of any deterministic online factorization algorithm.

[95] arXiv:2611.05605 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Transport along Local Annealing Paths: Wasserstein Geometry and Multimodal Sampling
Han Chen, Sifan Liu
Comments: 36 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation (stat.CO); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Variational approaches to learning transport maps for multimodal sampling can suffer from mode collapse. One way to mitigate this problem is to learn transport along a prescribed path of intermediate distributions defined by geometric annealing. We show that annealing can take a substantial detour in Wasserstein space: when mass moves between modes, the path can be much longer than the distance between its endpoints. We further link path geometry to transport learning, showing that long annealing paths can slow population optimization, while sufficiently regular paths permit rapid convergence. Motivated by these findings, we propose componentwise annealed transport (CAT) to reduce the need for mass transfer between modes. Starting from a mode-informed mixture reference, CAT constructs an exact mixture decomposition of the target and learns separate transport maps along componentwise annealing paths. We estimate the component weights separately and show that these estimates remain consistent even when the learned flows are inexact. We also develop adaptive annealing schedules guided by transport effort. Experiments on multimodal synthetic distributions and Bayesian inference problems demonstrate improvements in transport learning and sampling efficiency.

[96] arXiv:2611.05609 [pdf, other]
Title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation
Yichen Wang, Yufa Zhou, Siqi Zhu, Haozheng Luo, Jingzhi Bao, Zhichao Liu, Zijun Wei
Comments: 27 pages, 12 figures. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) to consolidate capabilities from multiple teachers. Although prior work reports near-perfect in-distribution (IND) distillation performance, we find that this can mask incomplete capability consolidation beyond the supervised distribution. A preliminary study on synthetic reasoning shows that OPD does not fully transfer teachers' generalization capabilities. We then extend this investigation to real-world tasks, evaluating extrapolative and compositional generalization across mathematical reasoning, coding, agent, and long-context capabilities using Qwen3 models. Across extrapolative settings, OPD and MOPD reach 96.04-102.73% of their teachers' IND scores. Yet their out-of-distribution (OOD) scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base model's. Across three compositional settings, MOPD improves IND performance over the base model, but its performance on composed tasks as OOD remains 18.19-24.34% below that of the best teachers. To understand these gaps, we examine teacher capability and data coverage as two potential bottlenecks. Jointly alleviating these bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in our experiments and suggests the potential for generalization beyond the teacher. (M)OPD also reduces OOD forgetting on average relative to its reinforcement learning (RL) baselines. Analysis of the associated update geometry reveals smaller and more spectrally concentrated updates on average than those of the RL baselines, along with greater shared update structure under MOPD. Motivated by these findings, we propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve OOD performance while largely preserving IND performance. Our findings identify a blind spot in capability consolidation via (M)OPD, highlighting the need for algorithms that explicitly support OOD retention and generalization.

[97] arXiv:2611.05611 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Hybrid Spark: Adaptive Speculative Decoding That Lets the Content Choose the Drafter
Ekagra Ranjan, Bharat Venkitesh
Comments: Speculative Decoding
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up large language model (LLM) serving, but its gain depends on the workload's \emph{shape}, such as batch size and context length, and on its \emph{content}. A model-based drafter proposes a short block on any content, while a model-free drafter such as n-gram lookup proposes long copies at almost no cost when the output repeats its input, as in code editing. Adaptive verification spends a batch-wide verification budget on the draft tokens most likely to be accepted, but it supports only one model-based drafter. Model-free drafters provide no per-token confidence, so they cannot take part in budget allocation, and deployments must either fix one drafter or split their GPUs between drafters. We present \sys, a framework that runs a model-based and a model-free drafter on every step and gives each request the better of their chains, within adaptive verification and entirely on the GPU, which keeps asynchronous scheduling intact. The key idea is a price per verified draft token: the goodput that slot would earn elsewhere in the batch. Once the model-free drafter's tokens carry calibrated acceptance estimates, fit once on general text, this price puts both drafters' chains on one scale. Instantiated with \dspark and an n-gram drafter in vLLM, \sys achieves 1.10--1.62\x the output throughput of \dspark on code editing at batch size~4 and 1.04--1.27\x at batch size~128, while staying at 0.97--1.01\x of it on chat at temperature~0. A single deployment can therefore serve both workloads.

[98] arXiv:2611.05612 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Whiel: A Neurosymbolic Platform for Certified Relational Program Verification
Jesse Comer, Fangzhu Shen, Shuo Zhang, Mayur Naik, Sudeepa Roy, Val Tannen
Subjects: Databases (cs.DB); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

We present the Whiel (a contraction of Whi(le-R)el) system for Lean-certified reasoning about imperative relational programs. The system can encode containment and equivalence problems for Datalog, its extensions with negation, and the core fragment of graph query languages. It can also represent optimized or incremental evaluation algorithms that are not expressible in the original query language, as well as first-order specifications of integrity constraints, schema mappings, and views arising in data integration, exchange, and sharing. Whiel's program states are database instances, and its imperative structure enables compositional Hoare-style reasoning with first-order relational specifications, using prophecy variables and leveled invariants to support inductive arguments. Whiel supports neurosymbolic discovery of loop invariants whose verification conditions can be checked using the Vampire first-order theorem prover. Counterexamples are fed back into the neurosymbolic pipeline, while proposed solutions are translated into Lean proof certificates. To validate the Whiel system, we evaluate its performance on a curated benchmark suite. In summary, we envision the Whiel system as a tool for tackling mathematically demanding, typically undecidable problems involving complex query and constraint languages, with a high degree of trust in its output.

[99] arXiv:2611.05614 [pdf, html, other]
Title: The CNF Encoding Complexity of Boolean Functions
Andrew Krapivin, Benjamin Przybocki, Bernardo Subercaseaux
Comments: 36 pages, comments are welcome!
Subjects: Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

We study the minimum number of clauses required to encode a boolean function into a CNF formula with auxiliary variables. Our main result is that if a boolean function can be evaluated in nondeterministic time $t$ (in the RAM model) with $m$ bits of advice such that at most $b$ bits of advice are accessed for each input, then it admits a CNF encoding with $\widetilde{O}(t + \sqrt{mb})$ clauses. This constitutes a nonuniform generalization of Robson's (TCS'91) variant of the Cook--Levin theorem, for which a naïve generalization would yield $\widetilde{O}(t+m)$ clauses; our applications leverage $b = o(m)$ to obtain significantly better bounds. Since preprocessed data structures can be modeled as computation with advice, our result allows us to translate space- and time-efficient data structures to compact CNF encodings. As an application, we derandomize a data structure of Larsen and Williams (SODA'17) to show that every $k$-CNF function on $n$ inputs can be encoded with $n^k/2^{\Omega_k(\sqrt{\lg n})}$ clauses. Notably, despite encoding a $k$-CNF function, the encoding itself necessarily contains clauses of unbounded width, since an information-theoretic argument shows that the minimum number of bounded-width clauses to encode such functions is $\Omega_k(n^{k}/\lg n)$ in the worst case. In general terms, our results imply that for a wide variety of NP-complete problems, one can reduce to CNF-SAT in a way that results in asymptotically fewer clauses than previously known methods.

[100] arXiv:2611.05615 [pdf, html, other]
Title: $\mathcal{C}^\infty$ Smooth Trajectory Planning with Application to Soft Robots
Reinhard M. Grassmann, Abdulaziz Y. Alkayas, Lingyun Chen, Sami Haddadin
Comments: 8 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

High motion performance and avoiding structural vibrations rely on smooth trajectory planning. The smoothness requirement depends on the robot's complexity in terms of the number of degrees of freedom and system order due to the flexibility of the joints and links. For industrial robots, the smoothness requirements have been determined and subsequently taken into account. Although unknown for soft continuum robots, the exact smoothness requirement can potentially be much larger than previously considered ones such as $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^4}$ for collaborative robots and $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^5}$ for quadcopter drones. To address this gap, we introduce a $\mathbf{\mathcal{C}^\infty}$-smooth trajectory generator that respects defined kinematic limits and generates infinitely differentiable trajectories. The generated path addresses and generalizes to all smoothness requirements, where a transition between sequential states is needed. Therefore, all trajectories have continuous velocity, acceleration, jerk, snap, crackle, pop, etc. Of particular interest is the case of null boundary conditions, i.e., all derivatives at the start and end of the trajectory are equal to zero. We verified and evaluated our proposed approach in simulations and on hardware.

[101] arXiv:2611.05616 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LACS: Distribution-Sensitive Label-Agnostic Confidence Selection for Dynamic Data Pruning
Heejin Choi
Comments: 40 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Training on large datasets motivates selecting which examples receive expensive training computation. Fixed quotas determine the amount of pruning in advance, while absolute confidence cutoffs depend on the score scale. We study a population-relative alternative that adapts the threshold and retained count together. We introduce LACS (Label-Agnostic Confidence Selector), a training-time rule based on maximum predictive confidence, requiring neither labels at selection time nor per-example gradients. LACS removes examples at or above a log-mean-exp reference plus a margin. We characterize its sensitivity to score gaps and mass, and derive an exact no-pruning condition. For $0<\rho<1$, the removed fraction is at most $\rho$ and at least one example remains. The unsigned score permits both confidently correct and confidently wrong examples to be removed. Neural execution studies reduce backward-active rows by 10-35%; on CIFAR-10, 29% fewer backward rows accompany accuracy means of 89.77% versus 89.82% for full CE. At a matched backward budget and number of optimizer updates, LACS is 1.0 pp above small-batch training and 1.2 pp above random selection over five seeds. Across 14 tabular datasets, quadratic boosting reduces mean test error from 23.36% to 22.96%. Its full training replays use about 30% fewer fitting rows; these counters span a different horizon from validation-selected accuracy. In one RBF-SVM case study, elapsed time falls by 37% with slightly lower error. These findings separate selective-work reduction from realized acceleration: the current exact-current-score neural implementation uses an additional scoring forward, so its backward sparsity does not yet translate into wall-clock acceleration. This overhead is an execution choice rather than a requirement of the selection rule.

[102] arXiv:2611.05617 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Barrier-State-Based Safe Navigation in Complex Environments Using Look-Ahead Safety Corridors
Yunlin Wei, Fangfei Li, Junhui Zhang
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Safe navigation in cluttered environments requires a safety representation that captures the available motion space along the planned path. A single local safe region may restrict progress through narrow passages and continuous turns. This paper presents a planning-guided look-ahead safety corridor framework for barrier-state-based navigation. Local safe convex polytopes are constructed around collision-free seeds along the forward reference path. Their facet constraints are combined using softmin, and the local functions are fused using softmax with entropy-based adaptive compensation. The resulting safe set remains within the union of the local polytopes while reducing the shrinkage caused by fixed compensation. A Poisson boundary-value problem then defines a differentiable interior safety field while preserving the prescribed corridor boundary. This field is embedded into the robot dynamics through one geometric barrier state. We establish sufficient conditions for corridor invariance based on barrier-state boundedness and active-corridor validity. Navigation simulations cover cluttered layouts, narrow passages, and moving obstacles. A differential-drive ground vehicle further demonstrates navigation through narrow passages and among obstacles absent from the prior map.

[103] arXiv:2611.05620 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ViBench 2.0: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Software Building
Daniel Furman, Preeya Kirani, Ibrahim Sheikh, Zhen Li, Peter Zhong, Michele Catasta
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Software Engineering (cs.SE)

On Replit, our agentic engineering platform, users now build entire products without writing code, through successive feature requests to an agent. Yet existing coding benchmarks evaluate single, fully specified tasks, and many are near saturation. We introduce ViBench 2.0, a benchmark for long-horizon software building that we use to select our platform's models. Its 17 full-stack web products, modeled on widely used software, grow over 241 feature requests and are judged only when finished, as a user would judge them: a browser agent runs 544 test plans, and a build passes only if every plan does, under a grading protocol validated to keep this strict score reliable. Evaluating nine models, we find a reliability gap: the three strongest pass up to 98% of test plans yet deliver a fully working product in at most 65% of builds, and no open-weight model delivers one. The gap is closing fast: across three releases of one model family, pass@1 on the public products rises from 3% to 53% while the cost per build falls by more than half. We release eight products with the harness and grader, hold out nine, and report lessons from production use.

[104] arXiv:2611.05625 [pdf, other]
Title: Personalized Visual Support After Automatic Speech Recognition
Beatriz Calero, Duarte Neves, Carlos Bruno, Luis Ricardo Santos, Mario Egea
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

Many spoken-language interfaces stop at producing a transcript. This project examines how a second layer of optional text and pictorial support can be adapted to individual needs. We specify four presentation levels and a behavior-based selection policy driven by replay requests, response latency and recent comprehension. After expert review of the mappings, we will compare fixed and adaptive presentation using counterbalanced spoken instructions. The study is designed to measure comprehension, usability and which modality listeners rely on, not to claim that transcript embellishment uniformly benefits listeners.

[105] arXiv:2611.05626 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Exact signal recovery from generative priors with sigmoid output activation
Matthew S. Scott, Yaniv Plan, Özgür Yılmaz
Comments: 9 pages
Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT); Signal Processing (eess.SP); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

We show exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward neural networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, with no assumption of expansivity. Consider a ReLU network of depth $d$ with a sigmoid final activation, whose input layer, of dimension $k$, is the narrowest, and let $K$ be the geometric mean of the widths of its layers. We show that, with high probability, all signals of the range whose entries lie in $[\delta, 1 - \delta]$ are uniformly recovered from $m \gtrsim k(d \log(K/k) + \log(1+\log(1/\delta)))$ measurements.

[106] arXiv:2611.05632 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
Mehdi Shajari
Comments: 81 pages, 3 figures
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Autonomous software agents can act through tools, delegate work, and change their models or execution environments while earlier authorizations remain in flight. We present Assurance-Conditioned Continuous Authorization (ACCA), an approach designed to be harness-independent, for maintaining operational authority according to currently justified assurance. It distinguishes evidence validity from contextual applicability, derives assurance claims from eligible evidence, and resolves a multidimensional effective-authority envelope within a principal-declared ceiling and applicable policy. A typed dependency graph supports selective re-evaluation of authorization-relevant changes. An authority epoch changes when effective authority changes; a distinct optional authorization-basis version supports revalidation of action-specific authorization conditions. Protected effect-time enforcement can reject stale actions before a consequential resource change, subject to the available commit mechanism. A compositional Domain Governance Profile expresses domain-specific semantics without granting authority. Controlled scenario tests implemented as a regression suite using a trading profile exercise default-deny rules, evidence-conditioned contraction and recovery, policy divergence, selective non-response, and stale-action rejection at a local gateway before the simulated-broker boundary. The study establishes implementation-level evidence in one domain, not a cross-domain guarantee of harmful-behavior prevention.

[107] arXiv:2611.05633 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Spatio-Temporal Multi-Order Interaction for Video Recognition
Kevin D. Nguetche, Lilian Hollard, Eric Granger, Marco Pedersoli
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Many temporal approaches for video recognition rely on explicit cross-channel aggregation projections, which have quadratic complexity in the number of channels, introducing significant computational overhead. In addition, the spatio-temporal representation used for video recognition is biased either toward local order interactions (for CNNs) or toward global order interactions (for transformers). Starting from the multi-order spatial representation of MogaNet, our method introduces two complementary contributions to tackle these problems. First, for the temporal modelling, we introduce parallel multi-order processing with depthwise-only convolutions and implicit gating-based aggregation, which is linear in the number of channels, inducing a considerable computational reduction. Second, we propose a dual interaction between spatial and temporal dimensions, which allows a better spatio-temporal representation without increasing the computational cost. By combining these two contributions, our proposed VideoMogaNet achieves performance on par with or better than state-of-the-art action recognition approaches across multiple video benchmarks (UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics-400, Diving48), while considerably reducing the cost of the temporal branch.

[108] arXiv:2611.05636 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Route to Remember: Adaptive Memory Selection for LLM Agents
Zeyu Fang, Jun Yin, Yongsheng Mei, Xu Han, Chaitali Joshi, Zhongkai Sun, Jie Hao, Bin Guo, Chengyuan Ma, Benjamin Z. Yao, Chenlei Guo
Journal-ref: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop PALM
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

The memory of production agents is increasingly becoming a bottleneck and is built almost exclusively from text: key points are extracted from out-of-limit context and retrieved into context at query time.
