Title: Learning to Tune with Biased Gradients: Iterative Feedback Tuning of Model-Free Control on Throttle Valves
Félix Martinez-Jiménez (GIPSA-INFINITY), Sander Miller-Murphy (GIPSA-INFINITY), Tobie Ondoa-Essomba (GIPSA-INFINITY), Emmanuel Witrant (GIPSA-INFINITY)
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Iterative feedback tuning (IFT) learns the parameters of a fixed-structure controller by stochastic gradient descent. At each iteration, two closed-loop experiments are run on the plant: the first one measures the tracking error, and the second one, driven by this error, provides the sensitivities from which the gradient of the cost is estimated. This estimate is unbiased for linear plants only. We study the biased case on automotive electronic throttle valves, whose friction and stiction vary between valves and runs, controlled by an intelligent proportional (model-free) controller, which is an incremental PI controller. We show that the mismatch of the controller state at the start of the two experiments, which stiction makes unavoidable, adds an error inversely proportional to the amplitude of the second experiment. On digital twins of ten valves, the IFT gradient is a descent direction in only 69\% of the low-cost region, friction being the cause, and all update rules plateau and then drift. On two hardware valves, the best update rule depends on the noise structure of the gradient. On the first valve, where one gradient component is buried in noise, Adam outperforms Gauss--Newton, its normalisation and its momentum each improving one parameter. On the second valve, where both components are consistent, the same normalisation amplifies a direction that Gauss--Newton rightly discounts, and Adam drifts to a controller worse than the initial one. The twins reproduce the mechanism but not this ranking.

[476] arXiv:2611.06342 [pdf, other]
Title: CoRTeC: A Differentially Private Release for Synthetic Tabular Data, Decodable by Any Generator
Calister Nnona
Comments: 29 pages, 4 figures. Code at this https URL and the releases, synthetic draws and score files at this https URL
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

The records that could train the most useful models, such as a hospital's patient files, are often the ones an institution cannot share. We propose CoRTeC, a method that releases synthetic versions of such records under differential privacy. Differential privacy places a proven limit on what the synthetic data can reveal about any person, and in particular on membership inference. CoRTeC spends the privacy budget once, on a small file of noisy counts designed for training a classifier. For each group of records, the file gives the group's size, its balance of outcomes, a histogram of every column for each outcome and the outcome rate in each of several non-overlapping cells. A reviewer can check every number before the file leaves the institution. Anyone can then turn the counts into synthetic rows, as often as they like and at no further privacy cost. A maximum-entropy decoder can do this without any language model, and so can each of the five frozen language models we tested. None of them ever sees a real record. A selection step then matches the rows to the released counts. Decoded without a language model, the automatically configured release at $\varepsilon = 2$ trains classifiers to within 0.02 AUC of a real sample of the same size on the Adult dataset, across three data splits. On NHANES and bank marketing, without the selection step, it stays within 0.05 AUC. On Adult, with a fixed cohort rule, the release carries the outcome rates a deployment names more closely than a real sample does, at some cost in accuracy on pairs of columns. Four controls show that most of the utility comes from the release and the selection step, and that a language model adds what it knows from the column names. No private row ever reaches a model, and no row CoRTeC generates copies a real one. The strongest membership attack stays far below the bound the budget allows.

[477] arXiv:2611.06343 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Prism: Bidirectional Self-Teaching for Unified Multimodal Models
Peng Zhang, Qian Chen, Xianyin Zhang, Yimin Tian, Ruite Fei, Dongyi Lv, Lifan Guo, Chi Zhang, Shuai Liu
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) aim to support visual understanding and generation within a single model. Existing post-training methods either use understanding as a fixed teacher to improve generation, or rely on ground-truth trajectories to supervise both understanding and generation. Prism instead derives bidirectional supervision from self-generated interleaved rollouts, constructing training targets according to the reliability of their text and image chains. We propose Prism, a bidirectional self-teaching post-training method for UMMs. Like a prism decomposing mixed light, Prism decouples a coupled interleaved trajectory into a text chain and an image chain, assesses the reliability of each chain, and constructs a corresponding training target from their reliability states. Experiments on both SenseNova-U1 and BAGEL show that Prism improves both understanding and generation. On the generation side, GenEval improves from 85.8 to 89.2 (+3.4), and DPG improves from 86.1 to 87.3 (+1.2) on SenseNova-U1. On the understanding side, the total MME score improves from 2282.6 to 2311.6, and MMVP improves from 58.0 to 62.0. Consistent improvements are observed on BAGEL. These results highlight that Prism enables coordinated improvements in generation and understanding by constructing reliability-guided self-training targets from self-generated trajectories, without relying on an external verifier or externally annotated corrected trajectories during target construction.

[478] arXiv:2611.06346 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
Moritz Diener, Daniel Hendriks, Philipp Spitzer, Gerhard Satzger, Joshua Holstein, Wei Sun
Comments: 30 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Moritz Diener and Daniel Hendriks contributed equally
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.

[479] arXiv:2611.06348 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
Hendrik Mehrtens, Florian Buettner, Oliver Stegle
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 36 pages, 3 figures, 25 tables. Code: this https URL (paper reproduction on branch neurips2026)
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form, and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d \mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

[480] arXiv:2611.06349 [pdf, html, other]
Title: PMRecBench: A Benchmark for Personalization in Recommendation Agents under Multimodal Queries
Xiaoyu Zhang, Yougang Lyu, Bin Wu, Sahan Bulathwela, Emine Yilmaz
Comments: 13 pages. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

On Web platforms for shopping and entertainment, recommendation agents under multimodal queries aim to deliver personalized recommendations that satisfy users' visually specified requirements and reflect preferences inferred from user histories. However, existing personalized recommendation benchmarks use text-only queries, while multimodal ones assess query matching without evaluating personalization based on real user histories. We introduce the Personalized Multimodal Recommendation Benchmark (PMRecBench), the first benchmark to evaluate the personalization of recommendation agents under multimodal queries. It pairs 510 quality-controlled image-text queries across clothing and movies with the corresponding users' real histories. PMRecBench features two key designs: (1) queries derived from consistent behavioral patterns in real user records, with reference images and targets linked to actual interactions; and (2) challenging diagnostic pools with candidate items rated highly by the user but violating requirements, and items satisfying requirements but never rated highly, testing requirement understanding and preference following, respectively. Extensive experiments on diagnostic pools reveal a personalization imbalance in recommendation agents: relative to personalization signals alone, adding multimodal queries weakens preference following, even though the additional information about query requirements improves overall ranking performance. Further analysis links this decline in preference following to image interpretation, where agents can prioritize resemblance to reference images over evidence from user histories, and stronger commercial backbones alone fail to resolve this imbalance. This personalization imbalance highlights a central challenge for recommendation agents: improving ranking performance while preserving preference following when responding to multimodal user queries

[481] arXiv:2611.06350 [pdf, html, other]
Title: On Existence and Computational Complexity of Quasi-strict Equilibria
Kristoffer Arnsfelt Hansen, Xinhao Nie
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

Quasi-strict Nash equilibrium, introduced by Harsanyi in 1973, is the Nash equilibrium refinement that requires every pure best response to be played with positive probability. Norde established that any bimatrix game admits a quasi-strict Nash equilibrium. We give a substantially simpler proof of this result that in particular avoids an intricate limit argument used in the final step of the proof by Norde.
Our existence proof allows us to positively resolve the outstanding open question of PPAD membership of the problem of computing a quasi-strict Nash equilibrium, thereby settling its precise complexity. In games with three or more players, a quasi-strict Nash equilibrium is not guaranteed to exist, leading to the natural problem of deciding the existence of a quasi-strict Nash equilibrium in a given strategic form game. We show that this problem is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete, strengthening a previous NP-hardness result.

[482] arXiv:2611.06353 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Traffic-VL: Reinforced Vision-Language Models for Generalizable End-to-End Traffic Signal Control
Xingchen Zou, Maonan Wang, Kemou Jiang, Jie Li, Yiqi Chen, Xi Chen, Hai Yang, Yuxuan Liang
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Existing traffic signal control methods typically rely on structured traffic states produced by dedicated perception pipelines. Emerging visual approaches often use idealized simulator images and convert them into intermediate representations before control, limiting their ability to directly exploit roadside visual observations. To bridge both the visual-domain and perception-to-decision gaps, we introduce SynTra-V and Traffic-VL. SynTra-V converts physics-based traffic simulations into photorealistic multi-view surveillance imagery across diverse road topologies and sensing conditions, and automatic semantic auditing checks that control-critical geometry, vehicle movements, and lane semantics match the simulator state. Traffic-VL is an eight-billion-parameter vision-language model that directly maps synchronized multi-view images and natural-language phase descriptions to signal decisions without intermediate structured states. Building on Traffic-R1's two-stage reinforced reasoning framework, Traffic-VL adapts its vision encoder via offline reinforcement learning on SynTra-V and freezes it during online visual stepwise trajectory policy optimization in closed-loop simulation. Experiments show that Traffic-VL matches structured-state Traffic-R1 while outperforming image-based controllers and general-purpose vision-language models, including Gemini 3 Pro. Evaluations on unseen topologies, degraded sensing conditions, real surveillance footage, and a three-week deployment across ten intersections further demonstrate robust visual generalization and effective constrained online control.

[483] arXiv:2611.06355 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FlashRelight: Portrait Video Relighting with Dynamic Lighting
Jiahui Sheng, Le Li, Limin Lin, Jiahao Li, Wansen Feng, Hong Gu, Shuhan Chen, Xiaorun Li, Rui Hu
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 23 pages, including appendix
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Portrait video relighting aims to modify the illumination of a portrait video while preserving photorealism and temporal stability. The task becomes particularly challenging under dynamic lighting, where illumination direction, intensity, and color vary over time. To tackle this problem, we introduce FlashRelight, a novel two-stage framework for dynamic portrait video relighting. FlashRelight first suppresses the source illumination through delighting, and then synthesizes the target dynamic lighting on an illumination-neutral portrait video. FlashRelight supports three complementary control modalities: envmap sequences for explicit frame-level lighting control, dynamic lighting text for semantic illumination editing, and lighting reference videos for visual lighting transfer. Training follows a low-cost hybrid strategy that combines static one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) data with generated dynamic-lighting portrait videos, covering both controlled illumination variation and realistic portrait motion. Extensive experiments show that FlashRelight achieves temporally coherent and photorealistic dynamic relighting while enabling flexible cross-video lighting transfer. Code is available at this https URL

[484] arXiv:2611.06356 [pdf, html, other]
Title: EEGDash Corpus: A Training-Ready Public Corpus for EEG Foundation Models
Kuber Shahi, Bruno Aristimunha, Arnaud Delorme
Comments: 8 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the Workshop on Machine Learning for EEG Signal Processing (MLESP 2026), IEEE BIBM 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Foundation models for electroencephalography (EEG) are pretrained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings, and their accuracy grows with that amount. Such data is hard to assemble. The largest sources are clinical archives that cannot be redistributed, and the public sources are spread over several archives, file formats, and licences. We release eegdash-corpus-v0, a training-ready corpus of 77 public EEG datasets, as the gated Hugging Face dataset EEGDash/eegdash-corpus-v0 with the SHA-256 of every file. REVE, the largest published EEG foundation model, names 89 datasets as its pretraining corpus. Twelve cannot be redistributed: four clinical archives that hold 82% of its hours, and eight under no-derivatives licences. The corpus holds the 76 others that REVE's sampling rate allows and one more from REVE's release card: 77 datasets, 14,075 hours from 7,272 subjects, 5.0 million 10-second samples and 6.21 billion tokens per epoch. Every dataset is fetched through EEGDash, converted once with REVE's recipe, and stored in its own buckets of a chunked Zarr store with its licence recorded beside it, so a model can train on the whole store or on any subset of datasets. To test that the store pretrains a model, we retrain REVE-Base from scratch twice with the authors' code, changed only in how it reads data, and score it on seven public OpenEEGBench tasks. It reaches 0.331 under linear probing and 0.273 after fine-tuning, against 0.333 and 0.325 for the released model and 0.200 and 0.205 for an untrained encoder. The converter, the conversion reports, and the loader changes are released with the corpus.

[485] arXiv:2611.06358 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Keeping Fuzzers on Duty: Repairing Fuzzing Build Breakages in Continuous Open-Source Fuzzing
Zhuang Zhao, Jiongchi Yu, Yao Zhang, Dongge Liu, Qiang Hu, Xiaohong Li, Yang Liu
Comments: 13 pages, 8 figures
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Continuous fuzzing platforms such as OSS-Fuzz provide sustained security testing for open-source projects, but long-term build breakages reduce security coverage and waste infrastructure resources. In OSS-Fuzz, around 20% of integrated projects remain in build-failure states, leaving their fuzzers off duty. These failures expose a maintenance gap between platform maintainers, who lack project-specific context, and project maintainers, who often lack fuzzing and infrastructure expertise. Existing program-repair techniques cannot be directly applied because fuzz build breakages span evolving project and infrastructure artifacts and require repeated infrastructure-aware diagnosis. We present FuzzMedic, an automated agent for fuzz build repair. FuzzMedic performs evidence-guided diagnosis across project and fuzzing-infrastructure artifacts. It explores repairs over a repair-state graph (RSG) that records the evolving workspace and build feedback. Branching and rollback enable FuzzMedic to recover from unproductive repair paths during long-horizon debugging. Candidate patches are validated to restore executable fuzz targets rather than merely suppress build failures. We evaluate FuzzMedic on 128 reproducible OSS-Fuzz build failures extracted from 1,820 real-world failures. FuzzMedic achieves a 48.44% repair rate and outperforms three representative program-repair baselines. In real-world use, it produces 29 patches merged into upstream or OSS-Fuzz main branches, including repairs for three failures that had remained unresolved for more than one year and two cases that had never built successfully.

[486] arXiv:2611.06359 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Vortex-Induced Torque in Grasping Soft Objects: Influence of Geometry and Pneumatic Parameters
Roman Mykhailyshyn, Tomohiro Motoda, Ivan Virgala, Ann Majewicz Fey, Yukiyasu Domae
Comments: Accepted for the SII
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Vortex grippers are commonly integrated into automated systems for handling objects with complex geometries in packaging, sorting, and assembling. However, their interaction with compliant objects remains difficult to predict, particularly with respect to the vortex-induced torque transmitted during grasping. This study investigates vortex-induced torque during the grasping of compliant objects and quantifies the coupled effects of supply pressure, tangential nozzle diameter, surface geometry, and curvature. The results show that increasing the tangential nozzle diameter primarily enhances the sensitivity of the generated torque to supply pressure rather than producing a uniformly higher torque. Surface geometry also strongly influences the rotational interaction, with dome-concave surfaces generally producing substantially greater torque than corresponding dome-convex surfaces, whereas the difference between cylindrical concave and convex surfaces is comparatively small. The strongest and most repeatable response was observed for a dome-concave surface exhibiting favorable object-gripper geometric matching. Among the evaluated machine-learning regression methods, Gaussian Process Regression provided the best overall predictive performance under repeated cross-validation, demonstrating that vortex-induced torque can be estimated from combined pneumatic and geometric parameters. These findings provide a basis for predicting and utilizing vortex-induced torque in the dexterous manipulation of soft objects.

[487] arXiv:2611.06364 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Estimating the Volume of a Union of Convex Bodies
Eeshan Banerjee, Aranya Kumar Bal, Debabrota Basu, Sourav Chakraborty, Debarshi Chanda, Uddalok Sarkar
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

The \textit{Union Volume Estimation problem}, i.e. yielding an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-approximation of the volume of the union of convex bodies, is a classical problem in computational geometry and formal methods.
In this paper, we first detect where and why the efficient union volume estimators with approximate sampling and PAC volume estimation oracles fail.
Specifically, we show that having only TV-distance guarantees on the approximate sampler does not suffice, and demonstrate this bottleneck by constructing the sunflower families of convex bodies.
In this context, we propose the concept of \textit{tail-controlled samplers} that can yield with high-probability almost-$\ell_{\infty}$ closeness.
Secondly, we leverage this concept to propose a generic algorithmic framework \texttt{Alpona} that properly combines a PAC volume computation and approximate point sampling oracles with tail-controls to yield an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-estimate of the union volume for any collection of convex bodies.
We show that \texttt{Alpona} needs only linear (in number of convex bodies) oracle calls to be $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-correct.
Finally, we provide a tail-controlled analysis of the Hit-and-Run sampler~\citep{lovasz2006fast}. We further provide a novel geometric analysis to improve the required walk length of Hit-and-Run.
We further instantiate \texttt{Alpona}'s correctness for the sparse frequency streams of convex bodies: a special case of the union volume estimation problem where no convex body intersects more than $\tau$ many other bodies.

[488] arXiv:2611.06365 [pdf, html, other]
Title: On the Optimality of Implicit Feedback in Markov Decision Processes over Imperfect Links
Romain Planchon, Federico Chiariotti, Federico Mason, Andrea Zanella, Deniz Gunduz
Comments: Submitted to IEEE INFOCOM 2027
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Goal-oriented communication protocols are explicitly designed to support the objectives of target applications, such as the monitoring and control of remote processes, while minimizing data traffic. This study considers a transmitter node that observes the environment state and sends it to a remote agent, which then performs control actions. This problem can be modeled as a remote Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), a subclass of decentralized POMDPs. Existing studies limit transmissions through communication costs, but neglect the effect of channel impairments and non-ideal or delayed feedback. In this work, we study the optimal joint transmission and control policies over lossy forward channels without explicit acknowledgments. We introduce \emph{revealing} policies, under which the receiver's action, observed directly by the transmitter, discloses the outcome of the forward transmission, keeping the two agents synchronized without a feedback channel. We derive sufficient conditions for the optimality of time-invariant policies in this implicit feedback regime for general POMDPs, along with strictly weaker sufficient conditions in the special case of contextual bandits. Our simulations over a family of remote POMDPs show that these conditions are conservative, and revealing policies are optimal over a substantially wider parameter range than the conditions warrant.

[489] arXiv:2611.06371 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Training-Free Character-Length Control in Summarization with Diffusion Language Models
Steffen Castle, Nils Feldhus, Christopher Ebert, Leonhard Hennig, Sebastian Möller
Comments: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference)
Journal-ref: Proceedings of EMNLP 2026, pp. 2803-2813
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Summarization with a fixed character length is important for tasks such as headline and article preview generation, where text must fit an exact space. Autoregressive language models (LMs) struggle with precise character-length control: training-based methods require task-specific fine-tuning, while zero-shot prompting strategies achieve only approximate compliance. We propose DELTA (Diffusion Expected Length Targeting Algorithm), a training-free inference-time method for masked diffusion LMs that estimates expected character length at each denoising step and dynamically inserts or removes masked positions to steer toward a target length. DELTA requires no fine-tuning and is designed for off-the-shelf masked diffusion LMs. Across three summarization benchmarks, it reduces character-length errors by an order of magnitude compared to baselines while maintaining competitive summary quality in both automatic and human evaluation.

[490] arXiv:2611.06372 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Give Up to Get More: Priors, Not Policies, Govern Test-Time Compute Allocation
Jinhyung Bae
Comments: 36 pages, 6 figures. Code, results and survey coding: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

When many inputs share a budget of repeated attempts by a large language model (LLM), a common rule gives harder inputs more. On public math, code and formal-proof samples, the best published difficulty-proportional rule captures half or more of the oracle gain on benchmarks the model mostly solves, but at most 13% on hard workloads, even given true pass rates. Because the value of one more attempt peaks at intermediate difficulty, the optimal static allocation is inverted-U and gives little to inputs that are hopeless at the current budget. In a strict survey of 221 LLM allocation papers, at least 13 give the hardest inputs the most attempts; their easier settings sit at budgets where this is near-optimal, so the cost appears on harder workloads. Acting on it requires knowing which inputs are solvable, so information, not the policy, drives the gain. With a verifier and a prior from a related model's past runs on the same inputs, Thompson Sampling raises the solved share on the hardest workload from 14% to 27%; without such a prior, no policy we tested beats round-robin. For the policies we tested, the gain vanishes between prior rank correlations of about 0.3 and 0.55, which cheap text-based priors barely reach on the weakest models, and it requires a verifier whose false acceptances are rare relative to the pass rate. On new Qwen2.5 samples the pattern holds, and tempering the prior avoids losses on easy workloads. We turn these results into a decision guide.

[491] arXiv:2611.06373 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Reassessing Dataset Quality and Fine-Tuning Practices for Vulnerability Detection on PrimeVul dataset
Norbert Sándor Szolnoki, Gábor Antal
Comments: Presented at EASE 2026 AI Models/Data track: this https URL
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Recent studies report promising results from supervised fine-tuning of pre-trained code language models for automated vulnerability detection on benchmarks such as PrimeVul. In this paper, we present a large-scale empirical evaluation of both model performance and dataset quality in this setting.
We systematically fine-tune three widely used encoder models (CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, and UniXCoder) across five imbalance mitigation strategies, extensive hyperparameter sweeps, and multiple random seeds, resulting in 770 independent training runs.
Our results reveal a consistent pattern. While standard metrics such as F1 and ROC-AUC occasionally suggest improvements, security-critical and calibration-aware measures tell a different story. Matthews Correlation Coefficient remains near zero, predicted probabilities are poorly calibrated, and evaluation under strict false-positive constraints reveals high false-negative rates. Neither imbalance handling, threshold optimization, nor post-hoc calibration recovers a meaningful discriminative signal.
We also conduct a data quality assessment of the PrimeVul benchmark and identify structural issues such as minimal semantic differences between vulnerable and fixed functions, and annotation noise introduced by commit-level labeling.
These findings suggests that the PrimeVul dataset, in its current form, presents significant challenges for reliable AI-based vulnerability detection in software engineering with the methodologies we used. Our study highlights the need for more robust dataset design, improved evaluation protocols, and rethinking of fine-tuning practices for security-critical tasks.

[492] arXiv:2611.06374 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Corralling AI Risks with Grassroots Contracts
Ehud Shapiro
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)

AI's inflection point is a fountain of alarming risks. Digital platforms in particular are vulnerable to three major AI risks, as those in control of global platforms cede control to AI, of the algorithms, of membership and of content: (1) AI control of global platforms, social and economic, used by the majority of humanity, resulting in the majority of humanity becoming vulnerable to AI control. (2) Unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously on social and economic digital platforms, side-by-side with humans, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals, operating under unknown restraints without accountability or culpability. (3) Unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, with people unable to distinguish them from genuine content and with their producers evading accountability and culpability.
Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two and show how they corral these major AI risks: (1) AI control of global platforms. (2) Unaccountable AI agents. (3) Unattributed deepfakes.

[493] arXiv:2611.06377 [pdf, html, other]
Title: NanoKV: High-Ratio KV Cache Compression for Autoregressive Video Generation
Jiacheng Lu, Haoyi Zhu, Sipei Yi, Enze Xie, Cheng Zhuo, Yu Li
Comments: 25 pages, 13 figures. Project page: this https URL . Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Autoregressive video models rely on historical key-value (KV) caches to preserve scene consistency over extended rollouts, making KV storage and repeated attention over history a growing memory and computational bottleneck. Aggressive compression can degrade generation quality, while reconstructing full-dimensional KV leaves attention computation largely unchanged. We introduce NanoKV, a frozen-backbone framework for generation-aware high-ratio KV compression. NanoKV exploits redundancy across tokens and attention heads by storing shared content in cluster centers and encoding joint head-channel residuals into low-bit coefficients. Crucially, NanoKV uses different fitting objectives for Keys and Values according to their distinct roles in attention: Key decoders are optimized to preserve downstream block outputs, whereas Value encoders and decoders are fitted for faithful reconstruction through the deployed quantization path. Building on the same compressed representation, the optional NanoKV-Fast variant reuses the stored coefficients for mixed-dimensional attention, reducing computation without modifying the video backbone. Across three autoregressive video backbones, NanoKV consistently improves the quality-storage trade-off. On HY-WorldPlay, NanoKV achieves $26.09\times$ effective KV compression, nearly twice that of KVTC, while improving PSNR by 1.0 dB. NanoKV-Fast retains $20.53\times$ effective compression and achieves an approximately $1.15\times$ end-to-end speedup over KVTC.

[494] arXiv:2611.06378 [pdf, html, other]
Title: UniLoop: Unified Loop Closure Detection from Retrieval to Geometric Verification and Relative Pose Estimation
Jingwen Yu, Pengyu Wang, Jin Wu, Weinan Chen, Ping Tan, Hong Zhang
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Loop closure detection conventionally cascades separate models for global retrieval, geometric verification, and relative pose estimation, leading to redundant computation and disconnected visual representations. We propose UniLoop, a unified framework that reuses the hierarchical representations of the pretrained geometric foundation model throughout this pipeline. A shared image encoder produces features for compact global descriptors; the same features are passed to the cross-view decoder for pairwise verification; and the original geometric predictions provide relative camera constraints for pose-graph optimization. Experiments on place recognition, loop verification, and relative pose estimation show that UniLoop improves loop-closure robustness and accuracy while reducing redundant backbone computation relative to modular pipelines. UniLoop achieves the best Recall@10 on MSLS (96.6) and Pitts30k (99.3) among the compared methods, while its verification branch reaches 95.63 AP and 96.29 ROC-AUC, surpassing the existing geometric verification baselines.

[495] arXiv:2611.06380 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Does Context Compression Preserve Refusal Alignment?
Anthony Nguyen, Wenjun Lin
Comments: Presented at Canadian AI 2026
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Context compression reduces inference cost by encoding inputs into compact representations while preserving semantic content. An open question is whether semantic preservation alone is sufficient to maintain downstream behaviours such as refusal alignment. We investigate this question and find that encoder-based compression systematically weakens refusal behaviour in instruction-tuned language models, despite high reconstruction fidelity. This effect persists across model families and compression architectures. Mechanistic analysis shows that compression attenuates activation along the decoder's learned refusal direction. We further explore Memory Steering, a lightweight inference-time intervention that restores refusal rates to near-baseline levels without retraining and operates entirely in compressed representation space. These results demonstrate that semantic preservation does not guarantee behavioural preservation under compression, highlighting the need to explicitly preserve alignment-relevant features in compression-aware systems.

[496] arXiv:2611.06381 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LegalEvolver: Agentic Legal Judgment Prediction via Rubric-Guided Self-Evolution
Xinyu Yang, Jiejun Tan, Chenlong Deng, Chenghao Zhang, Tongyu Wen, Zhicheng Dou
Comments: 20 pages, 5 figures
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

As LLM-based agents develop, they have been increasingly applied in the legal domain. Legal Judgment Prediction~(LJP) requires models to conduct multi-step reasoning and external legal evidence retrieval. Existing legal search agents' performance is often constrained by the quality of retrieval queries. They often formulate queries directly from the initial user request, overlooking latent legal issues and legally salient details. To address this issue, we propose \emph{LegalEvolver}, a query optimization framework specifically designed to generate legally informative queries for LJP-oriented retrieval. Sampling high-quality optimized queries and their corresponding search trajectories is challenging, as relying solely on unguided high-temperature rollouts is both inefficient and constrained by the model's initial capabilities. We therefore heuristically optimize queries as seeds, improving the efficiency of trajectory generation. Furthermore, we summarize rollout experience into rubrics and use them to guide multi-round iterative self-evolution. Iteratively performing rubric optimization and rubric-guided RL enables the model to surpass its initial performance ceiling. End-to-end performance on extensive benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of query optimization on LJP. Comparisons with direct SFT followed by RL demonstrate the effectiveness of rubric guidance. Evolving rubrics further outperform fixed rubrics, confirming the benefits of self-evolution.

[497] arXiv:2611.06382 [pdf, html, other]
Title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents
Xilin Xia
Comments: 61 pages, 12 figures, 13 tables, plus 19 pages of Supporting Information
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Dynamical Systems (math.DS); Geophysics (physics.geo-ph)

Dooge asked whether hydrology has laws at the catchment scale. We ask whether a low-dimensional system built under physical laws can match the accuracy of neural networks that outperform process-based models on the same inputs. Three laws constrain a lumped catchment model. Conservation makes it a flux-connected storage network, dissipation fixes the sign of every flux and aggregation determines how the unresolved composition enters the fluxes, through effective laws over threshold distributions and a memory of the forcing. These laws admit four kinds of refinement. A parsimonious model under them, CaRT (11 parameters per catchment), is refined in a loop assisted by AI agents. Each refinement addresses an observed deficit through a hypothesis from the literature. The result, CaRT+, has fourteen states, 35 parameters per catchment and no daily neural network. Most refinements follow from aggregation over thresholds or from variables that carry no water but modulate fluxes. On 602 British and 593 US gauged catchments, single CaRT+ models reach median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.863 and 0.765 in held-out years. A stateful LSTM reaches 0.869 and 0.751 and an entity-aware LSTM 0.862 and 0.754, while three-seed LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003-0.012 in median paired NSE. On 505 drier Australian gauged catchments unused in development, single CaRT+ models reach 0.778 against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs. The results suggest that catchment-scale laws exist as laws of form, with the constitutive families shared and only their parameters learned.

[498] arXiv:2611.06384 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation
Jatin Agrawal, Radhika Mamidi
Comments: 27 pages, 1 figure, includes appendices
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Typed decision models offer structured choices, scores, and probabilities for low-cost automated evaluation. We present a controlled audit of presentation sensitivity in Jev, Clef Flash, and Perplexity Decider across native choice and score interfaces. Across six datasets with 9,000 multiply annotated humor, helpfulness, and summarization items, we collect 702,000 judgments under interventions that vary positions, identifiers, authorship claims, endorsements, decision framing, and rating rubrics while preserving the evaluated texts. Jev's second-position probability advantage reaches 6.11 percentage points on summaries; reversing reader endorsements changes Perplexity's selected humor text on 40.40% of pairs; and rejection framing reduces Clef's summary agreement with human preferences by 23.36 points. Rating formats also shift score levels while often preserving rankings. Across these findings, repeatability, presentation robustness, and human alignment emerge as distinct properties of an evaluator. Reliable use therefore requires validating the decisions and score interpretations on which an evaluation pipeline depends.

[499] arXiv:2611.06385 [pdf, other]
Title: Spatial Differences Analysis of Nodal Frequency Considering Frequency-Voltage Coupling
Xiaodan Li, Donghai Zhu, Zining Liu, Zhu Guo, Jiabing Hu, Hong Rao
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

The rising penetration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) brings rich control dynamics that can amplify spatial differences in nodal frequency through frequency-voltage (F-V) coupling. Existing analyses often neglect voltage dynamics or only examine the aggregate frequency, leading to overoptimistic evaluation of frequency security. To address these drawbacks, this paper develops a unified model of synchronous generators (SGs), grid-following (GFL)-IBRs, and grid-forming (GFM)-IBRs based on the magnitude and phase dynamics of equivalent internal electromotive force (EMF). Integrating these source models with network equations yields a sparse implicit closed-loop model, which fully captures the device-network F-V coupling without transfer-matrix inversion. Then, the obtained nodal responses are decomposed into common and differential modes. Using this decomposition, coupling indices and pole-residue analysis reveal how F-V coupling can amplify spatial differences in nodal frequency and how source configuration and parameters modify this effect. Finally, case studies on the modified IEEE 39-bus and 118-bus test systems validate the proposed model and demonstrate its computational efficiency.

[500] arXiv:2611.06386 [pdf, other]
Title: Shoot on (Core)Sight: Re-enabling Secure Debug on the RP2350 with Photon-Emission Microscopy and Laser Fault Injection
Antoine Plin
Comments: pre-print
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Fault-resistant policy storage does not guarantee fault-resistant enforcement. We demonstrated this distinction on the RP2350A4 using differential photon-emission microscopy (PEM) and laser fault injection (LFI). PEM narrowed the area for laser scanning, which found two sites where pulses set the DEBUGEN bits enabling core~1 Secure debug. An online attack sequence using only Serial Wire Debug (SWD) feedback restored sustained access. After rescue reset, the sequence recovered a 128-bit test secret. This reset reloads the secret's runtime page lock from a stored policy that permits Secure reads and prevents user firmware from tightening the lock.

[501] arXiv:2611.06387 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Partially Dynamic Algorithms for Single-Source Temporal Paths
Davide Bilò, Bartłomiej Bosek, Jadwiga Czyżewska, Evangelos Kipouridis, Karol Węgrzycki, Anna Zych-Pawlewicz
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We present efficient partially dynamic algorithms for maintaining earliest arrival times from a fixed source in temporal digraphs with $n$ vertices.
For the incremental scenario where updates are arc insertions, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the total number of arcs added to the arc-less graph. For the decremental scenario where updates are arc removals, our algorithm has a constant query time and requires a total update time of $O(n + m \log m)$, where $m$ is the number of arcs in the graph upon its initialization. We also consider earliest-arrival queries with an arbitrary departure-time threshold and develop an incremental algorithm with $O(n+\Delta_s m\log m)$ total update time, $O(\log m)$ query time, and $O(n+m)$ space, where $\Delta_s$ is the number of distinct departure times of arcs leaving the source. All of our algorithms are also capable of reporting an earliest arrival path from the source to the queried vertex $v$ in constant time per edge once the earliest arrival time at $v$ is known.
We complement our positive results with conditional lower bounds based on the Online Boolean Matrix-Vector Multiplication conjecture (a.k.a. OMv conjecture). For both the incremental and the decremental scenarios, we show the non-existence of an algorithm with $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ amortized update time and $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ amortized query time, even if the algorithm is randomized and latencies on the arcs are uniform. For arbitrary departure-time queries, we also establish an OMv-based conditional lower bound showing that our incremental algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors on dense temporal graphs. Thus, efficient total running time is essentially the best outcome we can get. Our conditional lower bounds hold also for the case of undirected temporal graphs.

[502] arXiv:2611.06389 [pdf, html, other]
Title: MA-Mesh: Resilient Multi-Agent Collaboration via Role-based Self-Healing
JunYong Lee, Woo Kyung Kim, Honguk Woo
Comments: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (Main)
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Effective collaboration in multi-agent systems requires mechanisms for coordination and adaptability in dynamic and uncertain environments. However, existing multi-agent systems rarely model resilience explicitly, instead relying on ad-hoc output correction that limits systematic, runtime management of robustness. In this work, we propose Multi-Agent Mesh (MA-Mesh), a framework that constructs a role-based self-healing layer on top of a collaboration pattern. Specifically, MA-Mesh generates resilience-aware system specifications and synthesizes them into executable multi-agent policy code. To enhance resilience, we introduce two self-healing mechanisms: Cross-agent reflection, a mechanism that allows agents to evaluate not only their own outcomes but also the performance of their peers, enabling informed behavioral adjustments and collective policy refinement; Role-based failover, a strategy which dynamically reassigns roles and enables agents to substitute for one another when sub-tasks fail or agents underperform, ensuring continuity of task execution. Experimental results across diverse tasks (e.g., software development, tool use, scientific reasoning) demonstrate that MA-Mesh significantly outperforms existing multi-agent systems in both task performance and robustness under system uncertainty.

[503] arXiv:2611.06394 [pdf, html, other]
Title: KolTa: A Physics-Informed Active Learning Framework for Formulation Discovery with Limited Data
Boyong Tang, Tao Wang, Lei Yang
Comments: 21 pages, including 11 pages of supplementary material; 4 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Finding high-performing formulations is difficult when few have been measured and experimental budgets are limited. We propose KolTa, an active learning framework that selects batches to discover the top 5% of formulations at a target temperature under a fixed query budget. KolTa combines a three-stage predictor of component contributions, role-conditioned interactions, and anchored temperature response with task-specific soft physics constraints. Its Physics-Residual-Calibrated Upper Confidence Bound (PRC-UCB) acquisition rule combines predicted utility, ensemble disagreement, and a target-temperature physics residual, with nonnegative exploration weights fitted to out-of-fold signed errors. We evaluate the framework on three measured tasks and one simulated task covering binary-mixture viscosity, drug solubility, ionic-liquid viscosity, and electrolyte conductivity. KolTa ranks first or second in mean area under the learning curve (AULC) on every task and outperforms seven of the eight comparator strategies in paired tests, winning 75 of 78 paired comparisons across tasks and seeds against those seven strategies. Across the three measured tasks, its largest gap to the best mean AULC is 0.032, compared with at least 0.056 for every comparator. On Drug, reaching 80% average recovery of the remaining targets across drugs requires an estimated median of 348 additional formulation queries, about 18% fewer than the fastest comparator. Researchers can adapt the framework to diverse formulation problems through component roles and physical constraints.

[504] arXiv:2611.06395 [pdf, html, other]
Title: GIST: Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection for Offline RLVR
Xuliang Huang, Tianxiang Zhao, Chengwei Qin, Yao Shu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Offline reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on a fixed pool of sampled responses and typically supervises every token of every response, although responses and tokens are not equally informative. We study which ones to supervise through the Gibbs-optimal policy of KL-regularized RLVR, which offline training targets, and measure the mismatch between a policy and this target with a bidirectional KL divergence. At the reference policy, this mismatch factorizes exactly and separates the two outcomes: correct responses contribute mainly through the forward term, concentrated on their low-probability tokens, and incorrect responses through the reverse term, concentrated on the responses the policy generates often and on their high-probability tokens. Based on this analysis, we propose GIST (Gibbs-Targeted Hierarchical Data Selection), a two-level selection method that approximates these principles with signals available before training. GIST uses the sampling temperature to select correct responses on-policy and incorrect responses near the policy's mode, and it uses the initial policy's token probabilities to supervise only the tokens where the mismatch lies. Applied to two offline training objectives, GIST raises the average accuracy over GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP for all three models under both objectives. In a controlled comparison on Qwen3-0.6B/GSM8K, it outperforms seven selection baselines that choose from the same candidates while supervising 66.6% fewer tokens than training on all candidates of the same prompts.

[505] arXiv:2611.06397 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse
Yuxing Peng, Zhiqing Tang, Weijia Jia
Comments: 36 pages, 6 figures, 34 tables
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches. To find where a small repair budget should be spent, we vary the chunks around the answer-bearing one (the target) across three 7B-8B models and four datasets of dialogue memory, open-domain QA and API documentation. Reuse loses 19-100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the other chunks are of the same kind as the target. Because the recoverable damage is spread over these other chunks, restoring a few of them recovers little, and the budget is better spent on the target. This works through contextual compatibility: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings tested, although the recomputed KV stays far from the full-prefill KV. Question attention over reused caches, however, selects the target in at most 18.8% of development questions. A retriever finds it more often, and recomputing its top chunk after moving it next to the question significantly beats InfoFlow-style reordering at the same 5% budget in six of nine open-domain QA and API-documentation settings. On dialogue memory, though, recomputing chunks never significantly beats the token-level selector chosen for each setting.

[506] arXiv:2611.06402 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Interpretable Text Embeddings Based on Hierarchical Questions
Kohei Oda, Po-Min Chuang, Kiyoaki Shirai, Natthawut Kertkeidkachorn
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

QA-based text embeddings represent texts as vectors consisting of 1/0 answers to yes/no questions. Although these embeddings provide detailed information for interpretation and achieve high task performance, they often require humans to examine a large number of questions. Furthermore, the relationship between the number of questions and the appropriate level of question granularity has not been sufficiently studied. To address these challenges, we propose a method for constructing hierarchical questions for text embeddings. As the hierarchy deepens, questions become more specific and their number increases. During interpretation, we reduce the number of questions that humans need to examine by replacing questions at deeper levels with aligned questions at shallower levels. The question hierarchy is constructed through recursive clustering, contrastive prompting, and question alignment. Experimental results on general-purpose tasks show that our method improves interpretability while maintaining task performance. It is also found that, when only a limited number of questions are available, questions at shallower levels tend to achieve higher task performance than those at deeper levels, even with the same number of questions.

[507] arXiv:2611.06403 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Ruby-OPD: Enhancing Pronunciation Controllability and Accuracy for Flow-Matching Text-to-Speech via On-Policy Distillation
Rui Hu, Xiaolong Lin, Zhenpeng Zhan
Comments: 5 pages, 3 tables, work in progress
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Achieving both high pronunciation accuracy and fine-grained controllability remains a central challenge in Japanese text-to-speech (TTS), as Japanese is an unsegmented language mixing logographic Kanji and phonographic Kana with extensive polyphony. Traditional cascaded systems convert text into phoneme sequences via a front-end, ensuring pronunciation control but discarding lexical semantics and prosodic cues in surface orthography. Conversely, recent zero-shot TTS models directly consume raw orthographic text to improve naturalness, yet suffer from polyphone errors and lack explicit pronunciation control. To bridge this gap, we propose a two-stage framework for flow-matching TTS. First, we investigate Ruby text representations with orthography perturbation to jointly preserve surface forms and target pronunciations for reliable control. Second, we introduce On-Policy Distillation (OPD) on large-scale text-only corpora to enhance pronunciation accuracy on raw orthographic text without paired speech. On the Joyo-Kanji-Yomi benchmark, our model achieves 97.13% Accuracy, 2.02% Target PER, 0.70% Sentence PER, and 4.21% Sentence CER under raw text while retaining strong controllability.

[508] arXiv:2611.06408 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A volume-conserving ALE continuous Galerkin method with residual-based Dirichlet--Neumann fluxes for nonlinear free-surface waves
Fan Wang, Yinhua Xia, Yan Xu
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We develop an arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian continuous Galerkin finite element method for two-dimensional fully nonlinear free-surface potential flow. An isoparametric finite element method computes the interior potential on the current fluid domain, while a residual-based Dirichlet--Neumann flux drives the surface evolution. The residual-based flux satisfies a global discrete balance inherited from the interior variational formulation. When combined with compatible mesh motion, surface projection, and quadrature, this balance yields conservation of the discrete fluid volume at the semi-discrete level. An optional volume-conserving sixth-order surface dissipation controls high-frequency oscillations, and the surface equations are advanced with fourth-order Runge--Kutta integration, updating the mesh and interior solution at every stage. Numerical experiments confirm the expected spatial convergence for linear free-surface waves and demonstrate reduced mesh sensitivity for nonlinear waves over flat and curved bottoms. A rotating-wavemaker example further illustrates the treatment of moving solid boundaries.

[509] arXiv:2611.06409 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Zero-Shot Coordination among LLM Agents
Adrian Hayler, Shashank Reddy Chirra, Andrei Lupu, Johannes Forkel, Bidipta Sarkar, Siheng Feng, Jakob Foerster
Comments: NeurIPS 2026 Poster. ICLR 26 MALGAI Workshop Oral. The first two authors contributed equally
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

We study zero-shot coordination (ZSC), where independently developed agents must coordinate at test time. While ZSC has been well studied in the RL literature, far less is known about the performance of LLM agents despite their increasing deployment in such settings. Existing work on LLM coordination often relies on specialised scaffolding that independently developed agents are unlikely to share in practice. Moreover, evaluations on complex environments (e.g., Hanabi) make it difficult to pinpoint the sources of coordination failure. In contrast, we focus on simple, general-purpose scaffolds in minimal environments designed to isolate specific coordination challenges. Our results show that even in these controlled settings, frontier LLM agents struggle to coordinate, largely due to limited understanding of the coordination problem and weak reasoning about their partner's beliefs. While LLMs introduce semantic information as an additional axis for coordination, they nonetheless fail to exploit this structure effectively. Towards this, we propose Coordination-friendly definitions (CFDs) as a principled approach for enabling robust coordination among LLM agents. Finally, we show that CFDs can be discovered automatically, removing the need for manual engineering. Code is available at this https URL.

[510] arXiv:2611.06410 [pdf, other]
Title: Polynomial $(2α+\varepsilon)$- and Quadratic $4$-Approximation Algorithms for the Biased Traveling Salesman Problem in Bipartitioned Networks
Jingyang Zhao, Trung Q. Duong, Een-Kee Hong, Hyundong Shin
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is one of the fundamental problems in combinatorial optimization that asks for a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle in a complete undirected graph with $N$ vertices. For the metric TSP, where edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality, a long line of work has produced constant-factor approximation algorithms, culminating in the best-known approximation ratio $\alpha<3/2-10^{-36}$. The biased TSP (BTSP) generalizes the metric TSP to bipartitioned networks: the vertex set is partitioned into two subsets, edge costs satisfy the triangle inequality within each subset, while edges crossing the partition may violate it by a certain bias factor. This model captures heterogeneous routing scenarios in which distances are metric only locally but may be distorted across different regions or vertex types. Previously, the only known result for the BTSP was a $7/2$-approximation algorithm with running time $O(N^3)$. In this paper, we present two new approximation algorithms that significantly improve the state of the art. The first achieves an approximation ratio of $2\alpha+\varepsilon$ (strictly less than $3$) in polynomial time $N^{O(1)}$ for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, where the exponent grows at least linearly with $1/\varepsilon$. The second achieves a $4$-approximation in only $O(N^2)$ running time, reducing the previous cubic-time bound by a full polynomial factor. These advances directly support emerging networked systems---including multi-tier 6G architectures and hybrid quantum-classical networks---where cross-region transitions incur biased and non-metric overheads.

[511] arXiv:2611.06412 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Bag of Tricks for Defending Deep Learning-based Face Recognition Pipelines against Backdoor Attacks
Quentin Le Roux, Marti Jimenez, Yannick Teglia, Philippe Loubet Moundi
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

The protection of mature, multi-stage Face Recognition Systems is crucial to system providers. This technical report targets the threat model most relevant to industry practitioners: although model training is performed in-house, training data is sourced from possibly-compromised third parties. Given this setting, we present three practical defense "tricks" against data poisoning-based backdoor attacks. The first operates at training-time, detecting poisoned identities during training or prior to a pipeline's deployment. The last two operate at inference-time, filtering suspicious inputs before an answer can be sent back to a potential attacker. Each method is presented with their motivation, algorithms and computational impact, and evaluated on realistic face recognition workloads. Our goal is to provide actionable hardening techniques to system providers.

[512] arXiv:2611.06414 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Twists and Turns: A Graph-Based Benchmark and Framework for Long-Term Memory in Exploration Tasks
Chongyuan Dai, Yaling Shen, Zirui Song, Junfeng Liao, Jinpeng Hu, Xiuying Chen
Comments: 29 pages, 5 figures
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Long-term problem-solving processes, such as scientific research and software development, proceed along an evolving trial-and-error trajectory toward a central goal. We term these \textit{exploration tasks}, which require models to remember not only facts but also how solutions are tested against intermediate outcomes and early attempts are continually revised or revived. However, existing long-term memory research focuses on factual recall and updates, overlooking the interconnected nature of exploration. We observe that exploration processes naturally form graphs, with branching approaches linked by revisions and reconsiderations. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{LExMem}, a graph-guided benchmark designed to evaluate \underline{\textsc{Mem}}ory in \underline{\textsc{L}}ong-term \underline{\textsc{Ex}}ploration tasks. We model exploration processes as graphs and introduce an evolutionary mechanism to increase their structural complexity, yielding 224 dialogues and 2,018 question-answer instances derived from graph structures. Building on the same insight, we propose \textsc{LExGraph}, a graph-based memory framework that incrementally organizes dialogues into interconnected memory nodes and retrieves evidence through hybrid retrieval and neighbor expansion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that \textsc{LExMem} poses a significant challenge to existing retrieval- and memory-based systems, whereas \textsc{LExGraph} achieves superior performance and generalizes effectively to external benchmarks. Codes and datasets are available at this https URL.

[513] arXiv:2611.06415 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Entropogram-guided Visual Realignment Decoding: Capturing the Rhythm of Multimodal Reasoning
Jiaqi Deng, Zhe Fu, Yakun Chen, Dichang Zhang, Zonghan Wu, Xiaoshui Huang, Huan Huo, Guandong Xu
Comments: 22 pages, 9 figures
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Multimedia (cs.MM)

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress on cross-modal reasoning tasks, yet they continue to suffer from hallucinations in long-chain reasoning processes. In this work, we revisit hallucination in MLLMs from the perspective of reasoning generation dynamics. We argue that entropy is not merely a static measure of uncertainty but a structured signal that reflects how modality information is integrated throughout decoding. Through systematic analysis, we identify two characteristic entropy patterns associated with hallucination behaviors: (1) a generally high-confidence regime corresponds to premature convergence to inappropriate multimodal interactions; and (2) local abrupt entropy transitions are associated with reasoning instability and hallucination onset. Building on these observations, we propose an entropy-aware self-introspective framework for MLLM reasoning. Our method continuously tracks entropy dynamics during decoding and performs targeted visual re-alignment when suspicious hallucination states are detected, encouraging the model to re-examine salient visual evidence at critical reasoning stages. Extensive experiments across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks spanning nine distinct evaluation settings demonstrate that our approach delivers robust improvements in reasoning accuracy and hallucination robustness, while providing new insights into the generation dynamics underlying MLLM failures. The code is available at: this https URL.

[514] arXiv:2611.06422 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Unaligned Image Guided Denoising via Cross-modal Conditional Flow Matching
Runmin Zhang, Linshan Li, Si-Yuan Cao, Zhu Yu, Lingyu Zhu, Huaqi Zhang, Hui-Liang Shen
Comments: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

This work presents UGD-FM, a novel unaligned image guided denoising framework based on cross-modal conditional flow matching. Unlike previous approaches that assume spatially aligned inputs or only handle small-baseline rectified pairs, we address a more challenging setting where severe target noise and large-range two-dimensional cross-modal misalignment coexist. Specifically, we formulate guided denoising as a progressive flow matching process, allowing image restoration and aligned guidance aggregation to mutually reinforce each other. To support efficient few-step inference, we introduce a stage-focused and inference-consistent training strategy that focuses on task-critical denoising stages, and mitigates the training-inference mismatch. We further propose adaptive sparse guidance propagation for efficient and reliable large-range matching, regularized by perceptual and geometric auxiliary losses. Experiments demonstrate that UGD-FM achieves state-of-the-art denoising performance with only one or two inference steps, and is compatible with modern single-image restoration backbones.

[515] arXiv:2611.06425 [pdf, html, other]
Title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
Baoyou Chen, Ruiqiao Mei, Guancong Lin, Tao Song, Weihao Yuan, Qun Liu, Siyu Zhu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00$\times$ and 5.71$\times$ decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03$\times$ and 3.67$\times$ for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48$\times$. Code is publicly available at this https URL.

[516] arXiv:2611.06428 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Partially Interpretable Decision Trees
Ludovic Schwartz, Federico Berton, Tim van Erven
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Partially interpretable models extend simple interpretable models with the option to defer complicated inputs to an accurate but uninterpretable black-box model. By deferring more inputs, the model gets more accurate; by deferring fewer, it gets more interpretable. Existing procedures to train such partially interpretable models build on linear models or decision rules. We propose three algorithms for decision trees: a partially interpretable extension of the existing Branches algorithm, which performs exact search to optimize the tree; a conversion algorithm that we run on top of standard CART, which is computationally more efficient; and a generalized CART whose splitting criterion takes into account the option to defer while growing the tree. Perhaps surprisingly, the performance of the three algorithms is similar across many realworld datasets. We can explain this through a formal bound on the potential gain of smart tree construction, provided the black box accuracy is sufficiently homogeneous across the domain. We also construct a synthetic dataset where the accuracy of the black box is deliberately inhomogeneous. There, our deferral-aware generalization of CART does outperform regular CART and matches the performance of exact search. Finally, we evaluate an application to concept bottleneck models. Partially interpretable decision trees can replace uninterpretable neural networks after the bottleneck. On undeferred inputs, the model is fully interpretable, and deferring preserves accuracy.

[517] arXiv:2611.06429 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Neural Network-based Control Systems with Application to Flight Control, From Classical Neural Control to Reinforcement Learning
Seyyed Ali Emami, Paolo Castaldi, Mohammad Narimani, Mahdi Shahrajabian, Mostafa Ezabadi, Alireza Ettelaei, Hosein Saadatmanesh, Zahra Shahbazi
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

This book provides a comprehensive and systematic exploration of neural network-based intelligent control systems for aerospace applications, bridging foundational theory with practical implementation. It is structured into two primary parts: Part I covers model-based control design, detailing Feedback Error Learning (FEL), pseudocontrol strategies, and neural backstepping for strict-feedback systems, along with practical refinements such as learning rule modifications, composite learning, and discrete-time formulations, all grounded in rigorous Lyapunov stability analysis. Part II introduces model-free control, laying the groundwork for Reinforcement Learning and Approximate Dynamic Programming. Throughout, theoretical concepts are solidified through detailed case studies on quadrotor UAVs, fixed-wing aircraft (GTM), satellites, and hypersonic flight vehicles, complete with performance metrics, parameter sensitivity analyses, and discussions of actuator faults, input constraints, and wind disturbances, making the book an invaluable resource for students and practicing engineers seeking to design, simulate, and analyze intelligent flight control systems.

[518] arXiv:2611.06433 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
Benlei Cui, Chunyang Chai, Yiliang Zhang, Xiaoqian Xia, Chengwen Yao, Song Li, Longtao Huang, Yuwen Zhai, Haiwen Hong
Comments: 28 pages, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL . Model: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain prone to visual hallucinations when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. One line of post-training methods constructs visual contrasts through image retrieval, generation, or editing to improve fine-grained perception. However, these contrasts are not built around the model's own hallucinations, making it difficult to ensure that supervision targets its actual perceptual confusions. Another line suppresses hallucinated outputs through response correction or preference learning under fixed image conditions, but leaves the design of supervision signals on the image-input side underexplored. Inspired by how humans correct misconceptions, we introduce DreamRealm, a post-training framework that explores diverse latent hallucinated responses, minimally edits original images to make them valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. Our data construction pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. Using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B, we construct the Realized Hallucination Dataset (RealmSet). Our training objective, RealmMatch, constructs a likelihood score matrix across image--response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B model, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, including gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy. Together with ablation studies on data construction and training methods, these results demonstrate that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and mitigating hallucinations.

[519] arXiv:2611.06434 [pdf, html, other]
Title: EviSeek: An Evidence-Centric Agentic Framework for Embodied Active Information Seeking
Jintao Li, Zhiyong Cao, Baihua Xiao, Yu Bai, Börje F. Karlsson
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Active embodied question answering requires agents to acquire evidence through viewpoint changes and physical interaction. The central challenge is to avoid undirected interaction: taking plausible actions without specifying what evidence they should reveal for answering the question. Action plans and accumulated histories alone can leave the informational purpose of an interaction implicit. We introduce EviSeek, a training-free framework that makes question-derived evidence demands explicit acquisition objectives, linking observation-conditioned actions and selectively retained evidence to the information the agent seeks. On 3,436 ESI-Bench questions, EviSeek improves accuracy over the Single-model agent by 7.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL-32B and 3.7 points with Gemini 3.1 Pro, while improving visual-support-weighted accuracy and reducing mean token usage. These findings support making the informational purpose of interaction explicit, with action selection and evidence retention organized around what the agent needs to learn to answer the question.

[520] arXiv:2611.06436 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Hardwired Distributed Processing Units for Inference: Neural Decisions at the Sensor that Free the Host
Raj Mali
Comments: 8 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Companion to arXiv:2610.33107 and arXiv:2610.38752
Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We show that a hardwired distributed processing unit (HDPU) can take a neural decision at the sensor and so remove the inference from the host. Built for zebra-crossing detection on a low-cost Artix-7 FPGA, the unit decides on every camera frame in a fixed 2,269,477 clock cycles (34.04 ms depends upon Fpga clk ), inside the 37.49-ms frame period, and on the board it returns the same scores and decisions as its bit-exact software model on all 639 test images. The whole detection path, from camera pixels to decision, takes 1,814 LUTs, with no processor, no operating system and no full-resolution frame store. When the unit answers instead of reporting "not sure", 95.7% of its answers on street photographs are correct, and a hardware contrast stage lifts accuracy on camera-like dashcam frames from 47.7% to 78.2%. The host is spared all of the inference: 8.13 ms of a core in every frame period, where a full-precision ResNet-18 would need more than a frame period even on 16 threads. It also receives 16 bytes per frame instead of 614,400, 38,400 times less. The unit is an 80x60-pixel pipeline feeding a four-layer binarized CNN with 93,408 one-bit weights, verified bit-exactly from a Python model through RTL simulation to the board. Earlier HDPUs did pre-processing (edges, corners, steering); this one shows that the decision itself can move to the sensor.

[521] arXiv:2611.06438 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Understanding the Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
Nuo-Jing Liang, Xiao-Tong Yuan, Pan Zhou
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning substantially improves Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization mechanism remains theoretically underexplored. We study CoT as compositional OOD generalization: the target task lacks complete reasoning trajectories or direct input-output pairs, while training provides only in-distribution (ID) atomic step data. We show that CoT generalizes by repeatedly applying a shared single-step predictor to compose reusable ID transitions. Theoretically, let $T$ denote the number of reasoning steps in the target task, $n$ the number of training samples per sub-task, and $k$ the number of output tokens per step; then the OOD task risk is controlled by the sum of the ID sub-task risks, scaled by a coefficient of order $\mathcal{O}(k)$ that is independent of $T$, although the summed risk itself may still grow with $T$. A Rademacher-complexity analysis further shows that the estimation term is of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T/n})$, rather than linear in $T$, due to predictor sharing under a uniform capacity control on the shared class.
