For autoregressive Next-Token Prediction, the final-task risk is bounded by the best-in-class step-level risk scaled by the same coefficient of order $\mathcal{O}(k)$, plus an estimation term of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(k\sqrt{T/n}\big)$. A parity-coupled construction further shows that, for the sub-task empirical risk minimizer, the expected final-task risk is at least the best in-class risk plus $\Omega(\sqrt{T/n})$ when $T\le n$. Experiments on Atom-Task and GSM8K support the theory: CoT enables short-to-long and compositional generalization, while explicit state tracking is crucial.
Our code is available at this https URL.

[522] arXiv:2611.06441 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Graph Foundation Models Can Become Effective Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detectors
Zhuangyan Hu, Zhuoxuan Liang, Wei Li, Xiaohua Jia, Moustafa Youssef, Sumi Helal
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) relies on modeling both temporal dynamics and inter-sensor dependencies to identify complex system faults. Although graph-based detectors explicitly model sensor topologies, they train task-specific networks from scratch on limited target-domain data, remaining vulnerable to spurious correlations and unable to reuse transferable priors. While pretrained Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) offer transferable topological priors and anomaly discriminability, directly adapting them to MTSAD is hindered by cross-modal feature-topology mismatch, unreliable pseudo-anomaly supervision, and decision distortion during node-to-window aggregation. To fill these gaps, we propose a novel adaptation framework, Gfm4Mtsad, which unleashes pretrained GFMs for MTSAD. We introduce the Structure-and-Information Contract Alignment (SICA) module to bridge continuous time series and the pretrained GFM space. This module harmonizes principal subspace token projection, normal-prior-guided graph construction, and residual recovery to suppress spurious edges while retaining fine-grained temporal details. We propose a Mechanism-Aligned Pseudo-Anomaly Screening strategy (MAPS) to steer unsupervised learning. It applies localized dependency breaks while preserving empirical residuals, selecting hard negatives near the normal boundary for targeted supervision. We develop a Tail-Gated Evidence Calibration mechanism (TGEC) to eliminate node-to-window aggregation distortion. It calibrates multi-granular graph responses against normal operational references, strictly preserving benign score rankings while selectively refining extreme anomaly candidates in the tail distribution for reliable window detection and interpretable sensor evidence. Extensive evaluations with two GFM backbones demonstrate that Gfm4Mtsad achieves superior detection performance over existing baselines.

[523] arXiv:2611.06442 [pdf, html, other]
Title: TwinBridge: Digital Twin-Driven Policy and Reward Transfer for Real-World Reinforcement Learning in Laboratory Robotics
Shu'ang Sun, Yibo Qiu, Haoliang Ye, Zan Huang, Ao Tian, Kan Ding, Ronald Xu, Mingzhai Sun
Comments: 8 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Online reinforcement learning offers an effective approach to precise laboratory manipulation, yet costly real-world demonstrations and limited access to dense process rewards hinder its practical application. We present TwinBridge, a digital twin-driven framework that supplies policy initialization and dense visual rewards for real-world online learning. We construct digital twins by combining 3D Gaussian splatting with physics simulation. Here, simulator states provide task events and geometric progress under physical prerequisites and ordering constraints, yielding rewards for policy pretraining with simulated demonstrations and reinforcement learning. We distill this supervision into a visual reward model. During real-world interaction, its predictions are combined with execution history to compute dense rewards for human-in-the-loop policy refinement. Across five real-world laboratory tasks, TwinBridge achieves a final mean autonomous success rate of 98% with at most 25 minutes of real-world interaction per task. Experiments show that dense rewards improve interaction efficiency over sparse rewards, and simulation-based policy initialization further accelerates learning.

[524] arXiv:2611.06444 [pdf, html, other]
Title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
Yanli Wang, Zichen Bai, Tianyue Jiang, Kunming Shao, Junhao Shi, Xueqin Liu, Jinguo Sun, Muye Li, Tingting Bi, Yanlin Wang, Shaoqiang Zheng, Xuefei Diao, Zhuwei Zeng, Nan Duan, Peng Cao
Comments: 16 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables, including appendices
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Skills let language agents reuse experience across tasks as natural-language documents. Recent work evolves skills from interaction, but existing methods have limitations when skills evolve online. Prior methods update a skill offline from a batch of trajectories collected over many tasks. Some then adopt the new skill without any check, which can degrade the skill over time. Others keep it only if it improves performance on a held-out validation set, which is too slow and costly to run after every update. We introduce EvoGuard, a pairwise skill selector that mitigates skill degradation at low latency and cost. We first run the agent iteratively to build pools of skills and score each skill on a private test set to obtain utility labels. We pair the skills and use rejection sampling to keep only pairs with a clear utility gap. The selector is trained on the logits of two label tokens to pick the better skill. At deployment it decides in a single forward pass, which is significantly faster than evaluation on the private test set. Compared with adopting every new skill, EvoGuard improves success by 11.0% on ALFWorld, 5.9% on ScienceWorld, and 2.7% on LiveCodeBench.

[525] arXiv:2611.06445 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory
Jizhe Zhang, Ang Li, Chenheng Zhang, Yisen Wang
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Long-horizon language-model agents accumulate increasingly large interaction histories, making context compaction essential for efficient execution. Existing learned compaction methods often rely on downstream task outcomes or solver behavior, coupling training to specific tasks or agents. We introduce SumOne, a standalone summarizer trained to preserve information in agent histories through masked reconstruction. Given a summary of the expired history, a frozen reconstructor recovers randomly masked portions of the original trajectory; reconstruction quality, combined with a length penalty, provides a task-agnostic reward for optimizing the summarizer with GRPO. This yields self-supervision directly from raw trajectories, without reference summaries or downstream task execution. At inference time, only the lightweight summarizer is retained, enabling plug-and-play context compression for otherwise unchanged agents. We conduct a systematic evaluation of SumOne in long-horizon search and software-engineering tasks. SumOne reduces estimated inference cost by approximately 78\% on DeepSearchQA and 75\% on SWE-bench Verified relative to operating with full context, with absolute decreases of 0.04. The same checkpoint also transfers across downstream models and agent harnesses without additional fine-tuning.

[526] arXiv:2611.06447 [pdf, html, other]
Title: $A^3$-VLA: Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation
Shengzhe Zhang, Qi Zhang, Dazhong Shen, Chao Wang, Shaopeng Zhai, Hui Xiong
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions. However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability. To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself. Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline. These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions. Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

[527] arXiv:2611.06449 [pdf, html, other]
Title: AmbiHTMLBench: A Benchmark for HTML-based Visually Rich Document parsing
Boyu Niu, Yingjie Xiong, Shurui Li, Linhan Pang, Yuntong Zhang, Han Wang, Hao Wu, Kai Zuo, Xu Tang, Xuanhe Zhou, Fan Wu
Comments: Check latest benchmark info on this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Traditional document parsing systems use Markdown as their output representation, which is effective for linear text but does not fully preserve fine-grained spatial structure, table geometry, visual hierarchy, or rendering semantics. We show that HTML is advantageous for heterogeneous and layout-sensitive documents whose representations must remain editable, inspectable, and reusable, and introduce AmbiHTMLBench to systematically study this setting. In this benchmark, given a real-world document, a model must recover executable HTML that preserves its content, organization, and visual appearance. The benchmark contains 1,115 diverse pages with structured annotations and evaluates predictions in two different ways: The objective protocol aligns ground-truth and predicted rendered blocks and measures table fidelity, page-level text error, and a two-dimensional layout consistency; a complementary reference-anchored protocol measures perceived fidelity by aligning LLM judges with human preferences. Across ten primary multimodal systems, the best objective score is 0.8092, while the subjective winner is different, demonstrating that automatic decomposition and human-perceived fidelity capture complementary properties. We further fine-tune a small-parameter expert model and find that task-specific adaptation yields good performance on document-to-HTML reconstruction task. These results position AmbiHTMLBench as a diagnostic testbed for building smarter and more logical document parsing systems.

[528] arXiv:2611.06450 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Timed Games under Environmental Interference with Real-Time Objectives
Andrea Manini, Matteo Rossi, Pierluigi San Pietro
Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

Classical Timed Games formulations may be unsuitable, or require substantial modeling effort, to capture complex interaction patterns between a controller and its surrounding environment, in which non-determinism must be resolved after the controller has chosen which action to perform. In this paper, we develop the theory of Timed CLTLoc Games (TCGs), a Timed Game variant designed to facilitate the modeling of such patterns. Unlike classical Timed Games formulations, TCGs partition locations rather than transitions, and use Constraint Linear Temporal Logic over clocks (CLTLoc) to specify the controller's objectives. We develop algorithms for solving TCGs and synthesizing winning controller strategies for games whose objectives include formal properties such as reachability and safety. For reachability objectives, our synthesis algorithm yields winning controller strategies that minimize the number of moves required to reach a goal state. Solving reachability TCGs is EXPTIME-complete, matching the complexity of solving reachability Timed Games. All of our algorithms operate backwards and are implemented in our C++ region-based library TARZAN, leveraging OpenMP for efficient parallelization. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of TARZAN.

[529] arXiv:2611.06451 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Fourier Entropy Bounds via Approximations
Manaswi Paraashar, Nitin Saurabh
Subjects: Computational Complexity (cs.CC)

We establish upper bounds on the Shannon entropy $\mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2})$ of the Fourier distribution of Boolean functions. We prove that $$ \mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2}) =O\!\left(\log\bigl(1+\|\widehat f\|_{1,1/3}\bigr)\right), $$ where $\|\widehat f\|_{1,1/3}$ denotes the minimum spectral norm of a pointwise $1/3$-approximant to $f$. This implies $\mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2})=O(\mathsf R^\oplus(f))$, where $\mathsf R^\oplus(f)$ is bounded-error randomized parity-query complexity. We also bound Fourier entropy by the smaller of the two one-sided average unambiguous parity-certificate complexities. More generally, for any exact representation of indicator of $f$ as $\sum_C w_C\mathbf1_C$, with nonnegative weights and affine subspaces $C$, we prove $$ \mathbb H(\widehat f^{\,2}) =O\!\left(\sum_C w_C\,2^{-k_C}k_C\right), \qquad k_C=\operatorname{codim}(C). $$ The quantity on the right is the average conical junta degree of the representation. These results strengthen earlier bounds of (Arunachalam et al. 2021) by extending approximation-based entropy estimates to Shannon entropy and allowing one-sided and overlapping exact representations. The proofs use an entropy bound from a sequence of increasingly accurate approximants of $f$ with \emph{small} spectral norm.
Our techniques also find an application in quantum communication complexity, where it improves a lower bound for the bounded-error quantum communication complexity of XOR functions.

[530] arXiv:2611.06452 [pdf, other]
Title: Within-Family EfficientNet Scaling under Fixed-Resolution Transfer Learning for Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography Retinal Disease Classification
Shkelqim Sherifi
Comments: 46 pages, 20 figures, 18 tables
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Background/Objectives: CNNs perform well in retinal disease classification from spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), but whether EfficientNet's natural-image scaling hierarchy transfers to medical-image transfer learning at fixed resolution remains unclear. This study evaluates EfficientNet-B0-B7 for four-class SD-OCT classification and accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Methods: Eight ImageNet-pretrained variants (4.05-64.10M instantiated backbone parameters) were evaluated at 224x224 on the Kermany dataset. Grayscale images were replicated to RGB and processed using model-embedded preprocessing and augmentation. Training comprised frozen-backbone head training followed by partial fine-tuning. Metrics covered classification, discrimination, efficiency, and visual analyses. Results: Test accuracy varied non-monotonically from 95.93% (B0) to 96.95% (B1); B7 achieved 96.73%. B1 had the highest accuracy and Drusen F1 (0.8780), while B7 had Drusen F1 of 0.8720 and the highest Drusen recall (0.9177). Drusen had the lowest F1 across all variants and contributed 82.2% of the summed squared deviation in class-specific F1; class ranking remained Normal > CNV > DME > Drusen. The OCT accuracy ranking differed from the reported ImageNet hierarchy, where B7 ranked first. The accuracy-to-parameter ratio fell from 19.82 to 1.48 percentage points per million total parameters. The final train-test gap had a weak, non-significant association with test accuracy (r = 0.26, p = 0.53). Conclusions: Larger EfficientNet variants did not consistently improve SD-OCT classification. B1 achieved the highest accuracy and Drusen F1, whereas B7 showed a secondary accuracy recovery at greater model size and CPU latency, indicating task and protocol dependent scaling effects. As cross-partition duplicates have not been independently audited, results are conditional on the supplied split.

[531] arXiv:2611.06453 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Beyond Infraction Scores: Failure-Boundary Profiles for Closed-Loop Evaluation of Driving and Robot Navigation Agents
Milan Bulat, Gino Ardelean, Ellington Kirby
Comments: 16 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL. Data: this https URL
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.

[532] arXiv:2611.06455 [pdf, other]
Title: CoDecide: Content-Adaptive Video Decoding for High-Throughput Video Analytics
Shristy Shah, Thomas B. Moeslund, Kamal Nasrollahi
Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027. 12 pages including supplementary material
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Analytics on video archives are bottlenecked by decoding. In a dense pipeline that runs a detector on every frame, decoding is a small fraction of the runtime, but once the detector is restricted to selected frames, decoding takes over as the main cost. We introduce CoDecide, a retrospective analytics system that only decodes the frames where new content appears, using signals from the compressed bitstream to find them. Motion tells us something is moving, but not whether it is new to the scene or has been there the whole time. To make that distinction, we supervise a lightweight compressed-domain student on a label-free novelty signal from a frozen DINOv2 teacher, which fires on semantically new regions rather than on any motion. Consequently, the student model generalizes to new camera deployments without requiring per-camera retraining. At inference, it decides which frames to decode and which regions to reconstruct. Detections from the decoded frames are propagated to the skipped frames using motion vectors. We evaluate CoDecide with a leave-one-dataset-out protocol on VIRAT, MEVA, and ShanghaiTech. Against a dense per-frame detector, CoDecide recovers more moving-object detections than prior compressed-domain selectors at an equivalent decoding budget, outperforming even a competitor trained directly on the target camera. CoDecide runs 15 to 24x faster than a pipeline that decodes and detects every frame. Code is available at this https URL.

[533] arXiv:2611.06458 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Generative Learning on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
Zhenyu Yang, Yuhong Chen, Binli Luo, Xiaodong Li, Xiaolin Hu, Hui Li, Jintang Li
Comments: 10 pages, 7 figures, 7 tables
Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)

Dynamic text-attributed graphs capture evolving interactions among entities with rich textual information, but future-link prediction remains difficult when nodes have little interaction history or appear as new targets. We propose \method, a generative framework that represents nodes with compact semantic identifiers (SIDs) learned from text and autoregressively predicts a target SID conditioned on the source SID, recent interaction events, and relative time gaps. A lightweight structural calibration further incorporates repetition, co-occurrence, and popularity. At inference time, \method encodes each query context once and reuses SID likelihoods to rank prescribed candidates, providing a candidate-efficient prediction interface. Experiments on nine datasets show broadly competitive performance across domains and graph densities. Source-side inductive evaluations demonstrate that text-derived SIDs provide a useful representation when a test source has no observed interaction history, while two recommendation-oriented case studies evaluate controlled new-user adaptation and first-arrival ranking for inductive new items. Further analyses characterize SID uniqueness, capacity, and temporal stability. Overall, the results support combining text-derived SIDs with temporal histories for dynamic link prediction.

[534] arXiv:2611.06461 [pdf, html, other]
Title: eBPF-Driven Adaptive Lifetime-Aware Data Placement for Shared FDP SSDs
Hajin Moon, Taewan Noh, Chaeeun Yoon, Jeonghun Lee, Junyoung Han, Joo-Young Hwang, Youngjae Kim
Subjects: Operating Systems (cs.OS)

NVMe Flexible Data Placement (FDP) reduces SSD write amplification by separating data with different lifetimes to minimize garbage collection (GC) copying. However, on shared servers, multiple tenants generate more lifetime classes than the available placement handles. Existing approaches rely on static mappings or application-specific knowledge, failing to capture runtime lifetimes and adapt to changing workloads. The challenge is to identify which data die together and determine which classes should be separated to maximize GC savings under a limited handle budget. We present eFDP, an eBPF-based system that automatically learns data lifetimes and manages FDP placement for unmodified applications on a stock Linux kernel. By tracking writes and invalidations, eFDP identifies lifetime classes and estimates the GC copying saved by separating them. It first assigns each tenant a handle, then allocates the remaining handles to the separations offering the greatest savings. It also re-plans placement when active tenants change. With four database tenants on an emulated FDP SSD, eFDP eliminates twice as much excess write amplification as tenant-level isolation and improves every writing tenant's throughput by 19-23%. On an enterprise FDP SSD, given RocksDB's levels, it matches a manually optimized placement using three handles instead of five. After a tenant switch, eFDP re-plans within seven minutes and maintains 25% lower write amplification than the original layout even after an hour.

[535] arXiv:2611.06462 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Weaver: Unlocking Blockchain Transaction Parallelism through State-Decoupled Symbolic Execution
Ru Cheng, Maofan Yin, Liangrong Chen, Lizan Zhou, Chenyuan Wu
Comments: 15 pages, 9 figures, 1 table
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

Transaction execution remains a major performance bottleneck in blockchains. Existing parallel execution engines are still blocked by slow state accesses on each transaction's critical path, creating a hidden loss of parallelism. This paper presents Weaver, a state-decoupled transaction processing paradigm that enables execution flow to proceed in the absence of concrete state values. Weaver represents states as lightweight symbolic references and records subsequent computation as symbolic expressions while concrete values are fetched on the fly. To handle state-dependent control flow, Weaver predicts the most likely branch direction through hierarchical symbolic pattern matching. Weaver further introduces expression-granular scheduling that evaluates each symbolic expression as soon as its state dependencies are resolved, rather than waiting for the transaction's entire read set, fully exploiting fine-grained intra-transaction parallelism. Evaluation on real Ethereum blocks and synthetic workloads spanning four representative dApps shows that Weaver delivers 41%-63% higher throughput than state-of-the-art parallel execution engines and up to 7.5 times the throughput of serial execution.

[536] arXiv:2611.06471 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and segmentation
Yulu Xie, Zilong Li, Shen Xu, Yifan Bai, Liuhong Shi, Jiao Chen, Xianglei Kong, Wenchao Zhu, Na Shen, Xianghua Ye, Yang Yan, Jiaju Zheng, Yunsong Peng, Yanzhou Su, Chaohui Yu, Hao Luo, Fan Wang
Comments: 114 pages, including Supplementary Information; 7 main figures and 2 Extended Data figures
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, CT models have treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception. Here we present HoloCT, a generalist 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation by jointly modelling whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, providing 3D masks as evidence. We curated HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT-mask pairs. Across 346 tasks spanning segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperformed specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation across 11,455 clinical CT scans from five hospitals, HoloCT outperformed competing models in lesion segmentation and report generation by 18.2 and 15.3 points. It also achieved 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Further analyses revealed bidirectional semantic-spatial synergy: language-guided segmentation delineated unseen anatomical structures and lesions as well as diffuse free-text findings, outperforming the leading approach by 22.1 points, whereas prompting the model to generate corresponding 3D masks alongside its textual outputs significantly improved interpretation performance. HoloCT shows that clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned together within a single foundation model and offers a path towards more accurate and reliable CT analysis.

[537] arXiv:2611.06475 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Robocasa-Mem: Benchmarking Environment and Process Memory in Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
Sihang Chen, Chen Ye, Wei Chen, Xiaohan Lei, Zhipeng Tang, Sha Zhang, Yuan Zhang, Zixuan Chen, Jiajun Deng, Houqiang Li, Yanyong Zhang
Comments: 17 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

In the real world, mobile manipulation robots must perform complex object interactions and make multi-step decisions, often relying on task-relevant information that is no longer observable. However, existing benchmarks provide limited evaluation of such memory-dependent decision-making in mobile manipulation. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCasa-Mem, a new benchmark comprising nine mobile manipulation tasks that require agents to use interaction history at key decision points. Specifically, the tasks are grouped into two categories of memory: One is environment memory, which captures spatial locations, object attributes, and object relationships. The other is process memory, which captures single-task progress and multi-task scheduling. Particularly, we introduce Behavior-Conditioned Evaluation. For tasks with multiple valid execution paths, instead of fixing a single target or trajectory, the evaluator derives later task constraints from the robot's earlier actions. This allows us to evaluate whether later behavior is consistent with the robot's own interaction history while reducing shortcuts based on fixed target assignments. We provide 1,800 successful demonstrations for policy training. We also develop a baseline on our benchmark, namely Hierarchical Memory-Augmented Policy(HMAP). Its high-level planner uses structured entity and process memories to generate subtasks. Its low-level VLA controller uses subgoal-conditioned queries to incorporate VGGT-Omega geometry into action generation. Together, RoboCasa-Mem and HMAP baseline support systematic evaluation of memory-dependent behavior and the development of memory-aware mobile manipulation policies.

[538] arXiv:2611.06476 [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Alignment Tax Is Graded: Task-Selective Capability Loss Under Length-Normalized DPO with SFT Retention
Ye Yuan
Comments: 25 pages, 3 figures, 23 tables. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Setting. This is an empirical characterization study; we propose no new method and run no comparisons against alternative objectives. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B with sparse LoRA and length-normalized DPO plus an SFT retention term (the RPO objective) on structured financial-filing tasks, and track downstream capability as the implicit reward margin grows to $\sim 7$ $\beta$-scaled units (nf4 training; $\sim 3$ under fp16 measurement on the unquantized base). Question. Does margin growth degrade capability uniformly across tasks, or selectively? Findings. In a pre-registered study (8 seeds, 6 unseen at freeze) with artifact-aware scoring and TOST equivalence testing, the alignment tax is graded and task-selective: extraction is preserved ($\Delta = -0.55$ pts, equivalent at $\pm5$ pts), json loses little ($\Delta = -3.52$ pts, equivalence fails on a clustered item-level interval), and router degrades severely ($\Delta = -30$ pts). Router's loss concentrates in a margin 1-3 damage window containing a transient format-break spike. The margin is accounted for almost entirely ($\geq 96\%$) by suppression of rejected completions, with chosen reward approximately flat, consistent with the retention term anchoring it; we do not attribute the behavioral damage to any single gradient channel. Gold-logp deflation is task-selective (extraction $-0.15$, json $-1.04$, router $-1.47$ nats/token under fp16), with gold selectively protected relative to incorrect controls on extraction (8/8 seeds). QLoRA reward margins differ up to $3.4\times$ between nf4 training and unquantized fp16 measurement, with an axis-dependent gap. Scope. Length-normalized rewards with SFT retention, sparse LoRA on 8/32 layers, one 4B model, easily-separable synthetic preferences, three structured tasks. A no-retention control and a measured format-alignment metric are left to future work.

[539] arXiv:2611.06477 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Towards Early Warning of Real-World Vulnerabilities: An Evidence-Aware Decoupled Method for CVSS Vector Prediction Based on Unstructured Disclosures
Jianhong Ma, Wenhao Li, Xixing Li, Chenyu Yan, Haowen Chen
Comments: 21 pages, 12 figures; includes 3 pages of supplementary material
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Early assessment of Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) vectors from Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) can reduce the delay between initial public disclosure and official National Vulnerability Database (NVD) scoring. Existing predictors, trained mainly on standardized late-stage descriptions, degrade on noisy and incomplete pre-NVD reports. We introduce PARSE, a vulnerability-disclosure lifecycle model, and VPre, an early assessment framework built on two-level Evidence-Aware Decoupling. Decoupling Level I, Security-Evidence Screening, separates security-relevant evidence from noisy early reports at the report and sentence levels. Decoupling Level II, Evidence-Matched Routing, decouples the prediction task of the eight CVSS metrics into a scattered-evidence class and an explicit-evidence class based on validation-set measurements, matching each with a targeted predictor: large-language-model reasoning for the former, lightweight supervised classification for the latter. On the 851-report held-out test split of the 5,581-report VPre-Bench, VPre achieves a mean absolute error of 0.7239 -- 44.7% below the reproduced BERT-Small-NVD early-transfer baseline; paired timestamps across the full benchmark show an average 38-day lead before official scoring (observed range 21-60 days). Under the 38:1 PARSE-Triage noise setting, STDU's report-level screening reaches 0.98 precision, 1.00 recall, and 0.99 F1. Controlled ablations support the contributions of both decoupling levels.

[540] arXiv:2611.06478 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Beyond Gomory-Hu: All-Pairs $\times$ All-Pairs Mincuts in $O(n)$ Space
Koustav Bhanja, Merav Parter, Asaf Petruschka
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

For over four decades, two classical structures have offered complementary views of mincuts. The Gomory-Hu tree encodes one $(x,y)$-mincut for every vertex pair $x,y$ in $O(n)$ space, but retains only one mincut per pair. In contrast, for a fixed pair $x,y$, the Picard-Queyranne representation admits an $O(n)$ space vertex ordering that determines whether some $(x,y)$-mincut separates any given pair $u,v$ and reports such a cut. Can these complementary guarantees hold simultaneously in $O(n)$ space?
We answer affirmatively. For undirected graphs, we construct an $O(n)$ space structure encoding, for every four vertices $x,y,u,v$, an $(x,y)$-mincut separating $u,v$ whenever one exists. More precisely, given any terminal pair $x,y$, the structure recovers the Picard-Queyranne ordering in $O(n)$ time. Thereafter, separability queries take $O(1)$ time, and reporting a separating mincut $C$ takes $O(|C|)$ time. Thus, information for all $\Theta(n^4)$ choices of $x,y,u,v$ is encoded in $O(n)$ space. This is essentially the strongest information of this form that fits in $O(n)$ space: if one additionally requires the mincut to place $u$ on side of $x$ and $v$ on side of $y$, then $\Omega(n^2)$ space is necessary even for fixed $x,y$.
As a consequence, we obtain an $O(n)$ space all-pairs mincut sensitivity oracle for a single edge failure in multigraphs, with optimal $O(n)$ time to report a new mincut. This resolves an open question of Baswana and Pandey [SODA'22] on achieving $o(n^2)$ space and $o(m)$ query time simultaneously. Our construction substantially generalizes the $O(n)$ space nearest-mincut-hierarchy [SODA'27], which reports only the nearest $(x,y)$-mincut. Recovering the entire Picard-Queyranne ordering for an arbitrary pair requires new structural properties of the Dinitz-Vainshtein [STOC'94] connectivity carcass, extending its use beyond the Steiner mincuts it represents.

[541] arXiv:2611.06479 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Optimal Subcubic Byzantine Agreement with Plain PKI
Marc Dufay, Roger Wattenhofer
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

We consider Byzantine Agreement (BA), where $n$ parties run a distributed protocol to agree on a common value, despite $t$ parties being byzantine. In the synchronous setting, a choice must be made between the weaker unauthenticated setting, which only allows $t < n/3$ byzantine parties, and the stronger authenticated setting that allows up to $t < n/2$ byzantine parties. For this latter setting, BA can be solved with optimal resiliency and optimal bit complexity. However, so far, all optimal solutions rely on the use of threshold signatures. This shows a gap compared to regular signatures, where only protocols with cubic complexity are known for optimal resiliency $t < n/2$.
We wonder whether this cubic complexity is required without the use of threshold signatures and show that this is not the case. More specifically, given $\kappa$ an upper bound on the size of a hash or signature, we describe a deterministic protocol solving BA with bit complexity $\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{(\sqrt{13} - 1)/2} n^{(\sqrt{13} + 1)/2}) \approx \mathcal{O}(\kappa^{1.303}n^{2.303})$ while having optimal resiliency $t<n/2$ and round complexity $\mathcal{O}(n)$.

[542] arXiv:2611.06481 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
Jyotin Goel, Abhinav Arun, Tejas Prakash Agarwal, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
Comments: Preprint
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

[543] arXiv:2611.06482 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Computing Forest Degree Realizations with Minimum Cardinality Domination
Amotz Bar-Noy, Omri Kosary, David Peleg, Dror Rawitz
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM)

In the Degree Realization problem with respect to a family $\mathcal{P}$ of graphs the input is a non-increasing sequence $d = (d_1,\ldots,d_n)$ of positive integers, and the goal is to decide whether there exists a simple undirected graph $G \in \mathcal{P}$, whose degrees correspond to $d$, i.e., such that $deg(G) = d$. In this paper we consider the version of Degree Realization in which the realization is required to be a forest (i.e., $\mathcal{P}$ is the family of forests).
We consider \emph{optimized} Degree Realization in which the goal is to obtain a realization that minimizes an objective function $f$. That is, the goal is to find a realization $G$ that minimizes $f(G)$ among the realizations of the given input sequence. More specifically, we focus on the following functions: the size of an optimal \emph{vertex cover} and the size of an optimal \emph{dominating set}. We also consider the \emph{total} and \emph{paired} versions of both Min Vertex Cover and Min Dominating Set. We provide characterizations and linear time realization algorithms for all the above-mentioned problems. Since Min Paired Vertex Cover is closely related to Min Edge Dominating Set, our results for Degree Realization with respect to the former extend to the latter.

[544] arXiv:2611.06483 [pdf, html, other]
Title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?
Kejian Zhu, Zhuoran Jin, Shangqing Tu, Tianyi Men, Yupu Hao, Jiachun Li, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
Comments: Project Page: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

While multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning (RL) excels on long-horizon tasks, its performance gains remain highly sensitive to interaction constraints. Evaluating across sampling breadth $K$ and interaction depth $T$ via $Pass@(K,T)$, we show that trajectory-level RL advantages depend on sufficient turn budgets, diminishing significantly when budgets tighten. Besides, agentic RL does not uniformly elevate single-step decision quality; rather, its strength concentrates in error recovery and long-horizon resilience. To mitigate the deployment risks caused by this budget dependence, we provide a preliminary discussion on the benefits and limitations of process supervision signals and introduce BudgetMix RL as an alternative that varies interaction budgets during training. Experiments demonstrate that BudgetMix RL achieves robust performance across diverse execution settings. Project Page: this https URL

[545] arXiv:2611.06486 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Model Merging Does Not Require Uniform LoRA Ranks
Zirong Xie, Zainab Afolabi, Nikita Kozodoi, Jack Butler
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Model merging combines separately fine-tuned experts into a single model without retraining. Standard practice trains every expert at the same LoRA rank, which couples the rank choice across experts even though each domain has its own best rank. We show this coupling is a property of the merge method, not of merging. We train 36 experts on three domains (mathematics, instruction following, multilingual) at four ranks and three model scales, then merge with six methods at uniform ranks and at each domain's own best rank. Giving experts different ranks costs averaging and utility-based selection nothing, and gains them up to 1.8 pp of multi-domain accuracy, while the conflict-resolution methods are inconsistent and can lose up to 4 pp. The split has a simple cause. Merging keeps only a fixed share of the pooled spectral components, and methods that choose them by size discard many that would have reduced loss. They also tend to discard the same expert: the instruction adapter has the smallest singular values, so it is dropped almost entirely and IFEval falls by 16 to 25 pp. Choosing components by their effect on loss instead keeps all three experts, and leaves accuracy nearly flat across an 8$\times$ rank range (0.7 pp, against 6.7 pp for TIES at 4B scale). Rank can therefore be chosen per expert whenever the merge operator does not select by magnitude.

[546] arXiv:2611.06487 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Measuring the collaboration, not the agent
Xinxiao Li, Eisei Nakahara
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

Benchmarks for visualization agents score the agent alone; the human only supplies reference answers. For high-dimensional data this misses what matters: the knowledge of which variables count is held by on-site experts, not by the model, so the useful question is how well an analyst and an agent do together. We study one specific form of collaboration, the agent proposes a view, the analyst accepts, rejects, or modifies it, and those judgments are kept for later sessions, and propose five measures for it: complementarity, intervention efficiency, appropriate reliance, knowledge retention, and agency. The first four are computed from interaction logs alone. We test the measures, not people: in a testbed for parallel-coordinates design on public manufacturing data (UCI SECOM), with a simulated analyst whose behavior we control, all four are computable and respond to the controlled differences. Whether they reveal anything about real analysts is the next step; we release the testbed for it.

[547] arXiv:2611.06491 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FPTR: Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement for Deadline-Constrained Joint Beam and Resource Allocation
Minghao Kong, Zirong Liu, Jianhao Wu, Muyao Chen, Jianxin Wu, Rongjie Wang
Comments: 14 pages, 4 figures; includes appendix. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Performance (cs.PF)

Short-interval wireless schedulers must return a complete, feasible beam-and-resource allocation before each execution deadline, and a late or invalid output gives no utility in the current control cycle. Searching longer can increase transmitted traffic, but it may also miss the deadline or leave only an infeasible intermediate solution. We propose Feasibility-Preserving Transactional Refinement (FPTR), which always keeps a validated feasible allocation, the incumbent. Each refinement stage builds a separate candidate and leaves the incumbent unchanged. A candidate replaces the incumbent only if it is complete, passes the feasibility validator before its stage cutoff, and strictly improves the objective; otherwise it is discarded. Four refinement stages use this rule: buffer-aware resource selection, compatibility-group (CG) user sharing, beam-mask rebuilding from remaining demand, and joint reassignment of two resources. On 150 fixed synthetic instances, the full pipeline (Full) raises traffic by 3.83% on average over a lightweight beam-first reference and by 1.79% over its Base constructor. In a separate suite with matched inputs, Full exceeds six independent search baselines (ALNS, tabu search, GA, simulated annealing, iterated local search, and GRASP) by 6.68-8.35%, where outputs later than 100 ms receive zero utility. All 750 Full runs in the internal suite returned feasible allocations, and none exceeded 100 ms. Separating mandatory output construction from optional refinement lets spare computation time improve the allocation without endangering the incumbent. The open-source implementation supports independent reproduction.

[548] arXiv:2611.06494 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A $2.81^n$ upper bound on the number of stable matchings
Ebrahim Ghorbani, Matthias Mnich
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM); Combinatorics (math.CO)

We study the maximum number ${\rm SM}(n)$ of stable matchings in an instance with $n$ men and $n$ women. Karlin, Oveis Gharan, and Weber (STOC 2018) proved the first single-exponential upper bound; their argument gives ${\rm SM}(n)\le 2^{17n}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Palmer and Pálvölgyi (FOCS 2021) improved this bound to $3.55^n+O(1)$. We prove that ${\rm SM}(n)<2.81^n$. This brings the exponential base closer to $2.28$, the base of the best known lower bound. More precisely, we bound the number of stable matchings in each instance in terms of each person's number of stable partners, where a stable partner is someone matched to that person in at least one stable matching. Our proof assigns each person a weight determined by this number and uses these weights to bound the number of stable matchings by induction.

[549] arXiv:2611.06496 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LibriSpeech-Real-QA: A Benchmark for Streaming Question Answering
Zewen Zhan, Hui Lu, Xueyuan Chen, Huimeng Wang, Yikai Huang, Xixin Wu, Shiyin Kang, Bin Xia, Zhiyong Wu
Comments: 5 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Most speech large language models (SLMs) still process speech in an offline manner. They only start responding after they receive the complete speech segment. However, many real-world applications require streaming speech interaction, for which the audio continuously flows in and the machine is required to answer questions based on the so far received audio chunks. For example, a user may ask the system to continuously count how many times a person's name has been mentioned while they are speaking. We observe a lack of benchmarks and evaluation protocols for real-time speech interaction. Motivated by this, we propose LibriSpeech-Real-QA, a dataset and a benchmark for real-time speech interaction. We construct different types of real-time question-answer pairs from LibriSpeech to evaluate whether speech LLMs can identify target words in streaming audio. We evaluate several popular real-time commercial models and find that they still tend to respond only after the speech turn has finished. We demonstrate that we can enable a pretrained SLM to perform this task, where we explore several modeling designs and establish a solid baseline for future research.

[550] arXiv:2611.06498 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Georgios Feretzakis, Alexandros Papaspyridis
Comments: 20 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: this https URL (DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23948839)
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Offline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on edge devices is updated through signed knowledge packs that carry text and precomputed embedding vectors. A signature proves who published a pack, not that its vectors encode its text. We study this text-vector integrity gap. A verifier that recomputes vectors and accepts them within a cosine tolerance concedes a predictable share of queries to an attacker who controls the vectors: the hijack rate equals the distribution of angular retrieval margins at the tolerance (the margin law). Margins are small in five corpora and two embedding models, so an idealised tolerance at the level of floating-point noise leaves up to 5.5% of queries exposed (at most 1.2% in any corpus once exact duplicate documents are excluded), and a threshold calibrated from our CPU INT8-FP32 comparison of a small embedding model (at the empirical 0.1% quantile of honest cosines) leaves 98-100% exposed; on a Raspberry Pi 5 running a local language model, such an attack lowers correct answers from 0.75 to 0.39. Integrity audits of compressed vector stores fare no better: on a FAISS product-quantisation index over 57,638 documents, tampered vectors that all pass the audit put the attacker's document first for 25% of targets. Verifying quantisation codes instead, with ambiguity decided by the verifier, a calibrated guard band and canonicalisation, accepted every honest vector in our samples on three platforms and left the publisher no choice. We also show that common floating-point and dynamic-INT8 inference pipelines are not bit-reproducible across batch sizes or architectures, and report pre-registered negative results on abstention, context pruning and semantic screening. We release code and data.

[551] arXiv:2611.06499 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Energy-Accumulate-Then-Act Backscatter Communications With Retransmission Under Imperfect Feedback Detection
Rui Xu, Yinghui Ye, Guangyue Lu, Liqin Shi, Gan Zheng
Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT)

In this paper, we propose a threshold-triggered energy-accumulate-then-act backscatter communication system with retransmission under imperfect feedback detection. Under this system, harvested energy is accumulated across transmission blocks, and the backscatter device switches among different operation modes, including energy harvesting, initial transmission, and retransmission, according to its stored energy and decoded feedback. To characterize the resulting dynamics, the joint evolution of the packet-buffer and stored-energy states is modeled, based on which an embedded Markov chain is constructed to derive the steady-state energy distribution at the beginning of each update cycle. Subsequently, the average age of information (AAoI) is derived from the statistics of the inter-update interval and its correlation with the preceding packet system time, while the packet loss rate (PLR) caused by imperfect feedback detection is also obtained. Simulation results validate the analytical results and reveal that retransmission reduces PLR but may either improve or degrade AAoI, depending on packet-generation energy, data transmission rate, and feedback power. Moreover, lower feedback power shrinks the AAoI-favorable region of retransmission at low transmission rate, whereas the opposite trend emerges at higher rate.

[552] arXiv:2611.06500 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
Yuetong Liu, Zhehao Zhou, Yitong Zhang, Haorui Chen, Jia Li
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios.
In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at this https URL.

[553] arXiv:2611.06501 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CRESiST: Self-Enhancing Explorative Policy Learning for Simultaneous Speech Translation
Chenyang Le, Pei Zhang, Yuxiang Chen, Bing Han, Derek F. Wong, Baosong Yang, Yanmin Qian
Comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Sound (cs.SD)

Simultaneous Speech Translation (SimulST) requires balancing translation quality and latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in offline translation, current LLM-based SimulST systems predominantly rely on prefix-incremental generation. This paradigm suffers from redundant Key-Value cache recomputation and necessitates external Voice Activity Detection to process unbounded streams. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose an end-to-end interleaved read-write framework built upon an omni-modal LLM. By interleaving speech chunks and text tokens, our architecture achieves full KV cache reuse, natively supporting segmentation-free, infinite-length inference. Furthermore, to learn optimal streaming policies without rigid offline alignments, we introduce a novel Actor-Critic self-enhancement pipeline. An RNN-T Actor dynamically samples read-write trajectories, while an LLM-based Critic evaluates these paths via intrinsic semantic and latency rewards, distilling the optimal policy back to the Actor. Extensive experiments on sentence-level (FLEURS, CoVoST2) and document-level (MuST-C, ACL 60/60) benchmarks demonstrate that our model establishes new state-of-the-art quality-latency Pareto frontiers, substantially outperforming existing cascaded and static-alignment baselines.

[554] arXiv:2611.06504 [pdf, html, other]
Title: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria
Zainab Afolabi, Nikita Kozodoi, Jack Butler, Babs Khalidson
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce \naija, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, \yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49--50\% for the US/UK but 20\% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to \yoruba{} (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66--79\% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31\% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96\% on culture and 98\% on politics against 26\% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.

[555] arXiv:2611.06506 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Trace2Eval: Contextualized Evaluation of Coding Agents from Real-World Traces
Ji Shi, Lirong Jie, Lexiao Zou, Yaoming Zhu, Yifan Yang, Xuezhi Cao, Xunliang Cai, Miao Zhang
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Coding agents are increasingly used in real-world workflows across diverse domains, motivating evaluation grounded in real user tasks. Existing benchmarks, however, largely rely on static public tasks with reference patches or hidden tests. Next-generation coding-agent benchmarks should therefore move beyond correctness on fixed tasks toward continually renewed evaluation of overall artifact quality in real user workflows.
We propose Trace2Eval, a dynamically updatable pipeline that constructs benchmarks from real-world interaction trajectories. Trace2Eval employs a multi-agent reconstruction system to analyze the filtered trajectory, recover the original user query, restore the workspace files to their pre-interaction state, and rebuild a trajectory-equivalent execution environment. A candidate agent then executes the reconstructed query to produce an initial artifact.
To evaluate these artifacts, the pipeline iteratively refines human rubrics through inter-annotator alignment, and calibrates judge agents against human assessments using source-code and runtime evidence. Guided by feedback from the Trace2Eval pipeline, models revise their initial artifacts, yielding a mean score gain of 10.05 percentage points across 19 model-harness configurations and a maximum of 19.28 percentage points for DeepSeek-V4-Pro with Claude Code, which supports rubric feedback as actionable guidance for artifact improvement.

[556] arXiv:2611.06508 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ElecLoad: Adaptive Electricity Load Forecasting Guided by Multiple Events
Huajian Zhang, Mingyue Cheng, Xingpeng Gao, Xiaoyu Tao, Zhiding Liu, Jiqian Yang, Zhi Li
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Accurate electricity load forecasting provides critical decision support for energy procurement, generation scheduling, and supply-demand balancing, contributing to the economic efficiency and operational reliability of power systems. However, future electricity demand can be affected by the complex interplay of multiple events described in Web notices, weather alerts, and event schedules. Their effects vary over time and can reinforce or offset one another, making electricity load difficult to forecast accurately. While existing methods can incorporate context as additional input, how to use the effects of multiple events and their interactions to guide the load forecasting process itself remains to be explored. To address this gap, we propose ElecLoad, a context-aware agent for multi-event electricity load forecasting that adaptively organizes the forecasting process. Specifically, we train ElecLoad to combine historical load with context to analyze each event's relevance to the target load, the timing of its effects, and potential interactions among events. Guided by this analysis, ElecLoad adaptively chooses to forecast the entire forecast horizon directly or to partition it into segments according to changes in event effects. When the horizon is partitioned, sub-agents independently generate initial forecasts for each segment. The main agent then reviews these forecasts, and the sub-agents perform selective refinement guided by its feedback. Experiments on multiple electricity load datasets show that ElecLoad achieves state-of-the-art performance in most evaluation scenarios. Code is available at this https URL.

[557] arXiv:2611.06512 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Nowcasting Future Performance for Population Pruning in Survival-of-the-Fittest Training
Rico Städeli, Léo Meynent, Boris Knyazev, Damian Borth
Comments: Accepted at: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Training high-performing neural networks often involves evaluating populations of candidate models with varying hyperparameters, architectures, or random seeds. Training every candidate to completion is computationally expensive, yet stopping seemingly weaker runs early risks discarding models that would ultimately perform better, as learning curves can cross. To address this challenge, we investigate whether intermediate training checkpoints can predict future model accuracy and enable more informed pruning decisions. Our nowcasters predict test accuracy five epochs ahead or at the end of training. They are trained with accuracy and loss histories, weight statistics, and SANE representations as inputs. SANE is a transformer autoencoder that encodes a checkpoint as a sequence of latent tokens. We then use the nowcasters in Survival-of-the-Fittest (SOTF) training. SOTF repeatedly ranks runs during training by predicted accuracy and stops the lowest-ranked ones. Our results show that weight statistics work best for five-epoch forecasts, and SANE representations work best for final accuracy prediction. For evaluation, we compare SOTF with pruning the population by current accuracy. In homogeneous model zoos such as the CNN zoos, pruning by current accuracy already retains a final model only slightly worse than the best. Model zoos with a larger spread in performance, such as the ResNet-18 and ViT zoos, are more difficult to prune by current accuracy alone. In these zoos, SOTF with nowcasted final accuracy almost closes the gap to the best model.

[558] arXiv:2611.06513 [pdf, html, other]
Title: HELIX: HEterogeneous LLM Inference with FleXible and Fine-Grained Partitioning
Victoria Clerico, William Simon, Corey Liam Lammie, Orhun Görkem, Athanasios Vasilopoulos, Hsinyu Tsai, Jeronimo Castrillon, Abu Sebastian, Hadjer Benmeziane
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

LLM inference is inherently heterogeneous, with performance bottlenecks shifting throughout inference phases down to individual operators. This has motivated heterogeneous serving systems that disaggregate execution across specialized accelerators, typically through fixed partitions such as prefill/decode or attention/FFN. However, these approaches commit to a partitioning strategy in advance, limiting their ability to adapt to different workloads and model architectures while forcing emerging accelerators into predefined roles. We present HELIX, a vLLM-based software stack that discovers, compiles and dispatches workload-aware partitions across heterogeneous accelerators at the operator granularity. At engine initialization, HELIX automatically determines hardware-specific operator placements that minimize execution latency, accounting for profiled execution costs, communication overheads, device capabilities, and memory constraints. It combines dynamic programming, piecewise compilation, and heterogeneous subgraph dispatch, enabling accelerators with partial operator coverage to participate in LLM inference without predefined model partitions. HELIX provides an open-source unified framework for exploring, evaluating, and integrating heterogeneous accelerators for LLM inference, lowering the barrier to emerging hardware by exposing them as subgraph executors. In systems combining H100 and B200 GPUs with emerging accelerators, HELIX resolves LLM partitions that multi-query decoding latency by up to 3$\times$ for dense and sparse transformer models and up to 3.5$\times$ for hybrid state-space models, relative to standard attention-FFN disaggregation.

[559] arXiv:2611.06514 [pdf, html, other]
Title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case
Yousef Nejatbakhsh, Malihe Aliasgari, Parsa Safaee, Sina Shokoohyar
Comments: 18 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. Research code, datasets, and reproducibility materials are available at this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Applications (stat.AP)

Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength, and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal's meaning depends on the others: high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses. The proposed Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes such dependencies as four interpretable interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. We evaluate it on 55 acquisitions assisted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 2008-2024 by acquirers with a parent listed in the United States. Six financial inputs come from regulatory reports published before each failure; two deal terms, which the winning bidder knows when it bids but investors learn at the announcement, come from the regulator's press releases. The outcome, a positive three-day abnormal return around the announcement, records the market's initial reception, not realized success. Under grouped, nested cross-validation, the Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression on the same inputs and 0.632 for ridge regression; permutation tests that repeat the full model selection give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark. Thresholds tuned for the F1 score approve most acquisitions with negative returns and realize negative utility when each costs three times what a positively received acquisition gains.

[560] arXiv:2611.06515 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Scythe: Semantic-Aware Rewriting for Fast,Effective Program Reduction
Ioanna Moraiti, Charalambos Mitropoulos, Artem Anchikov, Sotirios Ioannidis, Dimitris Mitropoulos, Thodoris Sotiropoulos
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Automated program reduction shrinks a program into a smaller one that preserves a property of interest. Language-agnostic grammar-based reducers are easy to retarget across languages, but because they reason only about syntax, they cannot perform the coupled edits needed to remove whole declarations, e.g., a method cannot be deleted while it is still called. As a result, they waste oracle calls on edits that cannot succeed and often leave irrelevant declarations behind. We present SCYTHE, a fast, semantic-aware pre-processing step that runs in front of any grammar-based reducer without modifying it. SCYTHE encodes the program as a typed declaration dependency graph and applies a set of semantic-aware operators that decouple declarations from their use sites, making them removable while keeping the program well-typed. Fine-grained token-level minimization is then left to the downstream reducer. On 73 benchmarks across C, Java, and Solidity, combining SCYTHE with PERSES never yields a larger result than PERSES alone, and a strictly smaller one on 70 of 73 cases. On average, the combination produces programs 55.6% smaller (up to 95.5%) and is 2.3$\times$ faster (up to 7.4$\times$). SCYTHE also boosts LATRA, a reducer that, unlike the purely syntactic PERSES, also applies language-specific transformations: the combination produces programs 10.6% smaller (up to 61.8%) and is 2.4$\times$ faster on average. Video: this https URL

[561] arXiv:2611.06517 [pdf, other]
Title: Dialect Matters: A Dialect-Aware Baseline for Igala-English Machine Translation
Etuh E., Eli. A. Jiya
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

The massive permeability of intelligent systems in every sphere of human activities have greatly enhanced clarity, ease of work, and increased general global understanding which has significantly awaken the use of intelligent systems by all users. Intelligent systems greatly rely on precise dataset/corpus for the correctness of their output. Despite efforts by researchers to address Low-resource language in the Natural Language Processing (NLP), Igala still has zero parallel corpora despite efforts by researchers. We present a dialect-aware baseline for Igala-English machine translation, among first open systems and first with dialectal variation analysis. Our dataset of 1137 sentences (899 training) is first with dialect tags: Idah 459 (40.4%), Ankpa 297 (26.1%), Ibaji 160 (14.1%), Other 187 (16.4%), Ogugu 32 (2.8%). Same English yields 20-60 Igala forms. Mixed-dialect training achieves balanced BLEU 11.66 versus Idah-only model which drops 4.7 BLEU on Ibaji (13.2 on Idah, 8.5 on Ibaji), proving dialect fairness requires mixing. Fine-tuned from Helsinki-NLP/opus-mt-en-mul (78M), epoch ablation shows convergence at 8 epochs and overfitting at 15. BLEU 11.66, chrF 46.69. Analysis shows 899 sentences on log-linear trend consistent with African low-resource literature. This work provides first dialectal impact analysis for Igala and establishes baseline for future work.

[562] arXiv:2611.06518 [pdf, html, other]
Title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL
Mingzhe Zheng, Yue Wu, Jing Tan, Chang Zou, Dengyang Jiang, Zeyue Tian, Xuanhua He, Ryan Xu, Yunyang Ge, Sihui Ji, Yunlong Lin, Kaihang Pan, Hongru Yan, Sixiang Chen, Dianyi Wang, Julian Zhang, Weijie Kong, Changlin Li, Lanqing Guo, Zhao Zhong, Qifeng Chen, Harry Yang
Comments: 30 pages, 15 figures
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

[563] arXiv:2611.06519 [pdf, html, other]
Title: IDSISA: Influence-Distilled Sharded Training for Efficient Machine Unlearning
Deeraj SK, Sadhana Devarajan, Tanmoy Hazra, Anupam Shukla
Comments: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training examples to comply with privacy regulations. Full retraining gives strong guarantees but is computationally prohibitive at scale; approximate methods are efficient but lack formal guarantees. SISA (Sharded, Isolated, Sliced, and Aggregated training) achieves certified deletion through data sharding and independent retraining, but random partitioning scatters forget requests across most shards, and isolated retraining degrades utility. We introduce IDSISA (Influence-Distilled SISA), which uses influence functions to concentrate forget-prone samples into few shards and distillation from unaffected shards to recover utility lost to isolation. The deletion guarantee inherited from SISA's retraining step remains exact and requires no probabilistic qualification; the distillation-based utility recovery is a separately quantified, empirically bounded approximation ($\epsilon_{\text{cert}} \leq 0.015$ in expectation). We further formalize certification under sequences of repeated deletion requests, where cross-shard distillation can create dependencies between shards; we prove that a closure-based cascading retraining procedure restores the deletion guarantee to the full aggregated model under any deletion sequence. Experiments on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, ResNet-18/CIFAR-100, BiLSTM/IMDB, TCN/IMDB, and a fully connected network on Fashion-MNIST show $14-91\%$ better selective forgetting, up to $50\%$ better utility retention in relative terms (with consistent percentage-point gains on the other architectures, where a relative baseline is undefined), and unlearning-time changes ranging from $-6.7\%$ to $+6.4\%$ depending on architecture, relative to SISA.

[564] arXiv:2611.06521 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Deliberate Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
Haobo Zhang, Qiannan Zhu, Yutao Zhu, Zhicheng Dou
Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

Sequential recommenders are widely applied in real-world scenarios to model user preferences and behavior patterns based on user interactions. Recent advances in sequential recommendation enhance transformer-based models with latent reasoning to refine user representations by autoregressively generating intermediate reasoning vectors. However, exploring the optimal reasoning depth for diverse user histories remains challenging: existing methods typically employ a fixed number of reasoning steps for all users. This ``one-size-fits-all'' strategy often leads to suboptimal representation learning due to over-thinking in simple histories or under-thinking in complex ones. To address this issue, we propose DESRec, a deliberate latent reasoning framework that performs personalized latent reasoning to learn more informative reasoning states and enhance user modeling for sequential recommendation. Specifically, it designs a reasoning step selection module that identifies the optimal reasoning step for each user sequence during the training phase. Through a self-distillation mechanism, it compresses this most informative state into the final reasoning step, which serves as the final user representation for item ranking during inference. Moreover, it introduces a progressive preference extraction mechanism for personalized reasoning, which dynamically segments a user's history into a variable number of periods and summarizes each into a latent milestone representing the user's preference for that period. It will be used as the input of the subsequent reasoning. The number of milestones varies with the users' history, enabling a personalized reasoning over users' evolving interests. Extensive experimental results on six public datasets and four backbone recommenders demonstrate the superiority of DESRec over eight baseline models.

[565] arXiv:2611.06522 [pdf, html, other]
Title: From Admission to Retention: Predicting Durable Offspring in Quality-Diversity Search
Corrado Calamita, Matteo Mendicini, Luca Ferrari, Riccardo Bertamini
Comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems (EvoRobust)
Subjects: Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Automated failure discovery can be framed as a diversity problem: the objective is to expose distinct ways a system fails rather than a single critical adversarial case. Yet uniform parent sampling provides no way to allocate search effort toward individuals likely to produce durable archive contributions. We study this credit assignment problem in an unstructured Quality-Diversity (QD) archive, testing whether signals available before an individual has reproduced distinguish offspring that merely enter the archive from those still retained generations later. Across a planar-arm benchmark and two robotic-locomotion tasks, the same signals are often associated with entry and persistence in opposite directions. In particular, lineage depth is the clearest such signal, and its persistence discrimination grows with population capacity, which is associated with lower turnover. Biasing parent selection toward the signals with the strongest measured association to survival nevertheless does not improve search: moderate bias matches uniform sampling, and strong bias reduces QD-score.

[566] arXiv:2611.06523 [pdf, html, other]
Title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control
Xuemin Hu, Kaixin Li, Qingqing Xia, Yuxin Wang, Wei Xie, Bo Tang, Long Chen
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms.
