Comments: 25 pages, 7 figures, 12 tables, conference preprint
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.

[662] arXiv:2611.06732 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
Philipp Mondorf, Adrien Deliège, Solim LeGris, Claas Beger, Ryan Yi, Barbara Plank, Brenden M. Lake, Todd M. Gureckis
Comments: 23 pages, 14 figures
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.

[663] arXiv:2611.06734 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Smartphone-Aided VR Exergames for HIIT: Gamifying Fitness with Real-Time Pose Estimation
Abhiram Kothagundu, Pheelip Pritipal Raipure, Abhijit Chandrakant Patil, Himangshu Sarma, Christian Eichhorn, David A. Plecher, Johanna Pirker
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

This paper introduces an innovative virtual reality (VR) exergame system designed to gamify High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) workouts through 11 predefined combo moves, including squat-punch combinations, bilateral arm strikes, and diagonal stretch combos. Unlike conventional tracking methods that often rely on wearable motion capture suits or limited headset-based sensors, our system uses a standard smartphone camera placed on a tripod to capture full-body movement. This approach offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative, particularly well-suited to the fast, dynamic motions typical of HIIT routines.
The smartphone footage is processed in real time using a pose estimation algorithm, with extracted biomechanical data analyzed by a backend server built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to structured data sources and tools, and a GPT-4o large language model. The system generates personalized assessments of form accuracy, movement efficiency, exercise intensity, and potential injury risks, tailored specifically to high-impact, time-sensitive exercises.
A within-subject study involving 20 participants (ages 18-25) compared experiences in VR and Non-VR HIIT sessions. Results indicated significantly higher enjoyment (Mean = 3.5 vs 2.8, p = 0.02), improved immersion/focus (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.8, p = 0.03), and increased likelihood to recommend (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.7, p = 0.04) under the VR condition. Confidence to continue did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.15), while perceived intensity remained comparable. The MCP system showed strong agreement with expert evaluation (87.5%, N = 10 sessions, one certified trainer), supporting its reliability as a feedback tool.

[664] arXiv:2611.06737 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Data Center Agglomeration and Power Infrastructure Capacity in the United States
Yutong Ma
Comments: 10 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, conference paper that have been accepted after peer-review
Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR)

The continuous expansion of digital infrastructure, especially data centers, has imposed unprecedented, geographically concentrated stress on existing power grids. However, rigorous causal evidence quantifying how these facilities reshape local power-infrastructure supply remains limited. This study builds a comprehensive county-level US panel dataset spanning 2010-2024, uniquely integrating individual data center building footprints and power-plant additions. To mitigate endogeneity and high-dimensional confounding, this study deploys Double Machine Learning with five-fold cross-fitting, conditioning on county and year fixed effects alongside regional socioeconomic covariates. Baseline estimation identifies a significant positive causal effect robust across multiple rigorous specifications. The result holds following 1%-99% winsorization that downweights mega-clusters including Loudoun County: growth in data-center floor area drives meaningful increases in nearby power-generation capacity (ATE=1.982, P=0.000, CI: [1.25, 2.72]). Outcomes remain statistically significant using a one-year lagged treatment to address reverse causality, and are stable under state-level fixed-effect alternatives. An event-study framework augmented with historical agglomeration controls validates clear parallel trends and detects a sharp causal spike at t = 3, matching typical utility-scale grid-construction lead times. A placebo test further verifies these causal estimates cannot emerge from random chance. Substantial regional heterogeneity emerges: strong positive impacts concentrate in the West, while significant negative displacement-related effects appear within resource-constrained Northeastern counties. These results deliver timely insights for urban planners and energy regulators, stressing the importance of forward-looking grid-capacity investment to support ongoing digital transformation.

[665] arXiv:2611.06738 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Coupled Scene Graph Anticipation: When With-Constraint Recall Hides Structural Inconsistency
Zeno Nongmaithem, Anushttha Srivastava, Anshit Sinha, Apoorv Sisodia, Suman Chowdhury, Prerana Mukherjee, Rajesh P. Barnwal
Comments: Accepted at ICVGIP 2026 (Indian Conference on Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing), December 21-24, 2026, Kolkata, India. 9 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Scene Graph Anticipation (SGA) predicts object relationships in future video frames. Continuous-time SGA models evolve each subject-object pair with an independent Neural ODE, so relationships sharing an entity cannot influence one another during integration, and nothing prevents mutually exclusive predictions, such as "sitting on" and "standing on", for the same pair. We introduce CoupledSGA, which links such relationships through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and adds a Structural Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{SC}$) based on a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates.
Developing CoupledSGA revealed a limitation of the evaluation protocol. With-Constraint evaluation keeps one predicate per group for each subject-object pair, so its R@K and mR@K cannot capture the within-group violations targeted by $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$: we prove they are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and its score are held fixed. We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency.
On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.

[666] arXiv:2611.06741 [pdf, html, other]
Title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
Ruikang Li, Zixuan Chen, Jiarui Wu, Mingde Yao, Yiyuan Zhang, Yujin Wang, Hanming Deng, Lewei Lu, Tianfan Xue
Comments: 16 pages, 9 figures. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training. TailSteer follows a simple principle: keep early denoising dynamics close to those of the base model and concentrate preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. These corrections are learned from the editor's own on-policy denoising rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference without requiring curated ground-truth editing pairs. Experiments across the FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen families show that TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models after TailSteer, rather than by relearning their existing capabilities.

[667] arXiv:2611.06743 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Using AI Predictions to Augment Rather Than Replace Surveys
Lai Wei, Yifei Zhu
Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY)

LLMs can predict human survey responses with nontrivial accuracy. What this means for the future of social surveys remains hotly contested. Optimists anticipate a coming era of synthetic respondents; skeptics see a fragile and overhyped substitute. This article advocates a position: AI predictions cannot replace surveys, but they can augment them. Using prediction-powered inference (PPI), a statistical framework rooted in survey methodology and known in sociology as "mixed subjects design", the study tests whether AI predictions can improve the statistical efficiency of social surveys when combined with census-scale auxiliary information. Applying the framework to 83 social outcomes in the General Social Survey (GSS) and National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), with American Community Survey (ACS) being the auxiliary file, we find that supervised predictors yield effective-sample-size gains of about 7-12 percent when estimating the mean, while LLM gains are smaller but positive.

[668] arXiv:2611.06745 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Generalized Sorting via Four-Cycles
Soheil Behnezhad, Shane Ferrante
Comments: 22 pages, 2 figures
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We study the generalized sorting problem where only a subset of the pairs can be compared. Equivalently, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge graph $G=(V, E)$ where the vertex set $V$ is to be sorted, and the edge set $E$ indicates possible comparisons. The goal is to sort $V$ with as few (adaptive) queries to $E$ as possible.
When $G$ is the complete graph, the problem is equivalent to standard sorting for which $\Theta(n \log n)$ queries are sufficient and necessary. All classical sorting algorithms crucially rely on the ability to compare any pair and do not imply an $o(n^2)$-query algorithm in the general case. This was improved 15 years ago by Huang, Kannan, and Khanna [FOCS'11] who achieved a bound of $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$. Kuszmaul and Narayanan [FOCS'21] later gave a bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{m n})$, which is more efficient for sparse graphs, but matches the $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for dense graphs.
In this paper, we present an algorithm for generalized sorting that makes at most $\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})$ queries, therefore breaking the longstanding $\widetilde{O}(n\sqrt{n})$ barrier for all graphs. The key to our result is to query edges that belong to many (specific types of) four-cycles. We show that querying such edges allows the algorithm to verify the direction of many other edges (specifically, their opposing edges in the four-cycles) and thus achieve a much better amortized query cost.

[669] arXiv:2611.06747 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Fixed-Radius Neighbourhoods in Three-Dimensional Unit-Cube Graphs
Guangjian Zhang
Comments: 30 pages
Subjects: Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Combinatorics (math.CO)

We prove Conjecture 4 of Chan, Chang, Gao, Kisfaludi-Bak, Le, and Zheng (SoCG 2026): for every fixed integer $r\ge0$, the radius-$r$ neighbourhoods of a unit-cube graph in $\mathbb{R}^3$ have bounded VC-dimension. Our bound is $2^{2^{O(r)}}$, independent of the number of vertices. The main ingredient is a VC-dimension bound for reachability through arbitrary fixed-length sequences of three-dimensional generalized dominance relations. Its proof uses groups ordered in two coordinates, with neighbouring groups acting as barriers that preserve this invariant when one layer is removed. Combining these bounds with the existing interval-representation framework, we obtain a Las Vegas algorithm that, for every fixed integer $\Delta\ge1$, decides whether a graph given by $n$ cube centres has diameter at most $\Delta$ in expected $O_\Delta(n^{2-\varepsilon_\Delta})$ time, for an explicit constant $\varepsilon_\Delta>0$. Finally, for every integer $r\ge7$, we construct unit-cube graphs with rational centres whose radius-$r$ neighbourhoods have VC-dimension $\Omega(r^3)$.

[670] arXiv:2611.06748 [pdf, html, other]
Title: EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models
Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.

[671] arXiv:2611.06754 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Unified Framework for Extending Centrality Measures to Groups
Piotr Kępczyński, Oskar Skibski
Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)

We propose a unified framework for extending centrality measures from individual nodes to groups. For each centrality measure, we introduce four group variants---maximum, minimum, sum, and proportional---which differ in how individual contributions are aggregated at the group level. The framework builds on a new unified perspective on major classes of centrality measures, according to which the score of a node can be expressed as a sum of assessments made by individual nodes, pairs of nodes, or groups of nodes. Each of the four variants then corresponds to a different rule for aggregating the assessments of the members of a group.

[672] arXiv:2611.06759 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Continual Classification Beyond the Kernel Regime: Harnessing the Sparsity Bias of L2 Regularization in Diagonal Linear Networks
Gilad Karpel, Itay Evron, Ron Meir, Daniel Soudry
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We study logistic regression for continual learning with linear predictors in a high-dimensional statistical setting. Existing theoretical work has largely focused on continual linear regression with variants of L2 regularization, motivated by their analytical simplicity and connection to the kernel regime of neural networks. We first derive the optimal L2 regularization strength for continual linear classification and characterize its generalization performance, recovering behavior analogous to prior results for continual linear regression. Next, we examine the effect of L2 regularization in deeper models using a minimal two-layer diagonal linear network. In the single-task setting, L2 regularization on the weights of such models is known to promote sparsity in the resulting predictor, yielding a rich, sparse feature-learning regime beyond the kernel regime (a similar effect arises in two-layer ReLU networks). However, in continual learning, where L2 regularization is typically centered on previous-task weights, this sparsity bias is no longer preserved. We therefore propose a weighted variant of L2 regularization that extends this beneficial sparsity bias to continual learning. We show theoretically and empirically that, for a sufficiently sparse teacher, our variant converges substantially faster than directly learning a linear predictor with conventional continual L2 or L1 regularization, trading some long-horizon bias for markedly improved performance over moderate task horizons.

[673] arXiv:2611.06760 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Route First, See Later: Enabling Vision Agents to Reason Scientifically by Separating Routing Policy from Action Spaces
Shubhabrata Mukherjee, Jeffrey Donatelli, Daniela Ushizima
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Scientific image-analysis workflows require agents to select among diverse capabilities like description, detection, counting, and segmentation. Current multi-tool architectures conflate intent interpretation with visual execution, masking whether a failure arises from flawed reasoning (misrouting) or failed perception (invalid tool execution). This lack of auditability renders agents unreliable for high-stakes scientific automation. We introduce ZETA, an extensible architecture that operationalizes the decoupling of routing policy from action execution. ZETA resolves scientific intent before invoking specialized visual tools, treating measurement as a deterministic operation grounded in explicit geometry rather than generative output. This architecture exposes the "black box" of agent decision-making, allowing routing correctness and downstream execution to be evaluated as independent failure modes.
To our knowledge, we provide the first controlled study in scientific vision-agent routing that isolates explicit routing-policy specification while holding the legal action interface fixed. Evaluation on a zero-shot benchmark of 51 scientific-intent queries shows that explicit routing semantics can substantially improve routing accuracy, particularly at semantically adjacent action boundaries, although improvements vary across models. For Qwen 3.8, explicit routing-policy specification improves segmentation routing accuracy from 6.2% to 75.0% and detection routing accuracy from 60.0% to 100%. ZETA's execution traces make routing decisions and downstream artifacts separately observable, providing a basis for distinguishing intent-selection errors from visual execution failures. ZETA establishes the necessary infrastructure to isolate execution errors from interpretive ones, a critical requirement for deploying reliable scientific vision agents.

[674] arXiv:2611.06762 [pdf, html, other]
Title: U.S. State Guidance on AI in K-12 Education: A Comparative Content and Citation Analysis
Shahan Ali Memon, Anna-Maria Gueorguieva, Anukriti Kumar, Lucy Lu Wang, Jevin D. West, Nic Weber
Comments: 29 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables, Under Review
Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY); Digital Libraries (cs.DL)

In the years following the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, more than half of U.S. states have published formal guidelines around AI usage in K-12 education, creating a record of largely independent state education departments responding to a shared technological disruption. In this work, we analyze publicly available AI usage guidance documents from 35 states in the U.S. and Puerto Rico. We compare the guidance in these documents across various dimensions, including pedagogy and instruction, audience, actionability, workforce and career readiness, responsible use and equity, and alignment with state-level demographics and administrative capacity. Finally, we investigate who authored these documents and their cited sources, identifying epistemic foundations underlying their claims. We find that guidance priorities converge on topics anchored in laws such as data privacy and academic integrity, each addressed in 97% of documents. While most documents mention equity of access (86%) and algorithmic bias (97%), fewer discuss specific marginalized populations. Across documents, there is a common framing of urgency around AI integration to prepare students for workforce readiness (86%) and promote loosely-defined personalized learning (86%), which is not matched by specific guidance for capacity-building, actionability, or accountability. State priorities show no relationship to state demographics, capacity, or partisanship. Instead, we identify notable interdependencies between states with shared citations to non-profit organizations like TeachAI and this http URL, with some states reproducing TeachAI's model guidance near-verbatim, and peer citations concentrating on a few early states such as Oregon and Washington. No state includes parents as contributors on these documents, and only five include students.

[675] arXiv:2611.06764 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Rethinking Access Control for AI Agents: Recent Advances and Open Challenges
Chijin Zhou, Quan Zhang
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Large language model agents access data, invoke tools, and act on users' behalf. Keeping these actions within authorized bounds is challenging because agents choose their own execution paths while permissions and operating conditions may change. This paper surveys recent advances in agent access control across four areas: policy specification and derivation, identity and delegation, action and resource enforcement, and information flow control. We compare their control objects, enforcement boundaries, and assumptions to examine what individual mechanisms achieve and how they can work together. Building on this analysis, we rethink four aspects of authorization: plan selection shapes permission requirements; contextual information can inform decisions without itself granting authority; restrictions must retain their meaning across system interfaces; and authorization must be reassessed as workflows evolve. These insights motivate open challenges and future directions, together with concrete research questions and evaluation criteria. In particular, evaluation should examine both observed agent behavior and the unauthorized effects that remain enabled. Our analysis connects existing mechanisms to the requirements for preserving authorization throughout an agent workflow.

[676] arXiv:2611.06768 [pdf, html, other]
Title: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World
Qiang Wang, Jianxin Bi, Shulong Jiang, Ruiyang Si, Wenbo Huang, Kaiqi Chen, Jiaxin Li, Liyun Li, Xuanyi Li, Daquan Zhou
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

[677] arXiv:2611.06770 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management
Jiawei Zhang, Rizhao Cai, Dayan Guan
Comments: Accepted by IEEE AP-GARSS 2026; 4 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Fine-grained visual reasoning is essential for remote sensing in urban management, yet remains underexplored in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We introduce UMBench, a fine-grained urban remote sensing benchmark built from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) images for multiple urban management tasks such as traffic monitoring, urban construction, environmental quality, and disaster warning. Evaluations on UMBench reveal that current MLLMs often rely on scene-level priors and overlook fine-grained visual evidence. To address this issue, we further propose a novel evidence-first chain-of-thought method that directs models to inspect fine-grained visual evidence in a training-free manner. Experiments show that our method can improve the performance of both open-source and commercial MLLMs on UMBench.

[678] arXiv:2611.06772 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Energy Efficient Near-Threshold Voltage Massive MIMO Computing
MD Salman Sakib, Mehdi Safarpour, Pejman Ghasemzadeh, Shahriar Shahabuddin
Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR)

Near-Threshold Computing (NTC) offers a substan- tial energy savings, i.e., up to 10x, for digital circuits. However, due to Process, Voltage, and Temperature (PVT) variations, low voltage operating digital processors face increased susceptibility to timing errors. This work equips conventional massive MIMO algorithms with computational error detection mechanisms, en- abling reliable operation down to near-threshold voltages. While conventional hardware based Timing Error Detection (TED) systems introduce substantial overhead, this work modifies MIMO algorithms to seamlessly integrate low overhead Algorithm Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT). A co-simulation framework combining transistor level SPICE simulations and workload aware fault injection is developed to investigate reliability, Bit Error Rate (BER), energy savings, and overheads of modified algorithms operating at low voltages. The transistor-level characterization was performed in PSpice using generic Level-1 Shichman-Hodges CMOS transistor models with Monte Carlo parameter variations. No specific CMOS fabrication process node was assumed. Conse- quently, the reported energy savings are analytical estimates and are not specific to a particular CMOS fabrication technology. We evaluate Gauss Seidel (GS), ADMM based infinity norm detection (ADMIN), and Conjugate Gradient (CG) detectors using circuit derived fault models. Results demonstrate remarkable algorith- mic resilience. Although undetected computational errors in some trials near the Point of First Failure (PoFF) were observed, BER increases by only 0.7% to 1.4%, while beyond PoFF, ABFT reported nearly all erroneous cases. The proposed checksum based ABFT detects most arithmetic and memory errors, with an estimated overhead below 2% for a 64 x 16 MIMO system, decreasing further for larger configurations.

[679] arXiv:2611.06773 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Approximation and Hardness for the Data Validation Problem
Antoine Tinguely, G. Wessel van der Heijden
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

Finnah, Gönsch and Otto [Eur. J. Oper. Res. 2025] recently introduced the Data Validation Problem (DVP): Given a transitive directed acyclic graph $G$ on $n$ vertices (resp. tasks) and $m$ edges (resp. precedences) and a probing budget, a policy can successively pay a probing fee and probe an edge in $G$ as long as the total probing fees do not exceed the budget. If a probe succeeds, the targeted edge $e$ is removed from $G$ and we receive a reward; if the probe fails, the edge stays in $G$ and cannot be probed again. We seek a policy with maximum expected cumulative reward. Crucially, $G$ must stay transitive throughout the probing process, so a policy can only challenge the precedence between consecutive tasks, that is, only probe edges in the transitive reduction of the current precedence graph.
We show that DVP is strongly NP-hard and W[1]-hard with the probing budget $T$ as a parameter, even in the deterministic case (when every probe has probability $0$ or $1$ to succeed) and with unit probing costs and rewards. For the same setting, we give an approximation-preserving reduction from the Densest $k$-Subgraph (D$k$S) Problem, with the consequence that there is no polynomial-time $2^{(\log n)^{1-\delta}}$-approximation algorithm and no FPT $\sqrt{T}$-approximation algorithm for DVP, assuming the Almost-Exponential Time Hypothesis and the Strongish Planted Clique Hypothesis, respectively.
We also present the first known policies with provable worst-case guarantees for DVP, namely an $m$-approximation algorithm for instances with uniform probabilities and probing costs, a $2T/p_{\min}^T$-approximation algorithm for general instances, where $p_{\min}$ is the minimum probing success probability, and an exact FPT algorithm on tournament graphs, in the deterministic setting.

[680] arXiv:2611.06775 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Stability and Perfection in Constrained Weighted Network Games
Julien Fixary, Rémi Castera, Rida Laraki
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Theoretical Economics (econ.TH)

We introduce a general framework of constrained weighted network formation in which agents allocate resources across coalitional interactions while facing feasibility constraints. More precisely, we allow arbitrary coalitions of agents to be assigned a continuous weight, and we incorporate both coalitional capacity constraints and individual budget constraints into the model. This framework extends the weighted network formation model of Bich and Morhaim by combining continuous interaction intensities with endogenous feasibility restrictions. Within this setting, we introduce a new notion of stability -- called coalitionwise stability -- extending pairwise stability to constrained network games. Under standard continuity and componentwise quasiconcavity assumptions on payoff functions, we establish the existence of coalitionwise stable networks. We then investigate refinements of stability inspired by the notion of perfect equilibrium introduced by Selten, and by the notion of perfect pairwise stability developed by Bich and Teteryatnikova for network games. The presence of feasibility constraints fundamentally alters the geometry of the feasible set, which no longer possesses a product structure. As a consequence, trembling-hand type refinements become substantially more delicate, since perturbations of some interactions may render other interactions infeasible. Nevertheless, we introduce constrained analogues of both the trembling-hand and perturbative notions of perfect stability considered by Bich and Teteryatnikova, and study their existence and their relationship. In particular, we show the equivalence between these trembling-hand and perturbative formulations under some componentwise monotonicity assumption.

[681] arXiv:2611.06776 [pdf, other]
Title: Finding full immersions is fixed-parameter tractable in labeled tour graphs
Hadas Barabash, Jim Geelen, Rose McCarty, Caleb McFarland, Paul Wollan
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Combinatorics (math.CO)

We give an $O_H(n^5)$-time algorithm to test whether an $n$-vertex labeled tour graph has a full immersion isomorphic to a labeled tour graph $H$. A labeled tour graph is a connected $4$-regular graph whose edges are labeled by binary vectors of fixed length. To obtain a full immersion, a vertex may be removed only by pairing up its four incident edges and "splitting off" both pairs, summing the labels within each pair. Even for one-bit labels, no polynomial-time algorithm was previously known for arbitrary fixed $H$. Our main tool is of independent interest: we give an algorithmic min-max theorem that, in particular, characterizes the maximum number of odd-length circuits in a rooted circuit decomposition of an Eulerian graph.
Our results have implications for vertex-minors, whose study is motivated by applications in quantum networking, connections with graph minor theory, and the goal of developing an irrelevant vertex technique for dense graphs. For vertex-minors, circle graphs play the same role as planar graphs do for graph minors. As a corollary of our main theorem, we obtain a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for apex-vertex-minor testing in $k$-apex circle graphs. We also prove an irrelevant vertex theorem for such graphs of large rank-width. More broadly, our results are essential to forthcoming work of three of the authors proving a structure theorem for graphs with a forbidden vertex-minor. There, our min-max theorem plays the role of both the algorithmic $A$-paths and Two Paths Theorems.

[682] arXiv:2611.06777 [pdf, html, other]
Title: WISE: An Agentic Framework for Whole-page Multimodal Search Experience Attribution
Wenyi Xu, Renzhe Zhou, Songyang Li, Feiran Zhu, Ruoqi Zhao, Chenglei Dai, Xuanping Li, Kaiqiao Zhan, Jingwei Zhuo
Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

Algorithm-driven services, including search, recommendation, and advertising, rely on multi-stage model pipelines. While research prioritizes model optimization, post-deployment monitoring focuses on operational reliability. Yet operationally healthy systems may still produce poor-quality results, exposing a gap in existing evaluation and monitoring practices. However, a systematic problem formulation and benchmark for this task remain lacking. To bridge this gap, we formulate System Quality Diagnosis (SQD) for algorithm-driven services, a new task that extends quality evaluation beyond identifying poor outcomes to attributing their causes across system components. Focusing on industrial search, we propose WISE, an agentic framework for end-to-end quality diagnosis that discovers user-facing issues and traces their origins to underlying algorithmic components. To improve diagnostic reliability, we introduce ReTrace for constructing evidence-consistent trajectory supervision and Adaptive Harness-Policy Optimization (AHPO) for failure-guided optimization of the agent harness and model policy. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct WISE-BENCH, a real-world multimodal search benchmark that combines user-facing evidence, internal pipeline traces, and expert diagnosis annotations. Extensive experiments show consistent gains across model scales, with WISE achieving 75.20% end-to-end accuracy on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. In production, WISE supports quality auditing, online quality assurance, and model optimization, reducing diagnosis costs and improving downstream relevance models.

[683] arXiv:2611.06781 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Semantic Residual Vector Quantization for Sign Language Generation
Chang Liu, Ke Han, Niccolò Biondi, Gloria Isotton, Elisa Ricci, Davide Talon, Nicu Sebe
Comments: Accepted to WACV 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Sign language generation (SLG) maps written sentences into signing motion while preserving both lexical content and fine-grained articulation. This requires a model to decide what signs should be expressed and to realize them through precise handshape, trajectory, facial expression and body coordination. Existing pose-based systems and reconstruction-only motion tokenizers often entangle these two decisions, leaving the generator without an explicit text-aligned intermediate target for what to sign before refining how to sign it. To address this issue, we introduce Semantic Residual Vector Quantization (SRVQ), a framework for SLG that frames generation as a two-level process moving from semantics to kinematics. The newly introduced SRV Quantizer learns a hierarchy in which the first residual level encodes sign content and subsequent levels refine pose, handshape, trajectory, and body coordination, all within a single quantizer and without separate semantic representations or external planning stages. Through word-aware conditioning for hierarchical code generation, a masked semantic generator predicts semantic codes and a kinematic generator completes the residual codes for full SMPL-X motion synthesis. We evaluate using retrieval and FID in a shared text-motion embedding space, alongside standard geometric metrics. On CSL-Daily and Phoenix-2014T, SRVQ achieves R@1 of 82.3 and 70.3, outperforming the previous SOTA by 30 and 46 points, respectively.

[684] arXiv:2611.06782 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Target PageRank: Matching Prescribed PageRank Scores via Budgeted Edge Additions
Parth Gupta, Abhinav Jain, Avishek Mukhopadhyay, Amitabha Bagchi, Sayan Ranu, Abhijnan Chakraborty
Comments: 16 pages, 12 figures
Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)

PageRank is widely used to quantify the importance of nodes in directed networks. In applications such as recommendation systems, it is increasingly important that the PageRank distribution provides a fair representation of node exposure. This motivates the problem of making minimal changes to a graph so that the PageRank values of a given set of target nodes $T$ match a desired vector $\boldsymbol{t}$. In this paper, we study this problem under an edge-addition budget $B$, where exactly $B$ edges may be added to the graph. We show that deciding whether a multiset of exactly $B$ added edges can make the target nodes attain their desired absolute PageRank scores is NP-complete. After this, we define the $\ell_1$ \textsc{Target PageRank} problem in which we seek to minimize the $\ell_1$ distance between the target vector and resultant vector. We show that this optimization problem admits no polynomial-time multiplicative constant-factor approximation unless $P=NP$. Motivated by these hardness results, we propose two greedy heuristics for approaching the target PageRank vector. We additionally propose a Random Walk Hungarian (RWH) heuristic that addresses the addition of edges between dissimilar nodes by incorporating a penalty for such edges. Finally, we evaluate the proposed heuristics on several real-world and synthetic datasets and compare their performance in terms of PageRank accuracy, computational efficiency, and the relevance of the added edges.

[685] arXiv:2611.06783 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
Quan Minh Nguyen, Hoang M. Ngo, Bhakti Chowkwale, Yasaman Keshtkarjahromi, My T. Thai
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher this http URL across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.

[686] arXiv:2611.06786 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
Andrea Cambiaghi, Marco Tarini
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants.
We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays.
We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at this http URL

[687] arXiv:2611.06788 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
Yu Zhang, JingQi Liu, Shuangrui Zhao, Yuanyu Zhang, Yulong Shen, Xiaohong Jiang
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Signal Processing (eess.SP)

Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions require both semantic information reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy designs in SemCom mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source legitimacy. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation paradigm for integrated SemCom-identity protection to address active source impersonation and passive identity inference by treating each SemCom signal as an inherent carrier of both task-relevant semantic information and transmitter physical identity information. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for trustworthy decision making, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism under different operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic recovery quality is maintained to support anonymous sensing reports. The resulting outputs are jointly interpreted to support task decisions under mode-specific identity protection requirements. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.

[688] arXiv:2611.06789 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Ranking Agreement Does Not Reveal Paragraph-Edit Agreement in Two Released Paper Acceptance Predictors
Shaoliang Yang, Jun Wang
Comments: 38 pages including supplementary methods and results; 10 figures and 22 tables
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

A fast acceptance classifier could select revisions for a slower evaluator. We ask whether agreement on existing papers supports that use. We compare a classifier of word and document features with two released text-only acceptance predictors fine-tuned from the same language model with three billion parameters. For 198 papers from the International Conference on Learning Representations, we compare model rankings of the original papers and of paragraph rewrites screened automatically for unchanged facts, claim strength, and attribution. The classifier ranks original papers closely with one predictor and moderately with the other, but shows no detectable agreement with either on which rewrites raise scores. The tests specified in advance used reduced numerical precision. Rounding error dominated the small score responses. We therefore rescored the released weights in full 32-bit precision as a post hoc check; edit agreement remained near zero. At this precision, when each predictor chooses among five rewrites per paper, its average raw score is under two points out of 100 higher than with random choice. The evidence covers presentation rewrites and two open predictors from one family; transfer to costly evaluators remains untested. Revision selectors should therefore be checked against the intended evaluator on the revisions they rank.

[689] arXiv:2611.06791 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Frame-Level View and Image-Quality Annotation Tool for Fetal Echocardiography: Comparison with Spreadsheet Annotation
Mohamed Azzam, Ziyang Xu, Quinlan Couch, Zoe Keese, Andrea Cadlo, Christine Sedze-DeWolf, Micaiah Uhrmacher, Madelyn Graff, Catherine Fox, Lauren Vatter, Paige Jeffryes, Jason Christensen, Neil Hamill, Shibiao Wan, Ling Li, Jieqiong Wang
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)

Objective: To develop the Cardiologist Annotation Tool (CAT) for frame-level cardiac view and image-quality annotation in fetal echocardiography and compare it with spreadsheet-based annotation.
Methods: CAT provides cine playback, frame navigation, and keyboard-based labeling without manual frame-range entry. Experts annotated 25 studies using both methods, and spreadsheet annotations were audited for predefined data-entry errors. In a randomized crossover study, six medical students annotated two normal studies, one with each method, against an expert reference.
Results: Among 1,746 spreadsheet-annotated files, 6.2% contained major or critical data-entry errors, more frequently in congenital heart disease than normal studies (10.9% vs 3.4%). CAT yielded more annotated view segments per clip (3.6 vs 1.5). Rates of labeled and correctly labeled frames per minute were 1.77 and 1.68 times those with spreadsheets, respectively (both P = 0.031), with gains in all six students. No detectable difference in view-label accuracy was observed.
Conclusion: CAT eliminates manual frame-range entry and enables finer-grained, structured annotation of fetal echocardiography, providing a practical approach to preparing datasets for AI research.

[690] arXiv:2611.06793 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Transforming Integer Grids to Spatial Intuition: Perception, Not Planning, Governs ARC-AGI-3
Harsidak Singh Banwait
Comments: 24 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to the ARC Prize 2026 paper track. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Sample-efficient fluid intelligence requires agents that rapidly form working models of unfamiliar interactive environments. ARC-AGI-3 tests this across uninstructed visual games scored by Relative Human Action Efficiency, which penalizes exploratory waste quadratically. When frontier models read raw integer grids, serialization destroys spatial topology, and they spend hundreds of actions rediscovering basic boundaries and symmetries. We introduce SARBLOH, an open-weight agent built on the premise that spatial perception, not planning capacity, governs interactive reasoning on ARC-AGI-3. A zero-parameter O(HW) perception engine turns each frame, in 35 ms, into an object inventory with bipartite temporal tracking, a geometric briefing that separates proven invariants from affordance hypotheses, and an annotated canvas. Paired with a code-as-action runtime, the agent writes algorithmic hypotheses instead of low-level moves. Across eight presentations, grounded perception raises the rubric score from 3/28 to 25/28 points while cutting token use by 89.4%. On 23 held-out games, geometric invariants generalize with 100% accuracy, while single-frame affordance guesses fall to 6-50%, so active verification probes remain necessary. On the public set, Run A (briefing off) solved 143 of 183 levels in 8.2 hours at 59.4% single-pass efficiency; Run B (briefing on) reached 63.5%. Within the nine-hour budget on one Kaggle RTX PRO 6000 GPU, SARBLOH scored 16.53 on the hidden Kaggle evaluation, 13.7x the first Milestone winner.

[691] arXiv:2611.06796 [pdf, html, other]
Title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu
Comments: Project Page: this https URL Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.

[692] arXiv:2611.06801 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Message-passing graph persistence
Jorge Luiz Franco, Arthur Queiroz Moura, Moacir Ponti, Amauri Souza
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Message-passing graph neural networks (GNNs) are limited in expressive power by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman test. Persistent homology (PH) provides topological descriptors that can complement GNN representations, but existing approaches typically compute persistence separately from the representation learning process. In this paper, we introduce Message-Passing Graph Persistence (MGP), a family of topological descriptors that incorporates message passing into graph filtrations. At each filtration step, node embeddings are updated using the current subgraph and associated with persistence events. These embeddings also determine the representatives of connected components during persistence computation. We prove that MGP is invariant under graph isomorphism and that it is strictly more expressive than the PH-based descriptors it extends. We evaluate MGP on an expressivity benchmark and on several graph classification and regression datasets. Experiments show that MGP outperforms other PH-based descriptors on most of these datasets.

[693] arXiv:2611.06802 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
Kendra Givens, Taylor T. Johnson, Bryan C. Ward, Thomas Beckers
Comments: 8 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $\epsilon$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $\epsilon\tau$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $\epsilon$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

[694] arXiv:2611.06803 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Task-Efficient Agent Evaluation Using Cached Traces
Ben Johnson, Hayden Helm
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Efficient benchmarking estimates a system's full benchmark performance from a small number of task executions. Standard approaches rely solely on the binary correctness of executions from a collection of already-evaluated reference systems. An agentic system, however, produces a rich trace for each execution that can reveal substantially more about its capabilities. Leveraging this information requires useful trace representations. We propose representing a trace by extracting a structured summary of it with an LLM and embedding the summary with a standard text encoder. These representations preserve correctness- and task-related signal while minimizing the presence of system identity-, model family- and harness-related signals that dominate raw trace embeddings. Given this representation for each task execution from all reference systems, we construct low-dimensional representations of the systems and predict a new system's score from its position among the reference systems. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0, augmenting an item-response model with this geometry-based prediction reduces mean absolute error from 0.13 to 0.08 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-4}$) and from 0.14 to 0.12 (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-3}$), respectively, when provided a single random executed task. Further, given access to the full set of reference systems, our approach dominates baselines for any given number of executed tasks on both benchmarks.

[695] arXiv:2611.06804 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Monadically Dependent Graph Classes Have Almost Bounded Merge-Width
Jan Dreier, Nikolas Mählmann, Michał Pilipczuk, Szymon Toruńczyk
Subjects: Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Combinatorics (math.CO); Logic (math.LO)

A graph class $\mathcal{C}$ is monadically dependent if one cannot interpret all graphs in vertex-colored graphs from $\mathcal{C}$ using a fixed formula of first-order logic. We prove that every monadically dependent graph class has almost bounded merge-width, thereby confirming a conjecture of the first and the last author [STOC '25]. Our proof is algorithmic and the witnessing decompositions in the form of merge sequences can be computed in nearly-cubic time. This is a step towards the proof of fixed-parameter tractability of model checking first-order logic on monadically dependent graph classes, which is achieved in a companion paper.

[696] arXiv:2611.06806 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Measuring Risk, Not Harm: Detecting Psychological Harm Risk Factors in LLM Conversations
Nil-Jana Akpinar, Eugenia Kim, Natalie Isak, Amanda Minnich, Victoria Westerhoff, Matthew Dressman
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Psychological harms from interactions with large language models cannot be monitored directly because they may emerge over repeated interactions and depend strongly on subjective individual user context. We propose measuring risk, not harm: detecting observable AI behaviors that constitute risk factors for psychological harm at the AI response level and aggregating these signals to support longitudinal monitoring. We operationalize eight such behaviors and construct a synthetic multi-label corpus of 47,062 AI responses and 373,873 response-factor labels, with targeted human annotations for validation and evaluation. We then compare trained embedding-based classifiers, direct LLM judging, and a classifier--judge cascade. All detectors are model-agnostic and operate only on LLM outputs, requiring no access to internal model states. We apply these detectors to several out-of-distribution human-AI conversation data sets from prior research. On held-out human-labeled data, the best cascade achieves macro precision of 0.86, recall of 0.76, and F1 of 0.79. On WildChat, it reduces LLM-judge calls by 97.1\% relative to direct judging. On DelusionEval, risk-factor detections cluster within conversations. Together, our results show that response-level behavioral risk-factor detection can provide a scalable measurement layer for longitudinal psychological-safety monitoring without conflating observable AI behavior with latent user harm.

[697] arXiv:2611.06808 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
Lingfei Qian, Yan Wang, Xueqing Peng, Yupeng Cao, Yuechen Jiang, Zhuohan Xie, Anke Xu, Wenbo Cao, Jiarui Chen, Zehan Li, Jimin Huang, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Yuehua Tang, Sophia Ananiadou, Jian-Yun Nie
Comments: 20 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

[698] arXiv:2611.06812 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SAUCE: Summary Analysis Using Conversation Entailment
Man-Ling Sung, Hemanth Kandula, Jeff Ma, William Hartmann, Matthew Snover
Comments: Accepted and published to the ACL GEM workshop. Proceedings of the Fifth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics (GEM), pages 364-377, San Diego, California, USA. Association for Computational Linguistics
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)

With the growing need for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) and their applications to speech, challenges persist in summarizing and evaluating conversations that lack a clear end goal. We introduce SAUCE -- a reference-free, fact-based evaluation pipeline for cross-lingual conversational speech summarization. It measures the accuracy and the fact coverage of a summary through the entailment between conversation and text. We compare SAUCE against several popular summarization metrics and demonstrate the effectiveness of capturing information loss due to transcription and translation error and identifying broken summaries. Crucially, unlike black-box LLM evaluators or dense embedding metrics, SAUCE is inherently explainable: it maps summary scores to discrete, verifiable facts, allowing users to pinpoint exact hallucinations or omissions. We illustrate how this interpretability helps developers systematically profile LLM behaviors and gives end-users an actionable tool to verify summary accuracy in noisy, real-world conditions. Preliminary investigations show SAUCE strongly align with human judgment.

[699] arXiv:2611.06813 [pdf, html, other]
Title: The 3-Uniform Hyperclique Hypothesis is False
Timothy M. Chan, Reina Itakura, Zhiyuan Ma, Yuancheng Yu
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We present truly subquartic algorithms for detecting or counting 4-hypercliques in a 3-uniform hypergraph with $n$ vertices, disproving a popular hypothesis in fine-grained complexity. The result immediately implies a faster algorithm for finding a $k$-hyperclique in a 3-uniform hypergraph for all constant $k\ge 4$, and a faster exponential-time algorithm for Max-3-SAT.

[700] arXiv:2611.06816 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Boxicity of Power Graphs of Finite Nilpotent Groups
L. Sunil Chandran, Jinia Ghosh, Suraj Kumar Sahoo
Comments: 28 pages
Subjects: Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM); Combinatorics (math.CO); Group Theory (math.GR)

The \textit{boxicity} of an undirected graph $\Gamma$, denoted as $\operatorname{box}(\Gamma)$, is the smallest non-negative integer $d$ such that $\Gamma$ can be represented as the intersection graph of axis-parallel rectangular boxes in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The \emph{power graph} of a group $G$, denoted as $\operatorname{Pow}(G)$, is an undirected graph whose vertex set is the group itself, with two elements being adjacent if one is a power of the other.
We determine the exact boxicity of power graphs of finite nilpotent groups. For a cyclic group of order $n=\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i^{e_i}>1$, where the $p_i$ are distinct primes, we prove that its power graph has boxicity $\sum_{i=1}^{r}e_i-\max_i e_i$. For a finite nilpotent group $G$, let the number of noncyclic odd Sylow subgroups be denoted by $t(G)$. If $G$ has odd order or if $G$ has a cyclic Sylow $2$-subgroup, then $\operatorname{box}(\operatorname{Pow}(G))=\operatorname{box}(\operatorname{Pow}(\mathbb{Z}_{\operatorname{exp}(G)}))+t(G)$, where $\operatorname{exp}(G)$ denotes the \emph{exponent} of a group $G$. When the Sylow $2$-subgroup is noncyclic, and the odd part is nontrivial, the boxicity equals this value or one more, and we characterise precisely when each of these values is attained.
The boxicity of power graphs of arbitrary finite groups and the exact boxicity of the comparability graph of the Boolean lattice were posed as open questions in Discrete Mathematics, 349(7):115017, 2026. As a consequence of our results, we answer the latter question completely and the former question partially, by computing the exact boxicity of the power graphs of nilpotent groups.

[701] arXiv:2611.06817 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
Juncheng Ma, Jiaxin Li, Jiankai Tu, Bo Liang, Guodong Lv, Yufan Deng, Junzhe Tang, Liangzhu Yang, Chen Bian, Zicong Cao, Baohao Zhu, Jianxin Bi, Tengfei Yan, Yinyuan Zhang, Kewei Zhang, Xinglong Chen, Kaiqi Chen, Duomin Wang, Xiaotian Tang, Liang Tan, Li Li, Yuan Xu, Haosen Yang, Yuqi Wang, Jingfei Xia, Songyan Huang, Zhiyang Dou, Zhen Dong, Enze Xie, Tat-Seng Chua, Daquan Zhou
Comments: GitHub: this https URL Project website: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

[702] arXiv:2611.06822 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Excitability of High-Frequency Positive Feedback
Gustave Bainier, Arthur Fyon, Christian Fernandez Lorden, Alessio Franci
Comments: 6 pages, 7 figures
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

What is the threshold of an excitable system, i.e. the criterion that distinguishes rest from excitation? Previous research has shown that this question is far from trivial to answer. This paper studies the threshold of a simple excitable primitive in which excitability arises from the positive feedback interconnection of a first-order high-pass filter and a static, strictly monotone and strictly convex activation function. This threshold is a simple inequality on the difference between the instantaneous input and the motif's internal memory. While this result may help neuro-engineers characterize spiking in biological and artificial neurons, we argue that excitability is not always a desirable property, and that our threshold may also be relevant to safety considerations in fragile systems with rate-induced tipping points. We illustrate our framework with three examples: the FitzHugh-Nagumo model of neuronal dynamics, a model of stop-loss cascades in the stock market, and a social contagion model.

[703] arXiv:2611.06827 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Rules, Traces and Routing Statistics: Training and Calibration Data for Open Models on ARC-AGI-2
Nguyen Minh Thang, Trinh Thi Phuong
Comments: 39 pages, 7 figures, 23 tables
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

We study which training and calibration data help three open models solve ARC-AGI-2 tasks when the solver runs offline on four L4 GPUs for at most 12 hours. We compare data offline on public tasks and report 189 runs on the 120 hidden semi-private tasks. For the NVARC Qwen3-4B grid model, we built a corpus of 12,000 executable rules in a typed language and 95,993 tasks; a rule is admitted only if its behaviour on a fixed probe set differs from that of every admitted rule, and a task only if its pairs refute a shortlist of nearest competing rules and defeat 12 shortcut solvers. Continued fine-tuning on 1,920 real task records with revised four-GPU scheduling raised the semi-private score from 28.96 (mean of the released model) to 33.06 (mean of five runs, best 34.86); no checkpoint trained with synthetic tasks, even all 95,993 of them, improved on the real-task model. For the Qwen3.8-27B reasoning model, we fine-tuned on 1,036 of its own reasoning traces with correct final answers and compared sets that add traces of other models and synthetic tasks. With an inference procedure built around the model (a thinking cap enforced in the serving engine, a Python program checked on the demonstrations after each answer, a long first attempt per input), the score rose from 26.81 to 44.03, the level the ARC Prize Foundation measured for the base model without a time limit (42.36); most of the gain came from the inference procedure. For the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next mixture-of-experts model (125B parameters, 6B active), GPU memory limited concurrency. Pruning from 512 to 384 experts per layer by router-weighted activation saliency grew the key-value cache from 0.55M to 1.39M tokens; a 296-expert list adapted with ARC routing statistics, keeping experts for program tokens, plus an FP8 indexer cache, reached 1.96M. With a tool that checks programs, the model scored 56.67, our best result.

[704] arXiv:2611.06828 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
Gagik Amirkhanyan, Nuojin Cheng
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs.

[705] arXiv:2611.06829 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
David Rostcheck
Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.

[706] arXiv:2611.06832 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Coexistence-Aware Antenna Tilt and Resource Allocation for Cellular-Connected UAV Corridors
Tarun Singh Rawat, Pradyumna Kumar Bishoyi
Comments: 6 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in IEEE ANTS 2026 Conference WS-08
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)

Cellular-connected UAV corridors reuse terrestrial infrastructure to provide predictable aerial connectivity, but coexistence with ground users (GUEs) creates competing demands on antenna tilt and physical resource blocks (PRBs). Prior work optimizes tilt for signal quality alone and does not address joint tilt-PRB planning under corridor rate and GUE delay constraints, nor the allocation policy needed when combined resource claims exceed the PRB budget. We address both gaps by formulating a joint antenna-tilt and PRB-allocation problem that maximizes GUE sum-log-rate subject to a minimum UAV corridor rate and an $ M/G/1$-based GUE mean-delay bound. We decompose the problem into two subproblems: antenna tilts are adapted via projected gradient ascent, while PRB allocation follows a techno-economic approach. Under resource scarcity, we cast the PRB scarcity as a bankruptcy problem and apply the weighted Talmud rule to balance GUE and UAV claims. Simulation results demonstrate that relaxing the GUE delay bound consistently reduces UAV rate dissatisfaction under the proposed allocation.

[707] arXiv:2611.06835 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)
