Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.

[708] arXiv:2611.06837 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token
Tommy He, Thomas Jiralerspong
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated.

[709] arXiv:2611.06838 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Context-Aware Autoregressive Image Generation for Emerging Reasoning Properties
Jixuan Ying, Haoyu Liu, Timing Yang, Tingyu Zhu, Predrag Neskovic, Anand Bhattad, Cihang Xie, Zeyu Zheng, Alan Yuille, Feng Wang
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 16 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Autoregressive image generation has recently emerged as a competitive visual generation paradigm, yet its generation order is often predefined or heuristic, such as next-patch prediction, random-order prediction, or one-step generation for specific scales. We observe that these strategies can cause models to overlook important structural dependencies in images, thereby limiting both structural robustness and reasoning capability. In this work, we propose a context-aware autoregressive generation framework, where the model dynamically determines the next token location based on global context and current local information. Rather than following a fixed or random order, our method allows the generation process to adapt to image structure and semantic dependencies. Extensive experiments show that context-aware generation significantly improves structural robustness across different image AR paradigms, including masked autoregressive and scale-wise autoregressive models. Beyond quantitative improvements, we further observe emerging reasoning properties: the model can better understand complex semantic instructions and generate images that more faithfully follow the given guidance. These findings suggest that generation order is a critical yet underexplored factor in image autoregressive modeling, and that context-aware decoding can unlock stronger reasoning-aware visual generation capabilities. Code is available at this https URL.

[710] arXiv:2611.06839 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Before You Continue: Evaluating Time-Sensitive Safety Awareness in Conversational Assistants
Peidi Dong, Yunze Xiao, Yu-Lin Tsai, Yichen Zheng, Heyuan Huang, Weihao Xuan, Mark Dredze, Jen-tse Huang
Comments: Preprint
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large language model (LLM) assistants increasingly help users with everyday activities that involve time-dependent constraints. However, users may not mention these constraints in later requests, requiring assistants to recognize and adjust their advice accordingly. To evaluate such capability, we introduce TASC (Temporal Action Safety in Conversation), a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs apply time-dependent constraints when responding to conversational requests. TASC consists of 3,418 inputs derived from 128 templates, along with a separate set of 33 scenarios designed to compare models' ability to calculate elapsed time with their ability to apply that information. Across 13 models, assistants account for time-dependent constraints in only 30.5% of cases where the proposed action violates a rule, while rarely warning users unnecessarily. More importantly, models fail to apply these constraints in 62.1% of cases despite correctly calculating the elapsed time. Explicitly providing the timing resolves only about half of these failures, revealing a gap between temporal reasoning and its application in conversational advice.

[711] arXiv:2611.06840 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Same Layout, Different Count: What Number Words Do Past Ten in Text-to-Image Models
Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
Comments: 43 pages, including 32 pages of supplementary material; 14 figures, 44 tables
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Ask SD3.5-Medium for twelve of an object and then, from the same starting noise, for twenty-five. The picture keeps its layout, but the count changes about as much as it would under a new random seed, and in no consistent direction. We study what number words do once a request passes about ten objects, in five open text-to-image models. Holding the object and the starting noise fixed, we change one thing at a time, and people who never see the request count 3,088 of the images. Every model follows the number for small crowds, but only up to a point, its reach: SD3.5-M and FLUX.1-dev stop following it soon after ten, while FLUX.2 [klein] and Qwen-Image follow it loosely up to twenty-five. Beyond SD3.5-M's reach, the coarse part of the starting noise fixes the composition of the picture but not how many objects it holds: redrawing only the noise finer than an eighth of the image keeps the layout as well as a new number does, and already moves the count two-thirds as far. The number word still reaches the denoiser and acts in its first steps, but nothing we tried gives it a clear direction. Shown instead as a noised grid in the starting latent, the count is drawn: people find it in 59% of images, against 4% when it is only told. Past ten, an exact-match score barely separates a model that follows the number loosely from one that ignores it, and a relative-error score can even prefer a constant guess of sixteen. A same-noise test with a few requests per object tells them apart.

[712] arXiv:2611.06841 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
Xinrui Zhong, Zhiming Wang, Yongqi Liu, Zhaohui Wang, Shanglin Yang, Zikun Li, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.

[713] arXiv:2611.06844 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers
Yingying Yan, Jiaqi Tang, Wei Wei, Qianzhou Wang, Lei Zhang, Jianmin Chen, Yuyang Xia, Botong Geng, Jinjian Wu, Qifeng Chen
Comments: 24 pages (10 pages main text + references + appendix), 15 figures. Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA$^{I}$, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA$^{W}$) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: this https URL.

[714] arXiv:2611.06846 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness
Grant Shanklin, Jiří Němeček, Asia Biega
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.

[715] arXiv:2611.06848 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Persona Perspectives: Adopting Viewpoints Reorganizes Representations in LLMs
Austin C. Kozlowski, Avital Mintz, Madison Lee
Comments: 26 pages, 14 figures
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Common methods for monitoring features in large language models (LLMs) such as linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) assume that features maintain a consistent representation across contexts. LLMs, however, can flexibly adopt different perspectives or "personas" that suggest different underlying systems of conceptual relations. In this paper, we examine whether prompting an LLM to adopt a persona alters the representational geometry of the model's latent space. We extract representations of over 9,000 common words and 33 semantic axes from models adopting liberal and conservative political personas and compare these against two neutral baselines. We find that persona conditioning systematically alters both the projections of words onto semantic axes and the alignments among the axes themselves in directions consistent with the specified ideology. We then test the implications of this reorganization for two safety-relevant features: truthfulness and morality. Linear probes, SAE-based classifiers, and classifiers built from manually selected word representations, all trained without a persona, produce divergent results when applied to models conditioned on political personas, producing politically slanted ratings of truth and morality on controversial statements. These findings suggest that internal representations, as they are conventionally extracted, can exhibit different geometric relations when the model adopts personas, potentially undermining monitoring efforts.

[716] arXiv:2611.06849 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Trainspotting: Learning Object-Centric 3D Reconstruction from Found Photos
Hanyu Chen, Noah Snavely
Comments: project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

State-of-the-art feedforward reconstruction models perform poorly on in-the-wild object-centric photo collections. They are trained largely on single-session object captures whose images vary in viewpoint while the object and its environment remain nearly fixed. Public photo archives contain a different form of multi-view data. They hold found photos of the same object or design: photos taken independently by many people across years, environments, cameras, and sometimes physical units. In this work, we introduce Trainspotting, a dataset of 12,068 objects and 311,886 photos from Wikimedia Commons. We reconstruct each object to recover camera poses, multi-view stereo depth, and object masks. We categorize the objects into three regimes: objects fixed at one site, objects that move between sites, and designs shared by many physical units. Evaluating recent feedforward reconstruction models on Trainspotting shows that they fail most severely in the last two regimes. Fine-tuning VGGT-$\Omega$ on Trainspotting significantly improves camera pose, depth, and 3D geometry on held-out objects. We observe similar improvements on the independent NAVI in-the-wild benchmark, which contains photos of each object in different environments. Performance on conventional benchmarks remains largely unchanged.

[717] arXiv:2611.06850 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Extremal-Phase-Guided Sequential Convex Optimization: Model Order Reduction
Mustafa Oğuz Yeğin, Hitay Özbay, Tomáš Vyhlídal
Comments: 20 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables, submitted to International Journal of Control
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Fixed-order frequency-weighted H-infinity approximation is a nonconvex problem, and local optimization methods can be sensitive to initialization. We present extremal-phase-guided sequential convex optimization (EPGSCO) for stable fixed-order rational approximation. We introduce a novel phase-guidance technique motivated by the all-pass structure underlying optimal Hankel-norm approximation, with a phase template fitted to the error-magnitude derivative at dominant peaks. We integrate this guidance with dominant-peak selection, focused frequency grids, and adaptive pole-residue and polynomial-coefficient updates to address stagnation and improve approximation accuracy. CD-player examples and benchmarks with known optimal errors evaluate the algorithm against established methods. Comparisons with classical sequential convex optimization (SCO) under shared settings for the common components assess the combined contribution of phase guidance and adaptive frequency refinement. Results demonstrate improved accuracy in most of the tested cases and attainment of the known optimum from four tested initializations for a constructed order-42 benchmark, with additional computation in some cases.

[718] arXiv:2611.06854 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
Pranjal Aggarwal, Sean Welleck
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at this https URL

[719] arXiv:2611.06856 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
Haoxiang Cao, Yuxuan Zhang, Penghui Du, Bo Li, Jiajiong Cao, Yingying Fan, Zimeng Wu, Yifu Luo, Mingzhe Zheng, Junwen Miao, Huaisong Zhang, Yang Yao, Yu Wang, Dongfu Jiang, Ping Nie, Wenhu Chen, Chaoqun Wang, Changqian Yu, Kelsey R. Allen
Comments: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: this https URL.

[720] arXiv:2611.06857 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Deterministic Fault-Tolerant Connectivity Oracles with Subquadratic Space
Merav Parter, Elad Tzalik
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Combinatorics (math.CO)

A fault-tolerant (FT) connectivity oracle for an $n$-vertex graph $G=(V,E)$ determines whether $G- F$ is connected for any query set $F\subseteq E$. When the number of failures is unrestricted, prior constructions exhibited a sharp contrast between randomization and determinism: randomized oracles use only $\widetilde{O}(n)$ space [Duan and Pettie, SICOMP 2020], whereas no deterministic construction was known to improve upon storing $G$ explicitly, requiring $\Theta(n^2)$ bits in the worst case.
The promise that $F\subseteq E$ is essential for subquadratic space: allowing arbitrary queries $F\subseteq V\times V$ forces quadratic space. For queries containing at most $f$ failures, Khanna, Konrad, and Putterman [SODA 2027] recently constructed deterministic oracles using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{f}n)$ space that also report approximate distances with polylogarithmic stretch. Their result improves upon the classical $O(fn)$ space bound for deterministic connectivity oracles [Pătraşcu and Thorup, FOCS 2007], but offers no space savings over storing $G$ when $f=\Theta(n^2)$.
We present the first deterministic connectivity oracles with subquadratic space for failure sets of unrestricted size, using $\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})$ space. We also establish the first polynomial separation between deterministic and randomized connectivity oracles, proving that every deterministic oracle requires $\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})$ bits in the worst case. For queries containing at most $f$ failures, we obtain deterministic connectivity oracles using $\widetilde{O}(f^{2/5}n)$ space, improving the dependence on $f$ in the bound of Khanna et al., and prove a lower bound of $\widetilde{\Omega}(f^{1/4}n)$ bits.

[721] arXiv:2611.06858 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
Xinrui Zhong, Zhifeng Li, Zhiming Wang, Yongqi Liu, Shanglin Yang, Yang Zhou, Zikun Li, Zhuoming Chen, Beidi Chen
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

[722] arXiv:2611.06859 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings
Kai Ponel, Marco Polignano, Erasmo Purificato, Aylin Julia Temizkan, Marco Levantesi, Giovanni Semeraro, Ernesto William De Luca
Comments: 29 pages. Authors' version of the open access article published in Information Sciences (CC BY 4.0). This version corrects the second affiliation of Marco Polignano (Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg); the published version lists the European Commission, Joint Research Centre (JRC) in error. Marco Polignano is not affiliated with the JRC. No other content has been changed
Journal-ref: Information Sciences 763 (2027) 124271
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Hierarchical text embedding models offer variable-length representations, while quantization reduces numerical precision; both aim to improve computational efficiency. This work is an empirical benchmark study of how these two orthogonal, already-established techniques interact. We evaluate 38 tasks from the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) using four transformer-based embedding models, covering 1D and 2D hierarchical representations combined with 32-bit, 8-bit, and binary quantization, for 168 configurations per task. We report each efficiency dimension separately: theoretical per-vector storage and end-to-end evaluation time. Under a Friedman test with Nemenyi post-hoc analysis, int8 quantization is statistically indistinguishable from float32 for pair classification and re-ranking and costs at most 1.5 percentage points overall, whereas binary quantization is significantly worse across every task category. Halving the embedding dimension once is not statistically detectable above $m=16$; two successive halvings always are. Combining an 8x dimensionality reduction with int8 yields a 32x reduction in per-vector storage at 94.4% of baseline effectiveness. Because evaluation times were measured once, we treat them as indicative: we find no evidence that quantization speeds up evaluation, whereas sampling from intermediate layers shortens it substantially. Retrieval degrades far faster than every other category, so we report findings per task category.

[723] arXiv:2611.06863 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
Siddharth Aphale, Ayushman Singh
Comments: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Learn@Deploy workshop
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

[724] arXiv:2611.06864 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CounterFactual Retrieval for Evidence-Aware Individual Animal Identification
Ankit K. Upadhyay, Aleksandr Algasov, Ekaterina Nepovinnykh, Fedor Zolotarev, Tuomas Eerola, Heikki Kälviäinen, Charles V. Stewart, Lukas Picek
Comments: 14 pages, 5 figures; accepted at WACV 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Automated identification of individual animals is moving from small curated studies toward shared benchmarks and reusable foundation models. This progress is useful, but current evaluation leaves the evidence behind a match unresolved, i.e., high retrieval accuracy does not show whether a model used animal features or identity-correlated shortcuts. We address this with Counterfactual Foreground Retrieval (CFR), an evidence-aware evaluation protocol. CFR evaluates the same query-gallery task under different views: full image, foreground-only, and shortcut-only. The full-image measures standard retrieval performance; the foreground-only measures foreground-supported retrieval; and shortcut-only view measure how much identity signal is recoverable from background, or silhouette. This turns a retrieval score into an evidence profile: how well the model performs on the original images, how much of that performance remains when only the animal is visible, and how much identity signal remains recoverable when the animal is removed. We release around 0.5M masks for 34 datasets and code for mask generation and CFR evaluation.

[725] arXiv:2611.06866 [pdf, html, other]
Title: GH-AWTrace: A Large-Scale Dataset of GitHub Agentic Workflow Execution Logs
Jasem Khelifi, Hao Li, Ali Ouni, Mohammed Sayagh, Mohamed Aymen Saied
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Agentic workflows enable AI agents to perform recurring repository tasks on schedules or in response to repository events. Existing studies examine workflow definitions and outputs, but provide limited evidence of what happens during execution. We present GH-AWTrace, a dataset linking 25,014 verified GitHub Agentic Workflows across 5,051 repositories to 4,112,526 run records and 562,877 nonempty execution log archives. The dataset preserves execution evidence subject to GitHub's log-retention limits and links it to repository metadata and generated workflow configurations. Illustrative cases show how the logs expose tool denials, provider failures, changes in an agent's approach, and delegation among agents. These observations enable research on execution failures, tool use, and the relationship between reported run outcomes and visible task progress. Coverage varies across workflows, and the logs provide partial observations rather than complete agent trajectories. Video: this https URL

[726] arXiv:2611.06868 [pdf, html, other]
Title: On Turn-Level Best-of-N Sampling for Scaling LLM Agents
Jalaj Bhandari, Dhawal Gupta, Hongli Zhan, Zhenting Wang, Varad Pimpalkhute, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric Xing, Rupesh Srivastava
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

In this work, we evaluate a simple inference-time scaling approach based on \textit{turn-level best-of-N sampling} (\method) for large language model (LLM) agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. We instantiate this using a \textit{generator-selector} framework with two LLMs; at each turn, a \emph{generator} model generates $N$ candidate actions and a \emph{selector} model selects one of them, which is then executed in the environment. This paper is closely related to the work of \cite{zainullina2025guided} who used critic models for guided search at inference time. Different from their work, we evaluate if off-the-shelf, open-weight LLMs can be effective at comparing different candidate actions directly. Experiments on long-horizon terminal tasks show that \method can lead to significant performance improvements, both in terms of accuracy (5--10\%) and consistency across repeated attempts. Analysis of agent trajectories reveal a shift in agent behaviour towards desirable patterns such as reduction in number of attempts to solve the task, improved task instruction following, debugging and testing.

[727] arXiv:2611.06870 [pdf, html, other]
Title: PixelSpline: Continuous Space-Time Video Super-Resolution via Endpoint-Anchored Shared Pixel Trajectories
Wanqi Yuan, Nianyi Li
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Existing continuous space-time video super-resolution methods often infer motion from only two endpoint frames and model the two motion directions independently, making them vulnerable to ambiguous correspondence and inconsistent trajectories. We introduce a continuous STVSR framework that combines long-context encoding, continuous HR feature lifting, and an endpoint-anchored PixelSpline. Long-range observations provide more reliable endpoint representations, while continuous upsampling constructs detailed appearance features directly on the requested HR grid. PixelSpline explicitly models each pixel's motion as a single continuous trajectory shared by both endpoints. Using this trajectory, our method warps endpoint colors into a coarse intermediate frame and aligns the HR features for residual reconstruction. Experiments across spatial and temporal upsampling settings demonstrate that the proposed framework offers a favorable quality--efficiency trade-off.

[728] arXiv:2611.06874 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Learning to Decode Linear Codes with Generalized Belief Propagation Network
Samira Malek
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Error correcting codes are a fundamental component of communication systems, enabling reliable data transmission over noisy channels. Recently, neural decoders have demonstrated notable performance gains over classical iterative algorithms. In this paper, we propose a Generalized Belief Propagation Network (GBPNet) that preserves message-passing symmetry while enhancing the decoder's learning capability. The architecture uses cascaded variable-node updates and learned element-wise message scaling while retaining the Tanner graph structure. We also introduce two training strategies, progressive training and high-SNR training, that improve decoding accuracy. Experimental results on several linear codes show that GBPNet achieves lower bit error rates than conventional belief propagation and the evaluated state-of-the-art neural decoders.

[729] arXiv:2611.06876 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.

[730] arXiv:2611.06879 [pdf, other]
Title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
Benjamin Jacob Bodner
Comments: 29 pages, 8 figures, 19 tables. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; this https URL).

[731] arXiv:2611.06881 [pdf, html, other]
Title: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Uksang Yoo, Xinyue Zhu, Meadow Shen, Jaimyn Drake, Eugen Solowjow, Lionel Gulich, Alexander Millane, Rafael Cathomen, Tuur Stuyck, Sangeeta Subramanian, Yichao Pan, Bruce McGowan, Michael Benedict, Linxi Fan, Yuke Zhu, Spencer Huang, Ken Goldberg
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

[732] arXiv:2611.06888 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
Siyi Yu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); General Economics (econ.GN)

Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

[733] arXiv:2611.06890 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Procedural Adversarial Learning
Jack Nugent, Jia Deng
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

For many computer vision tasks, neural networks can be trained to produce a low average error, yet they still fail on seemingly simple scenes. Reducing these failures requires first finding them, but they may not be in a fixed dataset. We study procedural adversarial learning (PAL), a framework of minimax training and adversarial evaluation which searches the input space of a procedural generator for difficult instances. The procedural generator is an interpretable program mapping a low-dimensional vector of control parameters (e.g. layout, lighting, pose) to a rendered image and its label. We introduce the Simple-PAT algorithm, which uses zeroth-order optimization in the procedural generator's parameter space to propose adversarial training samples that are generated on demand. We also create PAL-Dojo, a collection of efficient procedural generators for surface normal estimation, image segmentation, and human pose estimation. Against a cross-model black-box adversary with 50M aggregate queries, Simple-PAT reduces worst-case error by a geometric mean of 3.15x compared to standard training and 2.63x compared to the strongest robust training baseline. Code is available at this https URL.

[734] arXiv:2611.06891 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Strict Separation at $1-1/e$
Hossein Esfandiari, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

The matroid prophet-secretary problem asks an online algorithm to select an independent set of elements whose nonnegative values are drawn independently and revealed in uniformly random order. Its combinatorial-auction counterpart asks the algorithm to allocate disjoint bundles to arriving buyers with independently drawn XOS valuation functions. In both problems the distributions are known, and the benchmark is the expected offline optimum. Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for both settings. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits.
For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements.
For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are independent and identically distributed, every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.

[735] arXiv:2611.06894 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Nonuniform Buy-at-Bulk Network Design: Improved Approximation and LP Integrality Gap
Iman Gholami, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

In nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design, we are given an undirected graph and $h$ terminal pairs with positive demands, and we must route every demand at minimum total cost when each network resource has two independent parameters: a fixed buying price paid once if the resource is used, and a per-unit rental cost (or physical length) paid proportionally to the traffic it carries. Unlike the uniform-cost or single-sink variants, the general multicommodity problem allows unrelated buying and rental metrics across arbitrary source--sink pairs, arbitrary demands, and both edge and node resources.
We give a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$-approximation algorithm for undirected nonuniform buy-at-bulk network design. The guarantee holds for edge costs, node costs, and their combination, and applies to arbitrary positive rational demands with no dependence on the number of vertices or the numerical demand ratio. This improves upon the $O(\log^4 h)$ bound of Chekuri, Hajiaghayi, Kortsarz, and Salavatipour (2010) for unrestricted instances. Our result also establishes the same $O(\log^2 h / (\log\log h)^2)$ upper bound on the integrality gap of the natural affine multicommodity flow LP, bounding integral buying and rental costs separately against their fractional counterparts and preserving zero rental budgets exactly.

[736] arXiv:2611.06896 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Online Edge-Weighted Matching Beyond 0.55
Alireza Farhadi, Mohammad Hajiaghayi
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

We give a $0.556195$-competitive randomized algorithm for edge-weighted online bipartite matching with free disposal, improving the $0.5368$ guarantee of Blanc and Charikar. The result holds for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights and any input sequence fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. Our algorithm builds on online correlated selection, introduced by Fahrbach, Huang, Tao, and Zadimoghaddam, and its multiway extension due to Blanc and Charikar.
Our main contribution is a state-dependent primal--dual analysis of correlated selection. At each weight threshold, we track the state of the selection process jointly with an auxiliary failure event. The analysis accounts for arrivals below the threshold, which change the state without improving the matching value at that threshold. A potential function bounds the dual increase in both cases. We instantiate the analysis with an explicit win map that assigns a common score to an initial range of states. Its selection inequalities are verified by a finite computer-assisted proof covering every required candidate multiplicity and every real threshold; the verifiers are available in an accompanying repository. Triangular unit-weight inputs asymptotically attain the guarantee of the underlying ideal algorithm, proving that its analysis is tight.

[737] arXiv:2611.06897 [pdf, html, other]
Title: MCP-Eco: A Linked Dataset of MCP Servers, Consumers, and Development Activity
Khalid Tounoussi, Mohammed Sayagh, Ali Ouni, Yutaro Kashiwa
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to access external tools and data. Studying its software ecosystem requires connecting server interfaces, the projects that configure these servers, and their development activity. However, this information is scattered across directories, package registries, configuration files, and repository histories. We present MCP-Eco, a relational dataset that integrates these sources and links consumer configuration declarations to candidate server projects. Its frozen release contains 16,880,899 records across 19 Parquet tables, covering 78,302 candidate server projects, 16,165 candidate consuming repositories, and 9,200 configuration declarations. Of these declarations, 5,975 resolve to 5,138 distinct repository-server pairs. The dataset also includes tool, resource, and prompt descriptions, declared dependencies, and associated development records, including pull requests, reviews, issues, and commits. Provenance fields distinguish directory-reported capabilities from those observed through live probing and document discovery sources and declaration-matching methods. These connections support research on MCP interface design, configuration practices, and repository maintenance, while enabling practitioners to inspect tool schemas and existing integration configurations. The dataset and accompanying analysis scripts are publicly available at this https URL Demo video: this https URL

[738] arXiv:2611.06899 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Occlusion for Free: Detecting Occlusion from the Disagreement Between Two Monocular Distance Cues
Chibueze Praise Onyenweaku, Toyibat Adele, Sikirulahi Opeyemi Abdulkareem, Obed Honour Eje
Comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 GlobalSouthAI Workshop
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.

[739] arXiv:2611.06900 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Human Mobility Sensing Using Wall-Reflected Beamformed Millimeter-Wave Communication Signals
Tony DiMichele, Raees Matheen Mullah, Christian Lopez Garcia, Zahra Najafi, Mohammed E. Eltayeb
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Existing millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication beam patterns spatially weight human-scattered signals and shape the received-power signatures induced by human motion. We exploit these beam-shaped signatures for device-free walkingpace and walk-direction classification using a wall-reflected 60.8-GHz link with closely spaced phased arrays and fixed communication beamforming vectors. Human movement alters the interference between wall-reflected and scattered signals, producing power oscillations surrounding a central blockage fade. A beam-dependent interference model provides a physical interpretation of these signatures. Using received-power statistics from a continuous-tone experiment, we extract fade duration for walking-pace classification and pre/post-fade asymmetries for walk-direction classification. Measurements comprise 144 crossings from three participants along perpendicular and diagonal trajectories. Under leave-one-participant-out validation, logistic regression achieves 86.1% binary and 79.2% three-class walking pace accuracy, and 77.1% travel-direction accuracy. The results demonstrate mobility sensing using fixed communication beams without channel estimation, Doppler processing, or dedicated radar hardware

[740] arXiv:2611.06901 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Motion-guided Contrastive Regularization For Latent World Models
Yiwen Chen, Qiqi Hou, Jisoo Jeong, Yinhao Zhu, Huaizu Jiang, Amir Said
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.

[741] arXiv:2611.06905 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement
Michal Korniak, Marco Bagatella, Ralf Römer, Michal Nauman, Yarden As, Pranav Vignesh, Manan Agarwal, Leander Diaz-Bone, Piotr Zalewski, Mikołaj Czarnecki, Lenart Treven, Shashwat Saxena, Sreyas Venkataraman, Sarvesh Patil, Zhiyuan Zhou, Daniel Marta, Oier Mees, Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah, Carmelo Sferrazza, Bhavya Sukhija, Angela P. Schoellig, Andreas Krause, Max Simchowitz, Andrew Wagenmaker
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)

The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models.

[742] arXiv:2611.06906 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Simple Subquadratic Cut Query Protocol for Directed Reachability
Henry Fleischmann, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Swagato Sanyal
Comments: 17 + 22 pages
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We study $s$--$t$ reachability in an unweighted directed graph on $n$ vertices, accessed through a directed cut oracle: given $S\subseteq V$, the oracle returns the number of edges directed from $S$ to $V\setminus S$. Directed cut functions are submodular, and reachability asks whether the minimum $s$--$t$ cut has positive value. This connects the problem to the query complexity of submodular function minimisation. Whether or not reachability can be solved in truly subquadratic query complexity has been an outstanding open question for a decade.
We give a simple algorithmic blueprint with two randomised implementations. The first uses $\widetilde O(n^{9/5})$ outgoing-cut queries; the second improves this bound to $\widetilde O(n^{5/3})$. The common idea is to construct an alternative orientation with the same underlying undirected graph and vertex-wise degree imbalances, thereby preserving reachability. We first approximate the target imbalances using an averaging and rounding procedure, then correct the remaining error with a flow.
An earlier manuscript, made available in August 2026 in an online AI repository, reports an $\widetilde O(n^{3/2})$ query bound. Our contribution is a simple and comprehensible alternative approach that already achieves a polynomial saving over quadratic query complexity.

[743] arXiv:2611.06908 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
Siyuan Hu, Abulikemu Abuduweili, Yue Meng, Shipeng Liu, Quentin Leboutet, Chen Chen, Matthias Müller, Vladlen Koltun
Comments: Code and videos at: this https URL
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See this https URL for code and videos.

[744] arXiv:2611.06910 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research
Bingran You, Wenjun Ke, Ria Rosenauer, Bo Liu, Wenbo Chen, Min Chen, Shuqi Xu, Yue Ma, Jiechao Feng, Bo Chen, Xiangkai Sun, Jiarui Liu, Jinen Guo, Zeyu Zhou, Xu Huang, Zhuohan Li, Haoyu Li, Heguang Lin, Lijie Ding, Yadong Zeng, Kangqi Zhang, Xinge Liu, Hanwen Liu, Zhenghong Li, Alexander von Recum, Yuchen Zhu, Felix Schwarzfischer, Yizhou Zhao, Jicheng Wang, Binxu Li, Qian Yu, Chan Li, Cheng Dai, Di Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Jiankai Sun, Kaituo Feng, Mian Qin, Ruihong Yin, Yiqun Luo, Weiwei Wu, Shihong Pan, Tsung Yeh Hsieh, Xiao Huang, Yan Zhang, Sihan Li, Zirui Ren, Zengji Tu, Kyoung Whan Choe, Ke Sun, Vincenzo Galia, Vaisakhi Mishra, Jiashu He, Hongyang Wang, Zhiheng Yang, Shubham Gaur, Yifan Gu, Shuyi Wang, Zihao Zuo, Steven Dillmann, Yiyou Sun, Xinyang Han, Hanchung Lee, Molei Tao, Yue Zhao, Shilong Liu, Yuchen Wu, Xuandong Zhao, Xiangyi Li, Florian Brand, Gerbrand Ceder, Hartmut Haeffner
Comments: 41 pages (10 pages main text), 19 figures, 11 tables
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

AI agents are playing an increasingly important role in physics research. However, existing physics benchmarks only evaluate fixed questions, isolated sub-tasks, or paper reproduction with given solutions, and rarely check research quality alongside correctness. We introduce FrontierPhysics, an end-to-end benchmark with 56 tasks made by 42 physicists based on their own research, covering nine domains across theoretical, computational, and experimental physics. Each task requires agents to review the literature, develop a research plan, conduct research and experiments, and produce structured outputs and scientific manuscripts. Combining deterministic verifiers with expert-authored rubrics, FrontierPhysics evaluates whether agents' research is correct and publishable. Across 22 models in 26 configurations, no configuration passes more than 46 of its 168 rollouts. Manual review of agent trajectories shows that frontier agents' main weaknesses are insufficiently rigorous reasoning and limited expert intuition, rather than gaps in physics knowledge or execution errors.

[745] arXiv:2611.06911 [pdf, html, other]
Title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
Fei Lin, Tengchao Zhang, Ziyang Gong, Xiaotong Yu, Bohan Zhang, Yifan Zhou, Qihao Yang, Ji Dai, Dong Li, Yining Jiang, Qinghua Ni, Jun Huang, Qiang Zhang, Yue Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Yonglin Tian, Fei-Yue Wang, Xue Yang
Comments: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets, Spotlight)
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs.

[746] arXiv:2611.06913 [pdf, html, other]
Title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
Balakumar Sundaralingam, Adithyavairavan Murali, Stan Birchfield
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

We present cuRoboV2-Fast, a GPU-accelerated planner that reduces both planning latency and execution time for collision-free, payload-aware, torque-limited motions. B-spline trajectory optimization reduces the required iterations, while accelerated robot computations and differentiable inverse dynamics reduce refinement cost and accommodate changing payloads. TimeOpt optimizes traversal speed along the fixed path under sampled velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque constraints, exploiting local spline support to solve banded Newton systems efficiently on the GPU. With a 3,kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast achieves 4.4 ms mean planning time on RTX 5090, 14.7x faster than cuRoboV2. Our method on Jetson AGX Orin plans faster than cuRoboV1 + TOPPRA on RTX 5090. A stereo-camera-based deployment on YAM achieves 5.93 s mean completed pick-and-drop cycles, 34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2. Code (Apache 2.0): this http URL , Project Page: this http URL .

[747] arXiv:2611.06914 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Framework for Context Enrichment and Selective Robustness in LLM Social Agents
Mattia Greiche, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maximilian Puelma Touzel
Comments: Accepted to the SocialAgent Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026. 12 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Researchers use large language models as agents in social simulations, where agents are prompted with observations and background information intended to shape their actions. Yet LLM agents have been shown to substantially change their behavior under meaning-preserving prompt variations, creating a validation problem for social simulation. One plausible hypothesis is that this brittleness reflects a lack of grounding and can be reduced by enriching the context provided to the agents. Whether richer context improves robustness remains unclear, in part because context richness and robustness are rarely defined in ways that support controlled comparisons. We address the first need with controlled context enrichment, a set of prompt substitution rules that systematically enriches distinct types of context: neutral padding, generic social background, descriptive decision grounding, and normative decision grounding. We address the second by introducing selective robustness as a validation criterion: insensitivity to meaning-preserving prompt variation combined with a directional response to decision-relevant changes in the social world. We demonstrate the framework in a Prisoner's Dilemma-like game, showing how it can be used to identify which forms of context enrichment produce more desirable and robust agent behavior. We find that these forms of enrichment produce distinct behavioral patterns that vary between the two models tested.

[748] arXiv:2611.06918 [pdf, html, other]
Title: From Pixels to Actions - Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies
Weichen Fan, Haiwen Diao, Penghao Wu, Siyuan Hu, Ziqi Huang, Tianqi Liu, Mingze Sun, Ziyi Wang, Zhongang Cai, Hanming Deng, Quan Wang, Lei Yang, Lewei Lu, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Dahua Lin, Ziwei Liu
Comments: Code link: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

Cross submissions (showing 70 of 70 entries)

[749] arXiv:2611.02216 (cross-list from q-bio.NC) [pdf, other]
Title: Do agents need to sleep?
Ido Haber, Giulio Tononi
Subjects: Neurons and Cognition (q-bio.NC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

[750] arXiv:2611.05398 (cross-list from q-bio.QM) [pdf, html, other]
Title: AgentCount: An Agentic Workflow for Traceable Colony Counting and Insight Generation from Agar Plate Images
Zhuosheng Liu, Austin E. Weber
Subjects: Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Colony counting is commonly used to evaluate microbial populations in food safety testing and microbiological studies. Despite its wide application, manual counting is time-consuming and operator-dependent, and the final count often lacks a record of the objects included in the measurement. To address these limitations, this study presents AgentCount, an open-source agentic workflow for colony counting and result interpretation from agar plate images. Plate photographs and plating metadata are processed through seven agents for image quality control, plate localisation, colony detection, counting, CFU calculation, validation, and reporting. Colony detection is performed using Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) with multiple text prompts and morphology-based filtering. After that, replicate statistics are calculated and a large language model (LLM)-based agent is used to generate a results narrative. Intermediate outputs, including quality scores, segmentation masks, detections, and warnings, are retained to support review of the reported values. The workflow also extends to skill-guided analysis of archived microbial population data. In a retrospective comparison with two previously published studies, we benchmarked 241 published endpoints, including all 216 mean +- SD values of the meat-analogue pathogen tables; on the 168 endpoints with a complete n=6 replicate source, 164 (97.6%) agreed within 0.01 log10 units. Overall, AgentCount demonstrates the promising potential of agentic workflows for applications in applied microbiology.

[751] arXiv:2611.05401 (cross-list from q-bio.GN) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Training-Free Socket for DNA in Frozen Language Models
Arash Fatehi
Subjects: Genomics (q-bio.GN); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Connecting a DNA foundation model to a large language model (LLM) usually requires training a connector, and often the LLM too. We show that a closed-form map is enough for gene-level questions. Our method, the socket, fits one ridge regression (the plug) from frozen Evo 2 features to the host LLM's own representation of the gene's symbol, name, and description at an early layer. The plug's output replaces the hidden state at placeholder positions, and no gradient passes through the host.
We test it on GeneHop, a five-way multiple-choice benchmark split by homology. In a single run on the held-out test set, under a frozen analysis plan, real DNA beats shuffled DNA on all four hosts: by +22.2 points [19.8, 25.0] on Qwen3.5-4B, +26.1 [24.3, 27.9] on Qwen3.6-27B, +16.7 [14.2, 19.7] on Mistral-7B, and +18.4 [16.2, 21.0] on OLMo-2-7B. All four survive Holm correction, every null control stays within two points of the sham level, and the development results agree within 2.3 points.
A layer rule that uses no task items was selected on three hosts; it predicted the working layer of the fourth before any DNA-plug scoring on it. A text-only linear map lets one plug feed any other host, at a cost of at most 0.9 points on test. The socket conveys gene identity: nearest-neighbour retrieval recovers 72-84% of the effect, but the plug beats it on every host by 3.0-5.2 points and keeps most of its effect without training homologs.

[752] arXiv:2611.05405 (cross-list from q-bio.GN) [pdf, html, other]
Title: VenusGenome: Genome-Aware Masked Autoencoding for Microbial Genome Representation Learning
Zhang Liang, Zhang Yukun, Tan Yang, Jiang Fan, Zhong Bozitao, Cheng Xiaoran, Hong Liang, Li Mingchen, Yu Yuanxi
Subjects: Genomics (q-bio.GN); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Genomic-context models have shown that contextualizing protein embeddings can improve predictions of microbial function. We observe that a gene's protein embedding is partially predictable from the embeddings of neighboring genes in the genome, motivating high-ratio masking that requires reconstruction from sparser genomic context. Genomic modeling must also distinguish biological relationships from assembly conventions, since the ordering of separate contigs does not imply adjacency and strand labels depend on the reference orientation. We therefore introduce VenusGenome, a gene-resolution masked autoencoder that combines visible-only encoding with genome-aware attention incorporating contig boundaries, relative strand orientations, and gene positions. We pretrain this model on a curated corpus of over 1.7 million microbial genome assemblies from isolate and metagenomic sources, using frozen protein embeddings as gene-level inputs. Across genome-level phenotype prediction and gene-level tasks, the resulting frozen representations achieve the highest mean performance among the evaluated models on nine of eleven primary metrics. An exploratory gene-input perturbation analysis further links representation sensitivity to experimentally measured fitness defects. Ablations support the contribution of genome-aware attention and show the benefits of masked autoencoding over BERT-style masked modeling, with further gains from higher masking ratios.

[753] arXiv:2611.05418 (cross-list from q-bio.GN) [pdf, html, other]
Title: BIOTRAM: Biochemistry-informed Transformer for Relative Abundance via Metabarcoding
Emma Boehly, Scott C. Lowe, Ken A. Thompson, Anthony Fuller, Will Armstrong, Iuliia Zarubiieva, Neelu Madan, Tiancheng Gao, Sameer Padhye, Jayme Sones, Kate H. J. Perez, Bess Hardwick, Brendan Furneaux, Evgeny V. Zakharov, Dirk Steinke, Jeremy R. deWaard, Stephanie L. deWaard, Jaclyn McKeown, Norman Monkhouse, Cole Pace, Sujeevan Ratnasingham, Raina Schmuck, Amy Thompson, Jorge L. León-Cortés, Luciano Cagnolo, Julieta Soledad Arena, Jeremías Domínguez Masciale, Errol Douwes, Elli Groner, Masae Iwamoto Ishihara, Shunsuke Matsuoka, Mailyn A. Gonzalez, Alexandre Antonelli, Renata S. Sousa-Lima, Armin Niessner, Patrícia Guedes, Elizabeth G. Biro, Zuania Colón-Piñeiro, Dezene P. W. Huber, Santosh Mazumdar, Magda Bou Dagher Kharrat, Eddie P. Mondejar, Pablo Luis Tubaro, Eugene Marais, Marie-Eugénie Maggia, Darío Alejandro Lijtmaer, Sean W. J. Prosser, Andrea Murillo-Vázquez, Paola Pulido-Santacruz, Paula Leitman, Thiago Arnt Dorigo, Nao Ito, Paul Knoops, Maria L. Kuzmina, Hikaru Morishita, Keishi Kimoto, Dimby Raharinjanahary, Rhian J. Smith, Solny A. Adalsteinsson, Kevin G. Borja-Acosta, Paul Amouroux, Angela M. Mendoza-Henao, Angélica Diaz-Pulido, Anamaria Dal Molin, Luke L. Powell, Diego Inclan, Alice Calvente, David Dunson, Brian Fisher, Tomas Roslin, Otso Ovaskainen, Paul D. N. Hebert, Graham W. Taylor
Subjects: Genomics (q-bio.GN); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Arthropod monitoring at scale begins with metabarcoding of bulk samples: trap collections of hundreds to thousands of specimens processed as one unit, extraction of DNA from the bulked specimens, then sequencing of the DNA from all specimens together. Metabarcoding reveals which taxa such a sample contains, but due to factors such as differing DNA amplification rates and body sizes, its read counts do not neatly correspond to how abundant the different taxa are relative to one another. This lack of relative abundance limits the data's utility for the multitude of ecological analyses that depend on it. We propose BIOTRAM: a neural network that estimates per-taxon specimen counts by dividing the observed read counts by a learned read yield per specimen, which it factors into the DNA each specimen contributes and how efficiently that DNA is amplified.
