Our main result is a simple exact sampling algorithm for $\pi_{n,\lambda}$ with expected running time $O\big((\min\{n,n\sqrt{\lambda}\}+1)\log n\big)$, which is optimal up to the logarithmic factor.

[984] arXiv:2605.22286 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: EmoTrack: Clinical-Semantic Modeling for Text-Based Depression Severity Estimation
Zhaomin Wu, Jiayi Li, Bingsheng He
Comments: 36 pages. Related LongCounsel-8 benchmark: arXiv:2609.03507
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Text-based counseling is widely adopted across online mental health platforms, where automatically estimating depressive symptom severity from transcripts is vital for client safety and clinical monitoring. We therefore study prediction of the standard eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) total score directly from counseling sessions. Existing clinical-based methods obtain structured assessments through large language model inference but summarize away individual client turns. Training-based methods preserve turn semantics but must learn clinical structure from limited labels. Integrating these representations requires preserving clinical-feature identity and selecting evidence relevant to each symptom. We propose EmoTrack, which jointly encodes clinical-feature tokens and frozen client-turn embeddings, then uses PHQ-8 item queries to estimate total severity. Optional gated memory incorporates evidence from the preceding session. To support controlled evaluation in the multi-session setting, we introduce CounselArc, a synthetic counseling dataset with session-level PHQ-8 supervision for predicting current-session severity with optional prior-session context. Across real DAIC-WOZ interviews, transfer to E-DAIC, and three longitudinal datasets, EmoTrack achieves the lowest normalized aggregate error. It reduces DAIC-WOZ mean absolute error by 12.5% and aggregate error by approximately 8.6%, each relative to the strongest baseline for that measure.

[985] arXiv:2605.23135 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Impact of AI Coding Assistants on Software Engineering: A Longitudinal Study
Annie Vella, Kelly Blincoe
Comments: Revised version. Accepted for publication in the ACM Transaction on Software Engineering and Methodology
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

AI coding assistants have become prolific in recent years. Through a longitudinal mixed-methods investigation, we examined how professional software engineers perceive the effects of AI coding assistants in regard to task focus, developer experience, and productivity. Two questionnaires were administered six months apart, yielding 158 eligible participants at the first time point, 101 at the second, and a matched longitudinal cohort of 95. Participants reported spending less time on most development tasks, with 82% reporting less on writing code. We found a broader shift in focus from creation to verification activities. We propose a new category of work we term supervisory engineering work, encompassing the direction, evaluation, and correction of AI output. This construct is broader than the extra review overhead that has been previously reported in literature since it encompasses directing and shaping AI output both before and during creation. We also identified a productivity-experience paradox: consistently positive productivity perceptions alongside eroding developer experience. These findings suggest that AI coding assistants may be reshaping both the nature of software engineering work and how engineers experience it.

[986] arXiv:2605.23262 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Designing Benchmarks for Knowledge Work
Yining Hua, Hongbin Na, Cyrus Ayubcha, Levi Lian
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Agent benchmarks have attracted substantial attention; yet, benchmarks for AI agents performing knowledge work are still mostly described only by their tasks, environments, and metrics. Starting from the definition of knowledge work, this paper derives four other design choices that often remain implicit. Three research threads on how knowledge work is organized each yield one choice: studies of professions, situated action, and boundary objects and coordination, while validity theory provides the fourth. Following this reasoning, we propose a benchmark representation centered on the work being performed. Based on this representation, we propose reporting practices for four largely missing fields: represented activity, tested setting, required work product, and evaluated result. Benchmarks designed in disparate ways thereby share a common description and can be compared side by side. To support the reporting of work activities, we cluster O*NET task statements into 18 shared work activities through unsupervised learning paired with human review. We then use this representation to analyze cases from three popular knowledge work benchmarks: GDPval, OfficeQA Pro, and APEX-SWE. Across all three benchmarks, the scope covered by the evaluated result is narrower than that of the required work product. We audited the tests of all 25 public APEX-SWE Integration tasks, independently coded by two authors. We found from the test code that in 13 of these tasks, a deliverable can alter established content from the source data and still pass all tests. We synthesize these four fields into a one-page record, accompanied by a worked example and a fillable template.

[987] arXiv:2605.24183 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: AvalancheBench: Evaluating Enterprise Agent-Driven Semantic Query Processing Through Latent World Recovery
Darek Kleczek, Fuheng Zhao, Alexander W. Lee, Julien Tissier, Pawel Liskowski, Ugur Cetintemel, Anupam Datta
Subjects: Databases (cs.DB); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

As LLMs improve, data agents are emerging as a new interface for analytics, while semantic query processing engines use LLMs to operate over structured and unstructured data. Existing benchmarks largely evaluate agents and semantic query engines in isolation, leaving it unclear whether agents can decide when and how to use semantic operators in end-to-end analysis.
We introduce AvalancheBench, a multimodal enterprise analytics benchmark that generates observed data from latent world specifications and evaluates data agents on their ability to recover that world. The benchmark's 3 validated tasks contain 58 questions spanning text, images, and documents. Questions are provided together as a multi-part analytical brief and may share intermediate results, exposing the avalanche effect: errors can propagate through legitimate dependencies, and inappropriate reuse can cause otherwise unrelated questions to fail. AvalancheBench measures analytical fidelity, monetary cost, and capability-adjusted token cost (CATC), a new metric that weights token use by model capability to separate technical efficiency from provider pricing.
We evaluate 5 model-harness configurations across 3 agent harnesses using Snowflake Cortex AISQL as the engine, with the best configuration reaching macro analytical fidelity of 0.82. Agents fail primarily in constructing the analysis: failing to recover facts that require semantic computation costs 45.1% of lost points, yet incorrect operator outputs account for only 2.5%, versus 36.3% from agents misusing or avoiding semantic operators. Misinterpreting requirements costs the most, at 51.5%. Errors also spread between questions: 29% of lost points come from reusing another question's results. Finally, monetary cost and CATC produce different Pareto frontiers, distinguishing economically attractive configurations from those that are technically resource efficient.

[988] arXiv:2605.24301 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: AcroRL: Learning Aggressive Quadrotor Inversion using Bidirectional Thrust
Gabriel Rodriguez, Henri Sayag, Abhishek Rathod, John Stecklein, Siddharth Saha, Christopher Barngrover, Wennie Tabib
Comments: 17 pages, 8 figures, Accepted to the 10th Annual Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Bidirectional thrust grants quadrotors a second equilibrium condition and increased control authority, expanding the envelope of possible aggressive maneuvers and enabling inverted flight, perching, and sensing. Prior geometric control approaches extend differential flatness through Hopf fibration-based attitude representations to support bidirectional thrust, but struggle with actuator saturation and motor reversal delay during inversions, requiring heuristic thrust posture scheduling and waypoint tuning. We propose a learning-based framework that modulates a constant reference trajectory to perform compact, position-constrained quadrotor inversions while remaining compatible with traditional trajectory generation and tracking across flight regimes. Separate policies are trained via reinforcement learning for nominal-to-inverted and inverted-to-nominal transitions. In JAX-based simulation, the proposed method achieves the lowest position deviation and settling time across all evaluated baselines, reducing position root mean square error (RMSE) by 32% and settling time by 57% relative to the strongest optimization-based baseline. Hardware experiments demonstrate successful inversion across multiple yaw configurations with position RMSE below 0.35m, and compatibility with downstream trajectory generation and control through circular flight in both regimes. Additionally, we provide an open-source implementation of the proposed framework.

[989] arXiv:2605.26647 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: More Expressive Feedforward Layers: Part I. Token-Adaptive Mixing of Activations
Mingze Wang, Jinbo Wang, Yikuan Xia, Kai Shen, Shu Zhong
Comments: 31 pages, accepted by NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Feedforward network (FFN) layers account for a large fraction of parameters and nonlinear expressivity in Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Despite the evolution from ReLU and GELU to gated variants such as SwiGLU, most FFN designs still use a single fixed activation function, applying the same nonlinear transformation to all tokens. In this work, we propose Mixture of Activations (MoA), a token-adaptive FFN design that mixes a dictionary of activation functions using lightweight input-dependent gates while sharing the same linear projections. As an input-independent counterpart, we also introduce learnable activations (LA), which form linear combinations of activation functions for both ReLU-type and SwiGLU-type FFNs. Theoretically, we establish strict finite-width expressive separations among fixed-activation FFNs, LA, and MoA: LA strictly contains fixed-activation FFNs, while MoA strictly contains LA, with the additional expressivity arising from input-dependent nonlinear hybridization. Empirically, we evaluate MoA through extensive pre-training experiments on dense and MoE language models ranging from 0.12B to 2B parameters under different token budgets, optimizers, and learning rate schedules. MoA consistently achieves lower terminal loss and exhibits more favorable scaling behavior than well-tuned baselines, with minimal parameter and computational overhead. These results suggest that token-adaptive activation mixing is a simple and effective mechanism for improving FFN expressivity in LLMs.

[990] arXiv:2605.26969 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Recon: Reconstruction-Guided Reasoning Synthesis for User Modeling
Alan Zhu, Mihran Miroyan, Carolyn Wang, Andrew Zhou, Lisa Dunlap, Narges Norouzi, Joseph E. Gonzalez
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

User modeling aims to use language models (LMs) to mimic an individual's behavior from a corpus of past context-action pairs (e.g., conversation turns), enabling the simulation of users in settings like behavioral science, human-AI collaboration, and market research. Recent approaches augment these corpora with synthesized reasoning traces, typically generated by conditioning on both context and action. However, action-conditioned traces are post-hoc rationalizations and need not reflect the user's underlying decision process. We propose Recon, which uses action reconstruction to score reasoning traces by their predictive power: given a context and candidate reasoning, a reconstruction model predicts the action, and reconstruction fidelity determines reasoning quality. Across four domains, Recon achieves a 54.7% win rate over Backward Synthesis, a standard post-hoc rationalization baseline. Further, we find that training a reasoning synthesis model with rewards derived from Recon improves downstream user modeling performance, achieving a win rate of up to 70.0% over baselines. We further show that Recon-synthesized reasoning transfers across models, and improves user modeling beyond the reconstruction model. Our work demonstrates that post-hoc rationalization is insufficient for reasoning synthesis, and that useful and interpretable reasoning should naturally elicit the action from the context.

[991] arXiv:2605.29300 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: MusTBench: Benchmarking and Advancing Temporal Grounding in Music LLMs
Daeyong Kwon, Qiyu Wu, Shinobu Kuriya, Junghyun Koo, Shuyang Cui, Zhi Zhong, Wei-Hsiang Liao, Hiromi Wakaki, Yuki Mitsufuji
Comments: Project page: this https URL | Github: this https URL
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Sound (cs.SD)

Recent Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have demonstrated promising abilities in understanding musical content. However, whether their responses are grounded in the correct temporal regions of the audio remains underexplored. This limitation is particularly critical for music understanding, where key information often occurs as temporally localized events, such as instrument entries and rhythmic transitions. To address this gap, we introduce MusTBench, a reliable benchmark with stem-wise data and music-expert validation designed to evaluate temporal grounding in LALMs through five temporally grounded question-answering tasks. To further improve temporal grounding in existing models, we propose MusT, a novel four-stage temporal optimization recipe spanning music encoder adaptation, LLM adaptation, LLM supervised fine-tuning, and RL-based optimization. Experiments on MusTBench show that existing LALMs face challenges in precise temporal grounding, while MusT consistently improves performance across different LALM backbones and scales. These results highlight temporal grounding as an important challenge in current LALMs and provide a benchmark and training recipe that may support future research on temporally grounded music understanding.

[992] arXiv:2605.30202 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Dual-Path Architecture for Scaling Compute and Capacity in LLMs
Markus Frey, Behzad Shomali, Joachim Koehler, Mehdi Ali
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Looped transformers apply a shared block multiple times and have emerged as a parameter-efficient route to scaling compute in language models. However, at fixed FLOPs a looped model has strictly less capacity than a baseline transformer. We argue that compute, the number of sequential operations applied to a hidden state, and capacity, the parameters available at a single step, are distinct scaling axes that standard transformer layers conflate. We propose a dual-path block that exposes both axes as parallel pathways within a single layer: a deep sublayer re-applied $K$ times with shared parameters, and a wide sublayer with an enlarged feed-forward network applied once, combined by independent per-token gates. At two FLOP budgets, the best dual-path configuration surpasses both iso-FLOP single-axis controls on aggregate language modelling, commonsense, and math metrics, while using 17-33% fewer parameters than the width-scaled baseline. The learned gates are directly interpretable and show systematic per-token allocation: function words and lexical content trend wide, while punctuation, symbols, and arithmetic tokens trend deep. Our results suggest that compute and capacity can be scaled separately, with the model balancing the two token by token.

[993] arXiv:2605.30749 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: FLAG: Flow Policy MaxEnt-RL by Latent Augmented Guidance
Sungha Kim, Gawon Lee, Jusuk Lee, Jonghae Park, H. Jin Kim, Daesol Cho
Comments: NeurIPS 2026, Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)

Maximum entropy reinforcement learning (MaxEnt-RL) enables robust exploration, yet practical implementations often restrict policies to simple Gaussians. While recent approaches incorporate expressive generative policies via importance-weighted supervised learning, they are prone to importance weight collapse, which limits their scalability in high-dimensional action spaces. Our key insight is to mitigate this limitation by localizing the sampling region, avoiding the weight degeneracy induced by importance sampling over the entire action space. To instantiate this insight, we introduce \textbf{FLAG} (\textbf{F}low policy with \textbf{L}atent-\textbf{A}ugmented \textbf{G}uidance). FLAG augments the state space with a flow latent variable and optimizes a provably consistent proxy MaxEnt-RL objective. We empirically demonstrate that FLAG enables expressive policy optimization with limited importance samples and scales to state-based high-dimensional control tasks. Furthermore, FLAG achieves state-of-the-art performance among expressive-policy MaxEnt online RL methods on state-based high-dimensional control benchmarks.

[994] arXiv:2605.31489 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Context-Conditioned Generative Models Enable Subnational Refinement of Sparse Humanitarian Surveys
